A company has hundreds of 1,000 GiB gp2 Amazon EBS volumes. Each volume delivers its baseline of 3,000 IOPS, which the workloads need. The company must reduce storage costs without downtime and without reducing performance.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Change each volume to gp3 in place by using Elastic Volumes.
options.rationale: gp3 costs about 20% less per GiB than gp2 and includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size. Elastic Volumes changes the volume type while the volume stays attached and in use, so there is no downtime. If you set no performance values, EBS matches the higher of the source gp2 performance and the gp3 baseline.

options.text: Create snapshots. Restore each one as a new sc1 volume.
options.rationale: sc1 is cold HDD storage with low throughput, and it is not designed for random IOPS, so performance would drop sharply.

options.text: Change each volume to io2 in place by using Elastic Volumes.
options.rationale: io2 provides provisioned IOPS and high durability, but it costs more than gp2 for this workload.

options.text: Stop each instance, and attach a new st1 volume as the root.
options.rationale: st1 cannot be used as a boot volume, and HDD volumes do not suit random I/O.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company runs a database on an m5.xlarge Amazon EC2 instance with a gp3 Amazon EBS volume that is provisioned for 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s. Under heavy load, throughput levels off far below 1,000 MiB/s, and the VolumeQueueLength metric is high. The volume's metrics show that it is well below its provisioned limits.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to improve throughput?

options.text: Move the database to an instance type with higher EBS bandwidth.
options.rationale: Each instance type has a maximum EBS bandwidth and IOPS. When the instance limit is lower than the volume's provisioned performance, the instance becomes the bottleneck and I/O queues up. A larger or EBS-optimized instance type with more EBS bandwidth raises that ceiling.

options.text: Increase the provisioned IOPS on the gp3 volume to 80,000.
options.rationale: The volume is already below its provisioned limits, so more IOPS would not help. The instance cannot drive the volume any harder.

options.text: Configure fast snapshot restore for the volume's snapshots.
options.rationale: Fast snapshot restore removes first-read latency on volumes created from snapshots. It does not raise ongoing throughput.

options.text: Change the volume type from gp3 to st1 for higher throughput.
options.rationale: st1 is an HDD volume for large sequential reads. It has higher latency and fewer IOPS, which does not suit a database.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company runs a critical database on a Nitro-based Amazon EC2 instance with a gp3 Amazon EBS volume. The database needs a sustained 150,000 IOPS on a single volume. The volume must have 99.999% durability. The company cannot accept downtime for the change.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Change the volume type to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) by using Elastic Volumes.
options.rationale: io2 Block Express provides up to 256,000 IOPS on Nitro-based instances and is designed for 99.999% durability. Elastic Volumes can change the volume type without detaching the volume or restarting the instance.

options.text: Increase the provisioned IOPS of the gp3 volume to 150,000 by using Elastic Volumes.
options.rationale: gp3 supports up to 80,000 IOPS and is designed for 99.8% to 99.9% durability, so it meets neither requirement.

options.text: Change the volume type to Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) by using Elastic Volumes.
options.rationale: st1 is a hard disk volume for sequential throughput. It cannot deliver this level of random IOPS.

options.text: Move the database to instance store volumes. Take a nightly backup to Amazon S3.
options.rationale: Instance store data does not survive stopping or terminating the instance, so it does not meet the durability requirement. A nightly backup also allows up to a day of data loss.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
During a disaster recovery test, a company creates a large Amazon EBS volume from a snapshot for a database. The database is slow for several hours because each block loads from the snapshot the first time that it is read. New volumes must deliver full performance as soon as they are created.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Configure fast snapshot restore for the snapshot in the Availability Zone of the new volume.
options.rationale: Volumes created from a snapshot load blocks from Amazon S3 on first access, so early reads are slow. With fast snapshot restore enabled for a snapshot in an Availability Zone, new volumes there deliver their full performance when they are created. It is billed while it is on, so disable it when it is not needed. A provisioned rate for volume initialization is a related option when you only need a predictable initialization time.

options.text: Create the new volume as io2 with more provisioned IOPS than the original volume had.
options.rationale: Provisioned IOPS do not change how blocks are fetched from the snapshot, so first reads would still be slow, and io2 adds cost.

options.text: Copy the snapshot to another AWS Region. Create the new volume from that copy instead.
options.rationale: A snapshot copy is stored the same way, so a volume created from it has the same first-read delay.

options.text: Take a new snapshot of the slow volume, and create a second volume from that new snapshot.
options.rationale: A volume created from the new snapshot also loads its blocks on first read, so the delay remains.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company runs a log analytics job that reads 2 TiB of data sequentially from an Amazon EBS volume every night. Throughput is important for the job, but low latency is not. The data is currently stored on a gp3 volume, and the company needs to reduce storage cost.

Which EBS volume type will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
options.rationale: st1 is a low-cost HDD volume designed for frequently accessed, throughput-intensive sequential workloads such as log processing. It costs much less per GiB than SSD volumes and suits a nightly sequential scan.

options.text: Cold HDD (sc1)
options.rationale: sc1 is the lowest-cost volume type, but it is meant for data that is accessed infrequently and has much lower throughput. A nightly 2 TiB scan would take far longer.

options.text: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)
options.rationale: io2 is for latency-sensitive workloads that need high IOPS and durability. It is the most expensive option, and its strengths are not needed here.

options.text: General Purpose SSD (gp2)
options.rationale: gp2 is an SSD volume that costs more per GiB than gp3, so it would increase cost.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A media company uploads video files of 20 GB to 80 GB from its data center to an Amazon S3 bucket. Uploads often fail partway through and restart from the beginning. The S3 bill also shows storage charges that are larger than the total size of the completed objects.

Which combination of steps will resolve these issues? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use multipart uploads to retry failed parts without restarting the whole file.
options.rationale: Multipart upload splits a file into parts that are uploaded independently and in parallel. If a part fails, only that part is retried. Objects larger than 5 GB must use multipart upload, and AWS recommends it for objects larger than 100 MB.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after a few days.
options.rationale: Parts from uploads that never complete are stored and billed until the upload is completed or aborted. A lifecycle rule with the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action deletes those leftover parts automatically.

options.text: Upload each file with a single PUT request to store it as one complete object.
options.rationale: A single PUT request can upload at most 5 GB, so it cannot handle these files, and any failure would still restart the whole upload.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning to keep failed uploads as earlier versions of each object.
options.rationale: Versioning applies to completed objects. It does not keep or resume failed uploads, and it can add storage cost.

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock to prevent partial uploads from being deleted by mistake.
options.rationale: Object Lock prevents the deletion of object versions. It would not help uploads finish and could make extra storage permanent.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company has users in Asia, Europe, and South America who upload large files from a browser to a single Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1. Uploads from distant locations are slow. The company must speed up uploads without changing the bucket's AWS Region or managing servers.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket. Use the accelerate endpoint for uploads.
options.rationale: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads to the nearest CloudFront edge location and then across the AWS backbone network to the bucket. It speeds up long-distance transfers to a single bucket, and clients only change the endpoint that they use.

options.text: Create a bucket on each continent. Use S3 Replication to copy files to the bucket in us-east-1.
options.rationale: This adds buckets and replication to manage, and files would reach us-east-1 later than with a direct accelerated upload.

options.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the bucket.
options.rationale: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between storage tiers to save cost. It does not speed up uploads.

options.text: Use AWS DataSync agents on each continent to copy the files from the users' browsers to the bucket.
options.rationale: DataSync agents run on hosts that you manage and copy data from storage systems. They cannot receive uploads from users' browsers.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company must copy 50 TB of files from an on-premises NFS server to Amazon EFS over an existing AWS Direct Connect connection. The copy must verify data integrity. After the first copy, only changed files must be copied each night until cutover.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent on premises. Create a task that runs on a nightly schedule.
options.rationale: DataSync copies data between NFS shares and EFS, verifies integrity, and copies only changed files on each run. Tasks run on a schedule and can use a bandwidth limit, so no custom scripts are needed.

options.text: Mount the EFS file system on an on-premises server, and run rsync from a cron job each night.
options.rationale: rsync can work, but scripting, monitoring, and retrying it is manual effort, and it lacks managed scheduling and integrity reporting.

options.text: Order an AWS Snowball Edge device for the first copy, and use the AWS CLI for the nightly changes.
options.rationale: The company already has Direct Connect, so shipping a device adds time, and the AWS CLI cannot sync NFS changes into EFS.

options.text: Use an Amazon S3 File Gateway to copy the files to Amazon S3. Copy them from S3 to Amazon EFS.
options.rationale: Copying through S3 adds an extra hop and an extra copy step, and it does not preserve POSIX metadata the same way.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company has an analytics application that writes 15,000 objects per second to an Amazon S3 bucket. Every object is written under the same prefix, logs/. The application receives many HTTP 503 Slow Down errors.

Which solution will MOST effectively reduce the errors?

options.text: Spread the objects across multiple prefixes, such as logs/shard-01/ through logs/shard-10/.
options.rationale: Amazon S3 supports at least 3,500 write requests per second for each partitioned prefix and scales by adding partitions. 15,000 writes per second to one prefix exceeds that, so spreading the writes across several prefixes lets S3 scale. Retrying with exponential backoff also helps while S3 scales.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to send the writes through edge locations.
options.rationale: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers. It does not raise the request rate for a prefix.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning to store more versions of each object at the same time.
options.rationale: Versioning keeps multiple versions of objects. It does not increase request throughput, and it adds storage.

options.text: Keep the single prefix. Use longer object names to spread the keys more evenly.
options.rationale: Request capacity scales with prefixes, not with how long the object names are. One prefix still has the same request rate.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company stores 400 TB of user-generated content in Amazon S3 Standard. Some objects are read heavily for months and others are never read again, and the pattern cannot be predicted. Reads must stay in milliseconds. The company must reduce storage costs without building analysis jobs.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Move the objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering by using a lifecycle rule.
options.rationale: Intelligent-Tiering moves each object between access tiers based on its own access pattern and moves it back when it is read again. The automatic tiers keep millisecond reads, and there are no retrieval fees, which suits unpredictable access. A small monthly monitoring fee applies for each object.

options.text: Move all objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days with a lifecycle rule.
options.rationale: Deep Archive retrieval takes hours, which fails the millisecond requirement, and objects that are still read heavily would incur retrieval costs.

options.text: Move all objects to S3 One Zone-IA after 30 days with a lifecycle rule.
options.rationale: One Zone-IA keeps data in one Availability Zone and charges for retrievals. Objects that are read heavily would cost more, and resilience would be lower.

options.text: Use S3 Storage Lens to find cold prefixes. Move them to S3 Standard-IA manually each month.
options.rationale: This is manual analysis and movement, which the company wants to avoid, and Standard-IA charges retrieval fees for objects that become popular again.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company is migrating a Windows-based line-of-business application to Amazon EC2. The application needs a shared file system that supports the SMB protocol, uses Microsoft Active Directory for permissions, and supports DFS namespaces.

Which storage service should a CloudOps engineer choose to meet these requirements?

options.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
options.rationale: FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed Windows file shares over SMB. It joins Microsoft Active Directory, uses Windows ACLs, and supports DFS namespaces and shadow copies.

options.text: Amazon EFS with Max I/O performance mode
options.rationale: EFS is an NFS file system for Linux workloads. It does not support SMB or Windows permissions that come from Active Directory.

options.text: Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to an Amazon S3 bucket
options.rationale: FSx for Lustre is a high-performance file system for compute-intensive Linux workloads such as HPC. It does not provide SMB shares.

options.text: Amazon S3 Files mounted on each instance
options.rationale: S3 Files provides NFS access to the data in an S3 bucket. It does not provide SMB shares or Windows ACLs from Active Directory.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company has a content management system that stores files on an Amazon EFS file system. The file system uses Bursting throughput mode and holds only 50 GiB of data, and traffic is spiky. During peaks, file operations become slow, and the BurstCreditBalance metric drops to 0.

Which solution will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Switch the file system to Elastic throughput mode.
options.rationale: In Bursting mode, throughput scales with the amount of data stored, so a small file system earns few credits. Elastic throughput scales up and down automatically with the workload, and you pay for the throughput that you use, which suits spiky traffic.

options.text: Add 1 TiB of placeholder files to earn more burst credits.
options.rationale: More stored data does raise baseline throughput, but placeholder files are a workaround that adds storage cost and must be maintained.

options.text: Switch the file system to Max I/O performance mode.
options.rationale: Max I/O is a performance mode for highly parallel workloads, and it has higher latency. It does not add throughput when burst credits run out.

options.text: Create a second mount target in the same subnet.
options.rationale: A file system can have only one mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount targets do not add throughput.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company's data science team keeps 300 TB of datasets in an Amazon S3 bucket. The team's Python tools and shell scripts need a shared POSIX file system, so engineers copy data to Amazon EBS volumes before each job. The company needs to stop copying the data.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a file system for the bucket with Amazon S3 Files, and mount it on the compute instances.
options.rationale: S3 Files makes an S3 bucket accessible as a shared NFS file system that compute resources can mount. The data stays in the bucket, changes made through the file system are synced back to S3, and there is no copy step or migration.

options.text: Copy the datasets to an Amazon EFS file system each night. Copy results back with AWS DataSync.
options.rationale: Nightly copies duplicate 300 TB of data and add sync jobs to manage, which is the overhead the team wants to remove.

options.text: Use Mountpoint for Amazon S3 on each instance. Change the tools that edit files in place.
options.rationale: Mountpoint for Amazon S3 does not provide full file system semantics, such as editing existing files in place, so the tools would need changes.

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server share. Use AWS DataSync to keep it in sync with the bucket.
options.rationale: FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB shares for Windows workloads. It does not suit Linux Python tools, and syncing it with the bucket keeps a second copy of the data.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance that shows high CPU utilization every day at 11:00. A CloudOps engineer needs to identify which SQL statements and wait events cause the load.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch Database Insights (formerly Performance Insights) to view DB load by top SQL and wait events.
options.rationale: CloudWatch Database Insights shows database load as average active sessions and breaks it down by dimensions such as top SQL and wait events, which identifies the statements behind the 11:00 load directly. It replaced Performance Insights in 2026. The exam guide still uses the older name, so know both.

options.text: Enable Enhanced Monitoring. Review the operating system process list for the DB instance.
options.rationale: Enhanced Monitoring shows OS metrics and processes. It shows that database processes use CPU, but not which SQL statements cause it.

options.text: Configure AWS CloudTrail data events for the DB instance, and search the trail for the SQL that ran at 11:00.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records RDS management API calls, such as modifying an instance. It does not record SQL statements that run inside the database.

options.text: Export the instance's metrics to Amazon S3, and use Amazon Athena to correlate CPU with query counts.
options.rationale: CloudWatch metrics such as CPUUtilization do not include individual SQL statements, so this analysis cannot find them.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company has an AWS Lambda function that connects to an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. During traffic spikes, thousands of function instances open new connections. The database reaches its max_connections limit, and requests fail with Too many connections errors.

Which solution will resolve this issue with the LEAST change to the application code?

options.text: Create an Amazon RDS Proxy for the database. Change the function to connect to the proxy endpoint.
options.rationale: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, so many function instances reuse a smaller number of connections to the database. Only the connection endpoint changes in the function's configuration. The proxy can also use IAM authentication and Secrets Manager for credentials.

options.text: Increase the max_connections parameter to the highest value allowed for the DB instance class.
options.rationale: A higher limit uses more database memory and only delays the problem, because each new connection still adds overhead.

options.text: Set the function's reserved concurrency to 0 during spikes.
options.rationale: Reserved concurrency of 0 stops the function from running at all, so the requests would fail.

options.text: Add an Aurora Replica. Send all of the function's connections to the cluster reader endpoint.
options.rationale: A reader endpoint accepts read-only work. Writes from the function would fail, and the replica has its own connection limit.

questions.topic: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

questions.question:
A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Load changes throughout the day without a fixed pattern. The company must keep average CPU utilization near 50%.

Which scaling policy will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: A target tracking policy on ASGAverageCPUUtilization with a target of 50
options.rationale: Target tracking works like a thermostat. You choose a metric and a target value, and EC2 Auto Scaling creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms and adjusts capacity in both directions to keep the metric near the target.

options.text: A step scaling policy with separate alarms at 40%, 50%, and 60% CPU
options.rationale: Step scaling can work, but you must create and tune the alarms and step adjustments yourself, which is more effort.

options.text: A scheduled action that changes the desired capacity every hour
options.rationale: Scheduled actions suit predictable patterns, and this load has no fixed pattern.

options.text: A simple scaling policy that adds one instance when CPU passes 50%
options.rationale: Simple scaling adds one instance at a time and waits for a cooldown before it acts again, so it reacts slowly to large changes. It also needs a separate scale-in policy.

questions.question:
A company runs a stateless API on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Load tests show that each instance handles up to 1,000 requests per minute before latency rises. CPU utilization stays below 40% even at that point.

Which scaling configuration will keep latency low?

options.text: A target tracking policy on ALBRequestCountPerTarget with a target of about 800
options.rationale: The instances slow down because of request volume, not CPU. Request count per target measures that load directly, and a target below the 1,000 limit leaves headroom while new instances start.

options.text: A target tracking policy on ASGAverageCPUUtilization with a target of 40
options.rationale: CPU stays below 40% even when latency rises, so a CPU target would not add instances in time.

options.text: A target tracking policy on ASGAverageNetworkIn with a target of 1,000
options.rationale: Network bytes in are not the same as requests, and 1,000 bytes is not a meaningful target for this API.

options.text: A step scaling policy that adds instances when HealthyHostCount drops
options.rationale: HealthyHostCount drops when targets fail health checks. It does not track the request load that causes the latency.

questions.question:
A company has an internal HR application that runs in an Auto Scaling group. The application has almost no traffic at night. Every weekday at 08:00, 4,000 employees sign in within 10 minutes, and the group's target tracking policy cannot add instances fast enough.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to handle the morning peak?

options.text: Add a scheduled action that raises the minimum capacity at 07:45 each weekday and lowers it in the evening.
options.rationale: The peak is predictable, so a scheduled action can add capacity before users arrive. Target tracking stays in place to handle changes during the day, and a second scheduled action lowers the minimum in the evening to save cost.

options.text: Lower the target value of the target tracking policy to run twice the instances that the group needs.
options.rationale: Running twice the needed capacity all day and night wastes money, especially at night when there is almost no traffic.

options.text: Change the default instance warmup to count new instances toward the group's metrics sooner.
options.rationale: Warmup controls when a new instance's metrics are counted. It does not start instances any earlier, so they would still be late.

options.text: Replace the target tracking policy with a simple scaling policy that has a shorter cooldown period.
options.rationale: A simple scaling policy still reacts only after the load arrives, so instances would still be late for the peak.

questions.question:
A company's retail website runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Traffic follows a repeating daily and weekly pattern. New instances take 8 minutes to boot and warm their caches. Capacity must be ready before traffic increases, without a manually maintained schedule.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Add a predictive scaling policy. Keep a target tracking policy for unexpected changes.
options.rationale: Predictive scaling uses machine learning on the group's history to forecast load and launches capacity ahead of the forecast, which covers the 8-minute boot time. Target tracking still reacts to changes that the forecast does not predict.

options.text: Create scheduled actions for each hour of the week. Update them every month.
options.rationale: A full set of scheduled actions must be built and kept up to date by hand, which the company wants to avoid.

options.text: Use step scaling with larger step adjustments to start more instances at once.
options.rationale: Step scaling still reacts after the load arrives, so new instances would still be 8 minutes late.

options.text: Enable detailed monitoring to evaluate the scaling alarms every minute.
options.rationale: More frequent metrics help scaling react slightly sooner, but capacity still arrives after the traffic does.

questions.question:
A company has an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances that run an initialization script that takes 12 minutes. During sudden spikes, users see errors until the new instances finish initializing. The company needs faster scale-out without paying for running instances that do not serve traffic.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Add a warm pool of pre-initialized instances in the Stopped state.
options.rationale: A warm pool keeps instances that have already run their initialization. Stopped instances incur no instance charges, only EBS storage, and they move into service much faster than new instances that start from scratch.

options.text: Raise the minimum capacity of the group by the size of a typical spike.
options.rationale: A higher minimum capacity keeps extra instances running without serving traffic, which is the cost the company wants to avoid.

options.text: Add a launch lifecycle hook that holds new instances in Pending:Wait.
options.rationale: A lifecycle hook gives an instance time to finish setup before it enters service. It does not shorten the 12-minute setup.

options.text: Lower the health check grace period.
options.rationale: A shorter grace period does not make initialization faster. Instances could be marked unhealthy and replaced before they are ready.

questions.question:
A company has an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances that write application logs to local disk. When the group scales in, the logs on terminated instances are lost. The logs must be uploaded to Amazon S3 before each instance is terminated.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Add a termination lifecycle hook that runs a script to upload the logs before the instance terminates.
options.rationale: A termination lifecycle hook holds the instance in the Terminating:Wait state. An EventBridge rule can run a script on the instance, for example with Systems Manager Run Command, that uploads the logs and then completes the lifecycle action so termination continues.

options.text: Enable scale-in protection for all instances to prevent the group from terminating them.
options.rationale: Scale-in protection stops the group from removing instances, which breaks scale-in and increases cost.

options.text: Set the termination policy to OldestLaunchTemplate to keep the newer instances.
options.rationale: A termination policy decides which instance is removed. The removed instance still loses its logs.

options.text: Increase the deregistration delay of the target group to give the logs time to upload.
options.rationale: Deregistration delay lets in-flight requests finish at the load balancer. It does not run scripts or upload files.

questions.question:
A company has an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The instances sometimes have a hung web server process. The ALB marks those targets as unhealthy and stops sending them traffic, but the Auto Scaling group never replaces them. The EC2 status checks pass.

What should a CloudOps engineer do so that the group replaces these instances?

options.text: Enable Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group.
options.rationale: By default, an Auto Scaling group uses only EC2 status checks, which pass because the instance is still running. When ELB health checks are enabled, the group also treats targets that fail the load balancer health check as unhealthy and replaces them.

options.text: Configure detailed monitoring for every instance in the Auto Scaling group.
options.rationale: Detailed monitoring adds 1-minute metrics. It does not change how the group decides that an instance is unhealthy.

options.text: Lower the ALB health check interval from 30 seconds to 5 seconds.
options.rationale: A shorter interval detects the failure sooner at the load balancer, but the group still ignores the load balancer's health status.

options.text: Add an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that reboots instances on StatusCheckFailed.
options.rationale: The status checks pass, so this alarm would never fire for a hung web server process.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer enables Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) health checks for an Auto Scaling group. New instances are now terminated and replaced repeatedly. Each instance needs about 6 minutes to install dependencies before the application responds. The health check grace period is 60 seconds.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Increase the health check grace period to longer than the startup time.
options.rationale: The grace period tells the group to ignore health check results for a new instance until it has had time to start. A value longer than the 6-minute startup stops the group from replacing instances that are still initializing.

options.text: Switch the Auto Scaling group back to Amazon EC2 status checks only.
options.rationale: This stops the loop, but the group could no longer replace instances whose application stops responding.

options.text: Lower the unhealthy threshold count on the target group to 2.
options.rationale: A lower threshold marks targets unhealthy even faster, which makes the problem worse.

options.text: Enable scale-in protection for each instance as it launches.
options.rationale: Scale-in protection affects scale-in decisions. It does not stop the group from replacing instances that it considers unhealthy.

questions.question:
A company runs a batch processing fleet in an Auto Scaling group. The workload can tolerate interruptions. The company must minimize cost, keep at least 2 On-Demand Instances at all times, and reduce the chance of Spot Instance interruptions.

Which configuration will meet these requirements?

options.text: A mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base capacity of 2, several instance types, and the price-capacity-optimized Spot strategy
options.rationale: The On-Demand base capacity keeps 2 On-Demand Instances, and the rest of the group can use Spot. Allowing several instance types gives Auto Scaling more Spot capacity pools, and price-capacity-optimized chooses pools that have low prices and a low chance of interruption.

options.text: A mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base capacity of 2, a single instance type, and the lowest-price Spot strategy
options.rationale: One instance type limits Spot to fewer pools, and lowest-price ignores available capacity, which raises the risk of interruptions.

options.text: A launch template for Spot Instances of one instance type, and a scheduled action that adds 2 On-Demand Instances daily
options.rationale: A scheduled action does not guarantee that 2 On-Demand Instances are always running, and one Spot instance type increases interruption risk.

options.text: Two Auto Scaling groups: one with 2 On-Demand Instances, and one with Spot Instances that use a single instance type
options.rationale: Two groups add management effort, and a single Spot instance type still increases interruption risk.

questions.question:
A company has worker instances in an Auto Scaling group that process video jobs that can run for up to 45 minutes. When the group scales in, it sometimes terminates an instance in the middle of a job.

How can a CloudOps engineer prevent the group from terminating instances that are processing jobs?

options.text: Have the worker enable instance scale-in protection when a job starts. Disable it when the job ends.
options.rationale: Instance scale-in protection stops Auto Scaling from choosing that instance during scale-in. Setting it through the API when a job starts and clearing it when the job finishes protects only busy instances, while idle instances can still be removed.

options.text: Change the termination policy to terminate the instance with the newest launch template.
options.rationale: The termination policy only changes which instance is chosen. A busy instance can still be terminated.

options.text: Increase the cooldown period of the scaling policy to 45 minutes to scale in less often.
options.rationale: A longer cooldown delays scaling activities but does not protect instances that are in the middle of a job.

options.text: Set the minimum capacity equal to the maximum capacity to stop the group from scaling in.
options.rationale: A fixed size removes elasticity and keeps idle instances running, which raises cost.

questions.question:
A company has an Auto Scaling group of worker instances that process messages from an Amazon SQS queue. Each instance processes about 100 messages per minute. The number of instances must grow and shrink so that any backlog is cleared within about 5 minutes.

Which scaling approach will meet this requirement?

options.text: Publish a backlog per instance metric. Use target tracking with a target of 500 messages per instance.
options.rationale: Backlog per instance is ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible divided by the number of running instances. Each instance clears 100 messages per minute, so 500 messages per instance is about 5 minutes of work. Target tracking on this metric adds and removes instances as the queue grows and shrinks.

options.text: Use target tracking on the group's average CPU utilization with a target value of 70%.
options.rationale: CPU does not show how many messages are waiting. Workers can run at low CPU while the backlog grows.

options.text: Use step scaling on the queue's NumberOfMessagesSent metric with one step for each 100 messages.
options.rationale: Messages sent shows the arrival rate, not the backlog, and it ignores how many instances are already running.

options.text: Use a scheduled action that sets the desired capacity to the queue length at the top of each hour.
options.rationale: An hourly schedule cannot react to a backlog that changes within minutes.

questions.question:
A company has a new mobile game that uses an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling enabled. Traffic is unpredictable and sometimes doubles within seconds after a social media post. Requests are throttled during these jumps.

Which solution will MOST effectively stop the throttling?

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode.
options.rationale: On-demand mode serves traffic without capacity planning and instantly accommodates up to double the table's previous peak. Auto scaling in provisioned mode adjusts over minutes, so it cannot keep up with spikes that arrive within seconds.

options.text: Lower the auto scaling target utilization to 50%.
options.rationale: A lower target adds more headroom, but auto scaling still reacts after the spike, so sudden jumps are still throttled.

options.text: Add a global secondary index to the table.
options.rationale: A global secondary index has its own capacity needs. It does not add capacity to the base table.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams for the table.
options.rationale: Streams capture item changes for other consumers. They do not add read or write capacity.

questions.question:
A company has a product catalog in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Reads outnumber writes by 50 to 1, and the same items are read repeatedly. The application needs microsecond read latency, and the company wants the fewest possible code changes.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster. Point the DynamoDB client at the DAX endpoint.
options.rationale: DAX is an in-memory cache built for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond read latency for cached items. It is compatible with the DynamoDB API, so the application mostly changes its client configuration to use the DAX endpoint.

options.text: Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and write cache logic for every read and write in the application.
options.rationale: ElastiCache can cache the data, but the team would have to write and maintain caching logic, which means more code changes.

options.text: Create a global table in a second Region. Send half of the reads to the replica table.
options.rationale: A replica in another Region does not bring read latency down to microseconds, and it adds cost and replication to manage.

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode.
options.rationale: On-demand mode changes how capacity is billed and scaled. It does not lower read latency to microseconds.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster that serves a reporting dashboard. Read traffic doubles during the last week of each month, and the reader instances reach 90% CPU utilization. At other times, one reader is enough.

Which solution will meet the read demand with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas with a target on average reader CPU utilization.
options.rationale: Aurora Auto Scaling adds and removes Aurora Replicas based on a target tracking policy, such as the average CPU of the readers. Applications that use the reader endpoint automatically spread reads across the replicas that it adds.

options.text: Add a cross-Region read replica each month. Delete it after the reporting week ends.
options.rationale: Cross-Region replicas are meant for disaster recovery and local reads in another Region, and creating them by hand every month is extra work.

options.text: Move the cluster to a larger instance class before each month end, and resize it back later.
options.rationale: Resizing by hand every month is manual work and can cause brief interruptions during each change.

options.text: Create an Amazon RDS Proxy for the cluster.
options.rationale: RDS Proxy pools connections. It does not add CPU capacity for read queries.

questions.question:
A company runs an application on an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Read-heavy reporting queries run throughout the day and slow down the application's writes. A CloudOps engineer must reduce the load on the primary DB instance. The reports can use slightly stale data.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance. Update the reporting queries to use the read replica's endpoint.
options.rationale: A read replica is a read-only copy that Amazon RDS updates asynchronously. Routing read queries to it reduces the load on the primary, and the small replication lag is acceptable for reports.

options.text: Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ deployment. Send the reporting queries to the standby instance.
options.rationale: The standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment cannot serve read traffic. It exists for high availability.

options.text: Increase the automated backup retention period. Run the reporting queries against the latest snapshot.
options.rationale: A snapshot cannot be queried directly, and a longer retention period does not reduce the load on the primary.

options.text: Restore a new DB instance from a snapshot each day. Run the reporting queries against the new DB instance.
options.rationale: This can work, but it needs a daily restore process and leaves the data up to a day old, which is more work than a read replica.

questions.question:
A company has a web application that stores user session data in the memory of each Amazon EC2 instance. The Application Load Balancer uses sticky sessions. When the Auto Scaling group scales in, users on the terminated instances are logged out. Load is also uneven across the instances.

Which solution will resolve these issues?

options.text: Store session data in Amazon ElastiCache. Disable sticky sessions on the target group.
options.rationale: Keeping sessions in a shared in-memory store makes the web tier stateless. Any instance can serve any request, so scale-in does not log users out, and disabling stickiness lets the load balancer spread requests evenly.

options.text: Increase the stickiness duration on the target group.
options.rationale: Longer stickiness makes the uneven load worse, and sessions are still lost when an instance is terminated.

options.text: Configure scale-in protection for every instance that has active user sessions in its memory.
options.rationale: Protecting instances that have sessions would block most scale-in and keep extra instances running.

options.text: Store session data on an Amazon EBS volume on each instance, and take snapshots of the volumes every hour.
options.rationale: Session data on a local volume is still unavailable to the other instances, and hourly snapshots cannot restore live sessions.

questions.question:
A company has an application that uses Amazon ElastiCache with a lazy loading strategy in front of an Amazon RDS database. After prices change in the database, users sometimes see prices that are several hours out of date. The cache must continue to serve most reads.

Which solution will reduce stale data with the LEAST impact on the cache hit rate?

options.text: Write the new value to the cache whenever a price is updated, and set a TTL on each key.
options.rationale: With write-through, the application updates the cache at the same time as the database, so reads see the new price immediately. A TTL acts as a safety net that expires any keys that are missed, while popular keys stay cached.

options.text: Disable the cache, and read every price directly from the RDS database instead.
options.rationale: Removing the cache sends every read to the database, which loses the performance benefit.

options.text: Flush the entire cache every 5 minutes to reload every key from the database.
options.rationale: Flushing everything causes a burst of cache misses and database load every 5 minutes.

options.text: Increase the TTL of each price key to keep items in the cache for a longer time.
options.rationale: A longer TTL keeps stale prices in the cache for even longer.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster with cluster mode disabled. The Evictions metric is rising steadily, and the cache hit rate is falling. The DatabaseMemoryUsagePercentage metric is near 100%, and CPU utilization is low.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Scale up to a node type with more memory, or enable cluster mode and add shards.
options.rationale: Evictions happen when the cache runs out of memory and removes keys to make room. More memory per node, or more shards that split the key space, increases the memory available for data, which reduces evictions and restores the hit rate.

options.text: Add more read replicas to the shard.
options.rationale: Read replicas hold copies of the same data, so they add read capacity but no extra space for more keys.

options.text: Set the maxmemory-policy parameter to noeviction.
options.rationale: With noeviction, write commands fail with errors when memory is full instead of removing keys, which breaks the application.

options.text: Scale up to nodes with more vCPUs, because evictions show that the engine is CPU bound.
options.rationale: CPU utilization is low, so the engine is not CPU bound. The evictions are caused by memory pressure.

questions.question:
A company's news website serves images and JavaScript files directly from an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to users around the world. During breaking news, the Amazon EC2 instances behind the ALB reach high CPU utilization because of requests for the same static files.

Which solution will MOST reduce the load on the instances?

options.text: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the site, and cache static files with long TTLs.
options.rationale: CloudFront caches static content at edge locations close to users. Repeated requests for the same images and scripts are served from the cache instead of reaching the instances, which removes most of that load.

options.text: Add more instances to the Auto Scaling group, and raise the maximum capacity of the group.
options.rationale: More instances absorb the load but cost more, and every request still reaches the origin.

options.text: Enable cross-zone load balancing to spread requests evenly across all instances.
options.rationale: Cross-zone load balancing is already on by default for an ALB. Spreading requests does not reduce how many requests there are.

options.text: Move the ALB into a larger subnet to create more load balancer nodes.
options.rationale: Subnet size does not limit request capacity in this way, and the instances, not the load balancer, are the bottleneck.

questions.question:
A company has a latency-sensitive API that runs on AWS Lambda functions. Users complain about slow responses for the first requests each morning because of cold starts. Traffic is high from 08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays and low at other times.

Which solution will reduce cold starts during business hours MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Use Application Auto Scaling to schedule provisioned concurrency on an alias during business hours.
options.rationale: Provisioned concurrency keeps execution environments initialized, so requests avoid cold starts. Application Auto Scaling can raise it on a schedule before 08:00 and lower it after 18:00, so you pay for it only when traffic is high.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency at the peak level on the function alias 24 hours a day, every day.
options.rationale: This removes cold starts, but it pays for peak provisioned concurrency during nights and weekends when traffic is low.

options.text: Set reserved concurrency on the function to the peak level.
options.rationale: Reserved concurrency limits and guarantees how many concurrent executions a function can use. It does not pre-initialize execution environments.

options.text: Invoke the function every minute from an Amazon EventBridge schedule to keep exactly one instance warm.
options.rationale: One warm environment does not help when many requests arrive at the same time, so most morning requests would still have cold starts.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon ECS service that runs on an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 container instances. During peaks, the service needs more tasks, but new tasks stay in the PROVISIONING state because the cluster has no free capacity.

Which combination of steps will let the service scale automatically? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure ECS service auto scaling with a target tracking policy on CPU.
options.rationale: Service auto scaling uses Application Auto Scaling to change the desired number of tasks based on metrics such as average CPU, so the service adds tasks during peaks.

options.text: Use a capacity provider with managed scaling for the Auto Scaling group.
options.rationale: A capacity provider with managed scaling scales the Auto Scaling group based on the capacity that tasks need. Tasks that are waiting for capacity cause the group to add instances so that the tasks can be placed.

options.text: Raise the desired task count of the service to the peak value permanently.
options.rationale: A permanently high task count wastes capacity at quiet times and still needs instances to run the tasks.

options.text: Change the task placement strategy from spread to binpack on memory only.
options.rationale: Binpack can fit tasks more tightly, but it cannot place tasks when the cluster is full.

options.text: Enable the deployment circuit breaker for the service in the cluster.
options.rationale: The circuit breaker rolls back failed deployments. It does not add tasks or instances.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon DynamoDB table that stores sensor readings. The partition key is the sensor model. Ten thousand sensors share only three model names. The table has plenty of total provisioned capacity, but writes are throttled.

What should a CloudOps engineer recommend to resolve this issue?

options.text: Use a high-cardinality partition key, such as the sensor ID.
options.rationale: A key with only three values sends all writes to a few partitions, which become hot and throttle even when the table has spare capacity. A key with many distinct values, such as the sensor ID, spreads writes evenly. Adaptive capacity helps with uneven load but cannot fix a key with only three values.

options.text: Double the table's provisioned write capacity, and keep the sensor model as the partition key.
options.rationale: Each partition has its own throughput limit, so the hot partitions keep throttling while cost rises.

options.text: Add a local secondary index on the sensor model.
options.rationale: Local secondary indexes share the partition key of the base table, so writes still concentrate on the same few keys.

options.text: Enable point-in-time recovery.
options.rationale: Point-in-time recovery protects against data loss. Throttled writes are rejected and never stored, so there is nothing to restore.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer adds an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect to a web server configuration. All targets in an Application Load Balancer target group then become unhealthy. The health check uses HTTP on port 80 with the path /health and expects a 200 response.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Exclude the /health path from the redirect.
options.rationale: The redirect makes the web server answer the health check with a 301 or 302 code, which does not match the expected 200, so every target fails. Returning 200 on the health check path, or adding the redirect code to the success codes, fixes the checks.

options.text: Change the health check protocol to TCP.
options.rationale: Target groups for an Application Load Balancer support only HTTP and HTTPS health checks, not TCP.

options.text: Increase the healthy threshold count.
options.rationale: A higher threshold makes targets take longer to become healthy. It does not change the redirect response.

options.text: Configure stickiness.
options.rationale: Stickiness affects how client requests are routed. It has no effect on health checks.

questions.question:
A company creates a new Application Load Balancer (ALB) for an existing fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. All targets fail health checks with the reason Request timed out. The application responds normally when a CloudOps engineer runs curl on the instances. The instances' security group allows inbound port 80 only from the company's office IP range.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Allow inbound port 80 on the instance security group from the ALB's security group.
options.rationale: Health checks come from the load balancer nodes, so the targets' security group must allow the health check port from the load balancer. Referencing the ALB's security group allows that traffic without hardcoding IP addresses.

options.text: Allow inbound port 80 on the ALB's security group from the instance security group.
options.rationale: The ALB's inbound rules control traffic from clients to the load balancer. The timeout happens on the path from the ALB to the instances.

options.text: Add a route to the ALB in the route tables of the subnets that contain the instances.
options.rationale: Traffic within a VPC uses the local route, which already exists. No extra route is needed.

options.text: Change the target type of the target group from instance to IP to skip security groups.
options.rationale: Security groups still apply to IP targets. Changing the target type does not bypass them.

questions.question:
A company has a Network Load Balancer (NLB) with nodes in two Availability Zones. Zone A has 2 targets, and zone B has 8 targets. The 2 targets in zone A are overloaded, while the targets in zone B are mostly idle.

Which solution will spread traffic evenly across all 10 targets?

options.text: Enable cross-zone load balancing for the NLB.
options.rationale: Cross-zone load balancing is off by default for Network Load Balancers, so each node sends traffic only to targets in its own zone. Each zone gets about half the traffic, so 2 targets receive as much as 8. Turning on cross-zone load balancing spreads traffic across all registered targets. Data transfer charges between zones can apply.

options.text: Configure sticky sessions for the NLB target group.
options.rationale: Stickiness keeps a client on the same target. It does not balance load between zones.

options.text: Change the NLB target group to use IP targets.
options.rationale: The target type does not change how traffic is split between zones.

options.text: Increase the deregistration delay of the target group.
options.rationale: Deregistration delay controls how long in-flight connections can finish when a target is removed. It does not change routing.

questions.question:
A company runs an application that handles uploads that can take up to 90 seconds. Users see failed requests every time the Auto Scaling group scales in. The Application Load Balancer target group uses a deregistration delay of 10 seconds.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Increase the deregistration delay to longer than the longest request.
options.rationale: When a target is deregistered, the load balancer stops sending it new requests but lets in-flight requests finish during the deregistration delay. A 10-second delay cuts off uploads that need up to 90 seconds, so a longer delay prevents the failures.

options.text: Enable slow start mode to give new targets a gradual share of requests.
options.rationale: Slow start helps new targets warm up. It does nothing for requests on targets that are being removed.

options.text: Lower the health check interval to remove targets from service faster.
options.rationale: Removing targets faster would cut off in-flight requests even sooner.

options.text: Disable cross-zone load balancing to keep requests in each Availability Zone.
options.rationale: Cross-zone settings control how traffic is spread. They do not protect requests during deregistration.

questions.question:
A company runs its primary web application behind an Application Load Balancer. Users must see a static maintenance page that is hosted in Amazon S3 whenever the application becomes unavailable. The switch must happen automatically.

Which Amazon Route 53 configuration will meet these requirements?

options.text: Failover routing: a primary alias to the ALB with Evaluate Target Health, and a secondary record for the S3 site
options.rationale: Failover routing answers with the primary record while it is healthy and with the secondary record when it is not. An alias record to the ALB with Evaluate Target Health uses the load balancer's target health, so Route 53 switches to the S3 maintenance page when the application is down.

options.text: Weighted routing that sends 90% of traffic to the ALB and 10% to the S3 site, with no health checks on either record
options.rationale: Weighted routing without health checks keeps sending 90% of users to the failed ALB, and it sends 10% to the maintenance page even when the site is healthy.

options.text: Latency-based routing with one record for the ALB and one record for the S3 site in the same AWS Region
options.rationale: Latency routing picks the record with the lowest latency. Both records are in one Region, and nothing here switches traffic based on health.

options.text: Multivalue answer routing that returns both the ALB and the S3 site
options.rationale: Multivalue answer returns several records for clients to try. It is not designed to show a maintenance page only during failures, and clients could pick it while the site is up.

questions.question:
A company uses Amazon Route 53 failover routing between two internal API endpoints that run in private subnets. The endpoints are not reachable from the internet, so Route 53 health checkers cannot connect to them. The company still needs failover based on endpoint health.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check that monitors the state of an Amazon CloudWatch alarm for each endpoint.
options.rationale: Route 53 health checkers run on the internet and cannot reach private resources. A health check can instead monitor a CloudWatch alarm, such as an alarm on the endpoint's error rate. The health check becomes unhealthy when the alarm is in ALARM, which drives the failover.

options.text: Open each endpoint's security group to 0.0.0.0/0 to allow the Route 53 health checkers to connect.
options.rationale: Opening the endpoints to the internet breaks the private design, and the subnets have no internet path anyway.

options.text: Associate the Route 53 health checks with the VPC to run the checks from inside the private subnets.
options.rationale: Route 53 health checks cannot be placed inside a VPC. They always run from health checker locations on the internet.

options.text: Replace failover routing with simple routing that lists both endpoints as values in a single record.
options.rationale: Simple routing with several values returns them with no health checking, so clients could still be sent to a failed endpoint.

questions.question:
A company keeps critical documents in an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1. For disaster recovery, a copy of every new object must be stored automatically in a bucket in eu-west-1.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable versioning on both buckets. Create an S3 Replication rule on the source bucket that targets the eu-west-1 bucket.
options.rationale: S3 Replication copies new objects to the destination automatically. Both buckets must have versioning enabled, and Amazon S3 needs an IAM role with replication permissions. To copy objects that already exist, use S3 Batch Replication.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function that copies each object. Invoke the function from an event notification on the source bucket.
options.rationale: This can work, but the company would have to write and maintain code for retries, large objects, and failures. Replication handles these without custom code.

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan for the source bucket. Run a weekly copy job to a backup vault in eu-west-1.
options.rationale: A weekly copy job leaves up to a week of new objects without a copy in the second Region.

options.text: Run the aws s3 sync command from an Amazon EC2 instance. Schedule the command by using a cron job on the instance.
options.rationale: An instance with a cron job must be patched and monitored, and new objects wait until the next run.

questions.question:
A company has an application that connects to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance by using the DB endpoint. During a test failover, Amazon RDS promotes the standby within 60 seconds, but the application continues to fail for 20 minutes until it is restarted.

What is the MOST likely cause of this issue?

options.text: The application caches the DNS lookup of the endpoint for longer than the record's TTL.
options.rationale: During a Multi-AZ failover, RDS updates the endpoint's DNS record to point to the new primary. The endpoint name stays the same, but an application or runtime that caches DNS results for too long keeps connecting to the old address. Honoring the short TTL, or connecting through RDS Proxy, shortens recovery.

options.text: The standby instance is in a different DB subnet group that the application cannot reach.
options.rationale: The primary and standby are in the same DB subnet group and VPC, so the application's network path is the same.

options.text: The standby needs 20 minutes to replay transaction logs before it accepts connections.
options.rationale: The standby is kept current with synchronous replication, and the scenario says the promotion finished within 60 seconds.

options.text: Multi-AZ failover creates a new endpoint name that the application must be updated to use.
options.rationale: The endpoint name does not change during a Multi-AZ failover. Only the IP address behind it changes.

questions.question:
A company runs Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. The company needs faster failover, typically under 35 seconds, and needs to use the standby capacity for read queries.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Move to a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment with two readable standby instances.
options.rationale: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable standby instances in three Availability Zones. Failover is typically under 35 seconds, and applications can send read queries to the reader endpoint.

options.text: Add a read replica in another Region. Promote it during an outage.
options.rationale: Promoting a cross-Region replica is a manual disaster recovery step that takes longer and changes the endpoint.

options.text: Enable RDS storage autoscaling.
options.rationale: Storage autoscaling grows storage when free space runs low. It has no effect on failover time.

options.text: Keep the Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Send read queries to its standby instance.
options.rationale: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the standby cannot serve reads. It exists only for failover.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster with a writer and three Aurora Replicas: two db.r6g.2xlarge replicas that the application uses, and one db.r6g.large replica for ad hoc reports. During a failover test, Aurora promoted the small reporting replica, and the application performed poorly.

How should a CloudOps engineer ensure that a large replica is promoted during failover?

options.text: Set the large replicas to promotion tier 0 and the reporting replica to tier 15.
options.rationale: Aurora promotes the replica with the highest priority, which is the lowest tier number. Tier 0 for the large replicas and tier 15 for the reporting replica makes Aurora choose a large replica. Among replicas in the same tier, Aurora picks the largest one.

options.text: Move the reporting replica to a different Availability Zone from the one the writer uses.
options.rationale: Availability Zone placement does not decide which replica is promoted.

options.text: Add the large replicas to a custom endpoint named failover for the cluster.
options.rationale: Custom endpoints group instances for connections. They do not affect which replica is promoted.

options.text: Enable Aurora Backtrack.
options.rationale: Backtrack rewinds a cluster's data to an earlier point in time. It does not control failover.

questions.question:
A company has a financial application that uses Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL in us-east-1. The company needs a disaster recovery plan for a Regional outage with an RPO of about 1 second and an RTO of a few minutes. The company also needs low-latency reads in eu-west-1.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Convert the cluster to an Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in eu-west-1.
options.rationale: Aurora Global Database replicates storage to secondary Regions with typical lag of under 1 second, and the secondary cluster serves reads locally. During a Regional outage, a secondary cluster can be promoted to accept writes within minutes.

options.text: Take hourly cluster snapshots, and copy each snapshot to eu-west-1 by using an AWS Backup plan.
options.rationale: Hourly snapshots give an RPO of up to an hour, and restoring a cluster from a snapshot takes much longer than a few minutes.

options.text: Create a Multi-AZ DB cluster in us-east-1 that spans three Availability Zones.
options.rationale: Multi-AZ protects against an Availability Zone failure, not a Regional outage, and it provides no reads in eu-west-1.

options.text: Export the database to Amazon S3 each night, and import it into a cluster in eu-west-1.
options.rationale: Nightly exports can lose up to a day of data, which fails the 1-second RPO.

questions.question:
A company has an application on Amazon EC2 instances in three Availability Zones. The instances share files through an Amazon EFS file system that uses the One Zone storage class. When the file system's Availability Zone had an outage, all instances lost access to the shared files.

Which solution will prevent this issue in the future?

options.text: Move the data to an EFS file system with Regional storage and a mount target in each zone.
options.rationale: Regional EFS file systems store data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones, and a mount target in each zone gives instances local access. The file system stays available if one zone fails.

options.text: Add mount targets for the One Zone file system in the two other Availability Zones.
options.rationale: A One Zone file system stores data in one zone and has a mount target only in that zone. Instances in other zones still lose access when that zone fails.

options.text: Configure EFS Replication to another One Zone file system in the same Availability Zone.
options.rationale: A replica in the same zone fails along with the source, so it does not protect against a zone outage.

options.text: Enable Elastic throughput for the One Zone file system.
options.rationale: The throughput mode affects performance, not where the data is stored.

questions.question:
A company runs an application behind an Application Load Balancer in three Availability Zones. During an incident, monitoring shows elevated errors in one Availability Zone, but health checks still pass. The company must move traffic away from that Availability Zone quickly and move it back later, without changing any infrastructure.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Start a zonal shift in Amazon Application Recovery Controller to move the ALB's traffic away from the zone.
options.rationale: A zonal shift moves traffic for a supported resource, such as a load balancer, away from one Availability Zone for a duration that you set. It works even when health checks pass, changes no infrastructure, and can be canceled or allowed to expire to restore traffic. The load balancer must be opted in to zonal shift beforehand, and the other zones need enough capacity to absorb the load.

options.text: Deregister the targets in the impaired zone from the target group, and register them again after the event.
options.rationale: Deregistering and registering targets by hand is slow and error prone during an incident, and it must be undone carefully.

options.text: Update the Auto Scaling group to remove the impaired zone's subnet. Add the subnet back after the event.
options.rationale: Changing the group's subnets terminates and relaunches instances, which is a slow infrastructure change.

options.text: Lower the health check thresholds.
options.rationale: Lower thresholds affect every zone and may not catch the problem if checks still succeed. They also stay in place after the event.

questions.question:
A company runs a critical application in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones with 4 instances in each Availability Zone. The application needs at least 8 instances to serve peak load. The application must continue to serve peak load if one Availability Zone fails, without waiting for new instances to launch.

Which configuration will meet this requirement?

options.text: Run 4 instances in each of three Availability Zones.
options.rationale: With 12 instances across three zones, losing any one zone leaves 8 instances, which is enough for peak load. This is static stability: enough capacity is already running, so recovery does not depend on launching instances during the event.

options.text: Run 6 instances in each of two Availability Zones.
options.rationale: Losing one zone leaves only 6 instances, which is below the 8 needed, so the group would have to launch more during the event.

options.text: Run 8 instances in a single Availability Zone only.
options.rationale: A single zone is a single point of failure. Losing that zone takes down the whole application.

options.text: Run 4 instances in each of two Availability Zones. Set the maximum capacity to 16.
options.rationale: A higher maximum lets the group scale out, but it must launch instances after the zone fails, which takes time and might be constrained during a zone event.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) replication group with one primary node and no replicas. When the primary node failed, the application lost its cache for 30 minutes while a new node was created and filled with data.

Which solution will provide the FASTEST recovery from a primary node failure?

options.text: Add a replica in another Availability Zone. Enable Multi-AZ with automatic failover.
options.rationale: With Multi-AZ and automatic failover, ElastiCache promotes a replica in another Availability Zone when the primary fails, and the replica already holds the data. The primary endpoint stays the same, so the application reconnects without configuration changes.

options.text: Configure daily automatic backups. Restore the latest backup whenever the primary node fails.
options.rationale: Restoring from a backup creates a new cluster, still takes a long time, and loses data written since the backup.

options.text: Change the node type to a larger size to start a new primary node and load data faster.
options.rationale: A larger node still has to be created and refilled with data, so recovery is not much faster.

options.text: Enable data tiering to store the cache data on SSDs that survive the node failure.
options.rationale: Data tiering extends capacity by using SSDs on the same node. It does not protect against that node failing.

questions.question:
A company must back up every Amazon EBS volume, Amazon RDS database, and Amazon DynamoDB table that has the tag Backup=Daily. Backups must be kept for 35 days, and a copy must be stored in a second AWS Region. New resources that get the tag must be included automatically.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan with a daily rule, 35-day retention, and a copy action to a vault in the second Region.
options.rationale: An AWS Backup plan defines when backups run and how long they are kept. A copy action sends each recovery point to a backup vault in another Region, with its own retention.

options.text: Assign resources to the backup plan by using the Backup=Daily tag.
options.rationale: Tag-based resource assignment includes every supported resource that has the tag, including resources created later, so no one has to update the plan.

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge schedule that invokes an AWS Lambda function to snapshot each tagged resource every day.
options.rationale: Custom snapshot code must be built and maintained for each resource type, and it still needs separate retention and copy logic.

options.text: Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager for all three resource types, with a cross-Region copy rule.
options.rationale: Data Lifecycle Manager manages EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs. It does not back up RDS databases or DynamoDB tables.

options.text: Configure Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication for the bucket where AWS Backup stores the recovery points.
options.rationale: AWS Backup stores recovery points in backup vaults, not in an S3 bucket that you manage, so there is no bucket to replicate.

questions.question:
A company has production AWS accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company's security team needs backups of the production accounts stored in a separate backup account, so that a compromised production account cannot delete them.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Enable cross-account backup in AWS Backup. Add a copy action to a vault in the backup account.
options.rationale: With cross-account backup enabled in the organization's management account, a backup plan can copy recovery points to a vault in another account. Production administrators cannot delete copies that live in the backup account, and a vault access policy can restrict access further.

options.text: Share each production backup vault with the backup account by using AWS Resource Access Manager.
options.rationale: Standard backup vaults are not shared through AWS RAM, and the backups would still be stored in the production accounts.

options.text: Give the backup account's IAM users permission to start backup jobs inside each production account.
options.rationale: Backups created inside the production accounts still live there and can be deleted from a compromised account.

options.text: Create a second backup vault in each production account. Copy every recovery point into it.
options.rationale: A second vault in the same account is still controlled by that account, so a compromise could delete both copies.

questions.question:
A company must keep backups for 7 years to comply with a regulation. No one, including the root user, can be allowed to delete the backups before the retention period ends.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Apply AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode to the vault, with a minimum retention of 7 years.
options.rationale: Vault Lock in compliance mode makes the retention settings immutable after the grace period ends. No one, including the root user and AWS, can delete recovery points early or remove the lock.

options.text: Apply AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode to the vault, with a minimum retention of 7 years.
options.rationale: Governance mode can be removed or changed by users who have sufficient IAM permissions, so it does not stop all deletions.

options.text: Add a vault access policy that denies backup:DeleteRecoveryPoint to all IAM users in the account.
options.rationale: Users with enough permissions, or the root user, can change the vault access policy, so it is not an immutable control.

options.text: Enable MFA delete for the backup vault.
options.rationale: MFA delete is an S3 bucket feature. Backup vaults use Vault Lock for this purpose.

questions.question:
A company stores shared files on an Amazon EFS file system in us-east-1. For disaster recovery, the company needs a copy in us-west-2 that is no more than about 15 minutes behind the source.

Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Enable EFS Replication with a destination file system in us-west-2.
options.rationale: EFS Replication keeps a read-only replica in another Region, with a recovery point objective of 15 minutes for most file systems, and it needs no scripts or schedules. During a disaster, you fail over to the replica.

options.text: Run an AWS DataSync task every hour from us-east-1 to an EFS file system in us-west-2.
options.rationale: DataSync is built for scheduled transfers, so it adds tasks to run, and an hourly schedule does not meet the 15-minute target.

options.text: Mount both file systems on an Amazon EC2 instance, and run rsync from a cron job every 15 minutes.
options.rationale: A cron job on a server must be patched, monitored, and retried, which is far more overhead than a managed replication feature.

options.text: Back up the file system with AWS Backup every day, and copy each backup to us-west-2.
options.rationale: A daily backup can lose up to a day of changes, which fails the 15-minute target.

questions.question:
