A company's auditors require monthly evidence that backups of critical Amazon RDS databases and Amazon EBS volumes can be restored, and how long each restore takes. The company's CloudOps team currently performs these restores manually.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS Backup restore testing plan that restores recent recovery points on a schedule.
options.rationale: Restore testing runs scheduled restores of selected recovery points, records whether each restore succeeded and how long it took, and then cleans up the test resources. This gives auditors monthly evidence with no manual restores.

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function that restores each backup monthly, times it, and saves results to a spreadsheet.
options.rationale: A custom function works, but it is code to build and maintain for each resource type.

options.text: Configure AWS Backup Audit Manager with a framework that checks that a backup plan covers each resource.
options.rationale: Audit Manager reports whether backup controls, such as plans and retention, are in place. On its own, it does not run restores to prove that they work.

options.text: Copy every recovery point to a second Region each month.
options.rationale: Copies prove that data was duplicated, not that it can be restored.

questions.question:
A company needs hourly snapshots of Amazon EBS volumes that have the tag Tier=Critical, kept for 48 hours. The company also needs daily snapshots of the same volumes, kept for 30 days. The company wants a policy-based feature that is built into Amazon EBS and needs no custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy that targets the tag and has two schedules.
options.rationale: Data Lifecycle Manager automates the creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots for volumes or instances selected by tag. One policy can have several schedules, such as hourly snapshots kept for 48 hours and daily snapshots kept for 30 days.

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that runs every hour and invokes an AWS Lambda function to snapshot the volumes.
options.rationale: Custom code must handle creating, keeping, and deleting snapshots, which Data Lifecycle Manager provides natively.

options.text: Enable fast snapshot restore for the tagged volumes.
options.rationale: Fast snapshot restore speeds up creating volumes from existing snapshots. It does not create snapshots.

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling scheduled action that creates snapshots of the volumes every hour.
options.rationale: Auto Scaling scheduled actions change a group's capacity. They cannot create EBS snapshots.

questions.question:
A company stores application logs in Amazon S3 Standard. The logs are read often for 30 days and rarely after that. The logs must be kept for 1 year for compliance and must be retrievable within hours. After 1 year, the logs must be deleted.

Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days and expires objects after 365 days.
options.rationale: S3 Lifecycle moves objects to a lower-cost storage class and deletes them at the end of the retention period without custom code. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval costs less than S3 Standard-IA and supports retrieval within hours, which meets the requirement.

options.text: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration that transitions objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and expires objects after 365 days.
options.rationale: This meets the requirements, but S3 Standard-IA costs more than S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for logs that are rarely read and can wait hours for retrieval.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function that runs each day to copy objects older than 30 days to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and delete objects older than 1 year.
options.rationale: This re-creates what a lifecycle rule does for free, and the company would have to maintain the code.

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 1 year. Keep all objects in S3 Standard for the full retention period.
options.rationale: Object Lock prevents deletion, which the requirement does not ask for, and keeping everything in S3 Standard is the most expensive choice.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer accidentally deleted several Amazon EBS snapshots and AMIs that were needed for recovery. The company must be able to recover deleted snapshots and AMIs for 14 days after they are deleted.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Create Recycle Bin retention rules for EBS snapshots and for AMIs with a 14-day retention period.
options.rationale: Recycle Bin keeps deleted EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs for the retention period of a matching rule. During that time you can recover them, and after that they are permanently deleted.

options.text: Enable AWS Config recording to restore deleted snapshots and AMIs from configuration history.
options.rationale: Config records configuration history. It cannot restore the data in a deleted snapshot.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon EBS to re-create each deleted snapshot from the trail.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records the delete API call. The snapshot data is gone and cannot be rebuilt from a log.

options.text: Add an IAM policy that denies ec2:DeleteSnapshot to all users, including the backup automation role.
options.rationale: Denying all deletions breaks the backup automation's retention cleanup, and snapshot costs would grow without limit.

questions.question:
A company has a production Amazon RDS for MySQL database. At 14:05, a developer accidentally ran a DELETE statement without a WHERE clause. Automated backups are enabled with a 7-day retention period. The company needs the data as it was at 14:04.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Restore the DB instance to a point in time of 14:04 as a new DB instance. Point the application to it.
options.rationale: Point-in-time restore uses automated backups and transaction logs to create a new DB instance at any second within the retention period, up to about 5 minutes before the current time. A restore always creates a new instance, so the application must be pointed to the new endpoint, or the instances must be renamed.

options.text: Restore the most recent daily automated snapshot onto the existing DB instance to overwrite its current data.
options.rationale: RDS restores always create a new DB instance. You cannot restore a snapshot onto an existing instance, and a daily snapshot would lose more data.

options.text: Promote the Multi-AZ standby instance, because the standby still has the data from before 14:05.
options.rationale: The standby is synchronously replicated, so the DELETE was applied to it as well.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance. Promote the replica to recover the data from before 14:05.
options.rationale: A new replica copies the current data, which already has the rows deleted.

questions.question:
A company runs a stateless web application on a single Amazon EC2 instance in one Availability Zone. An outage in the Availability Zone took the application offline. The application must remain available if an Availability Zone fails and must replace failed instances automatically.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group that spans multiple Availability Zones. Place an Application Load Balancer in front of the group.
options.rationale: An Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones replaces failed instances and rebalances capacity. An Application Load Balancer sends traffic only to healthy targets in the zones that are still working. This is the standard pattern for a highly available stateless application.

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group in the existing Availability Zone. Set the minimum capacity of the group to 4 instances.
options.rationale: All instances are still in one Availability Zone, so an outage in that zone stops the application.

options.text: Change the instance to a larger instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that uses the EC2 recover action.
options.rationale: The recover action helps with hardware problems on one instance. It does not protect against the loss of the whole Availability Zone.

options.text: Launch a second instance in another Availability Zone. Create an Amazon Route 53 simple record with both IP addresses.
options.rationale: A simple record has no health checks, so clients still receive the failed instance's IP address, and nothing replaces failed instances.

questions.question:
A company runs a production database on a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The database must fail over automatically if the Availability Zone fails. Committed transactions must not be lost, and the application must continue to use the same endpoint.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Modify the DB instance to use a Multi-AZ deployment with a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone.
options.rationale: A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone. Amazon RDS fails over automatically and updates the DNS record of the DB endpoint, so the application reconnects to the same endpoint.

options.text: Create a read replica in another Availability Zone. Promote the read replica during an Availability Zone outage.
options.rationale: Replication to a read replica is asynchronous, so committed transactions can be lost. Promotion is manual, and the replica has a different endpoint.

options.text: Take a manual snapshot every hour. Restore the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone during an outage.
options.rationale: A restore loses the changes made since the last snapshot, and the restored DB instance has a new endpoint.

options.text: Install PostgreSQL on an Amazon EC2 instance in another Availability Zone. Configure log shipping to the instance.
options.rationale: The company would have to patch and fail over this database itself, and log shipping does not fail over automatically.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon DynamoDB table with point-in-time recovery enabled. A bug in a deployment 2 hours ago overwrote attributes in thousands of items. The company needs the data as it was before the bug.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Restore the table to a point in time before the deployment as a new table. Copy the needed data back.
options.rationale: Point-in-time recovery restores a table to any second within its recovery period, which can be set from 1 to 35 days. The restore always creates a new table, so the team can copy the correct items back or switch the application to the restored table.

options.text: Restore the table in place to a point in time before the deployment.
options.rationale: DynamoDB cannot restore a table in place. Every restore creates a new table.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams, and replay the stream records from the last 2 hours in reverse order.
options.rationale: Turning on Streams now captures only future changes, so the earlier values are not available this way.

options.text: Use the on-demand backup that DynamoDB created automatically when point-in-time recovery was enabled.
options.rationale: Turning on point-in-time recovery does not create an on-demand backup. The two are separate features.

questions.question:
A global ecommerce company needs its Amazon DynamoDB shopping cart table to accept writes in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 at the same time. Changes must replicate between the AWS Regions automatically, and the application must continue to work if one Region fails.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Convert the table to a DynamoDB global table with replicas in both Regions.
options.rationale: Global tables provide multi-Region, multi-active replication. Applications can read and write in each replica Region, DynamoDB replicates changes automatically, and the application can keep working in one Region if the other fails.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams. Use an AWS Lambda function to copy writes to a table in the other Region.
options.rationale: Custom stream replication is code to build and operate, and handling conflicts and failures yourself is complex.

options.text: Take on-demand backups every hour, and restore them in the other Region.
options.rationale: Hourly backups lose up to an hour of carts, and restored tables are separate copies that cannot both accept writes and stay in sync.

options.text: Use AWS Backup to copy the table to the other Region every 15 minutes.
options.rationale: Periodic copies are not live replicas, so the second Region cannot accept writes that stay in sync.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon S3 bucket with versioning enabled. A user accidentally deleted an important report with a simple DELETE request that did not specify a version ID. The report no longer appears in the bucket listing.

How can a CloudOps engineer restore the report with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Delete the delete marker that is now the current version of the object.
options.rationale: In a versioned bucket, a simple DELETE adds a delete marker as the current version and keeps the earlier versions. Removing the delete marker makes the previous version current again, so the report reappears.

options.text: Rebuild the object from the S3 server access logs that recorded the upload.
options.rationale: Server access logs record requests, not object contents, so they cannot rebuild the report.

options.text: Create a new bucket with versioning enabled. Copy the object back from it.
options.rationale: A new bucket does not contain the deleted object, so there is nothing to copy back.

options.text: Ask AWS Support to recover the object from the bucket's deleted storage.
options.rationale: No support request is needed, because the earlier version is still stored in the bucket.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon S3 bucket with versioning enabled. The bucket stores files that are overwritten many times each day. Storage costs continue to rise because every old version is kept indefinitely. The company must be able to recover overwritten files for 30 days.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that permanently deletes noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent.
options.rationale: The NoncurrentVersionExpiration action deletes old versions a set number of days after they are replaced. Overwritten files stay recoverable for 30 days, and storage no longer grows without limit.

options.text: Suspend versioning on the bucket to stop keeping old versions of the overwritten files.
options.rationale: Suspending versioning stops keeping new versions, so overwritten files could no longer be recovered, and existing old versions would remain.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that expires the current versions of all objects 30 days after creation.
options.rationale: Expiring current versions deletes live files, which the company does not want, and it does not remove old versions.

options.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering to move the old versions to a cheaper tier after 30 days.
options.rationale: Intelligent-Tiering lowers the price of data that is not accessed, but it keeps every version forever, so costs still grow.

questions.question:
A company stores trading records in Amazon S3. Regulations require that no user can overwrite or delete a record for 5 years. Separately, the company's legal team sometimes needs to keep specific records indefinitely during an investigation.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock. Set a default retention of 5 years in compliance mode.
options.rationale: Object Lock in compliance mode prevents every user, including the root user, from overwriting or deleting a protected version until its retention period ends, and the retention period cannot be shortened.

options.text: Place a legal hold on specific object versions during an investigation.
options.rationale: A legal hold prevents an object version from being deleted or overwritten until the hold is removed. It has no expiration date, which suits investigations of unknown length.

options.text: Set a default retention of 5 years in governance mode with no extra permissions.
options.rationale: Users with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can delete objects in governance mode, so it does not meet a rule that applies to every user.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies s3:DeleteObject to every user except the root user.
options.rationale: Administrators can change a bucket policy, and the root user would still be able to delete records.

options.text: Enable MFA delete.
options.rationale: MFA delete makes deletions harder, but the root user can still delete versions, and it does not set a retention period.

questions.question:
A company enables Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication from a bucket in us-east-1 to a bucket in us-west-2 for disaster recovery. New objects replicate correctly, but the 2 million objects that existed before replication was configured are missing from the destination. The company also needs 99.9% of new objects replicated within 15 minutes.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run an S3 Batch Replication job to replicate the existing objects.
options.rationale: Replication rules apply only to objects written after the rule is created. S3 Batch Replication replicates existing objects, and objects that failed to replicate before, on demand.

options.text: Enable S3 Replication Time Control for the replication rule.
options.rationale: Replication Time Control replicates most new objects in seconds and 99.9% of them within 15 minutes, backed by a service level agreement, and it adds replication metrics and notifications.

options.text: Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration for the source bucket.
options.rationale: Transfer Acceleration speeds up client transfers to a bucket. It does not affect replication.

options.text: Suspend and then resume versioning on the source bucket.
options.rationale: Changing the versioning state does not replicate existing objects, and replication requires versioning to stay enabled.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that copies existing objects to us-west-2.
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules transition or expire objects. They cannot copy objects to another Region.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server share. Users often overwrite documents by mistake and open tickets to get earlier versions back. Users must be able to restore earlier versions of their files themselves from Windows File Explorer.

What should a CloudOps engineer configure to meet this requirement?

options.text: Enable shadow copies for the FSx file system on a regular schedule.
options.rationale: Shadow copies are point-in-time snapshots of the file system that Windows users can browse on the Previous Versions tab in File Explorer. Users can restore earlier versions of their own files without opening a ticket.

options.text: Configure daily automatic backups of the FSx file system with 30-day retention.
options.rationale: Automatic backups protect the whole file system, but restoring one creates a new file system. That needs an administrator and does not give users self-service restores.

options.text: Enable Amazon S3 Versioning for the bucket that stores the FSx file system data.
options.rationale: FSx for Windows File Server data is not stored in a bucket that you manage, so there is no S3 Versioning to enable.

options.text: Configure data deduplication for the FSx file system to keep copies of changes.
options.rationale: Deduplication saves storage by removing duplicate data. It does not keep earlier versions of files.

questions.question:
A company copies the AMIs of its application servers from us-east-1 to us-west-2 for disaster recovery. The AMIs' Amazon EBS snapshots are encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key that is in us-east-1. The copies must be encrypted with a customer managed key.

What must a CloudOps engineer specify when copying the AMIs?

options.text: A KMS key in us-west-2 to encrypt the copied snapshots, because KMS keys are Regional.
options.rationale: KMS keys are Regional, so a key in us-east-1 cannot encrypt data in us-west-2. When you copy an AMI with encrypted snapshots to another Region, you specify a key in the destination Region, such as a customer managed key or a replica of a multi-Region key.

options.text: The same KMS key ARN from us-east-1, because AMI copies keep the source Region's key.
options.rationale: A single-Region key exists only in its own Region and cannot encrypt the copies in us-west-2.

options.text: No key at all, because AMI copies across Regions are always left unencrypted by default.
options.rationale: Copies of encrypted snapshots are always encrypted. They cannot become unencrypted.

options.text: The AWS owned key for EBS, because customer managed keys cannot be used across Regions.
options.rationale: EBS uses the AWS managed key aws/ebs by default, not an AWS owned key. Customer managed keys work as long as the key is in the destination Region.

questions.question:
A company has an internal wiki. During a Regional disaster, the wiki can be down for up to 24 hours, and losing up to 12 hours of data is acceptable. The company needs the lowest-cost disaster recovery strategy.

Which strategy should a CloudOps engineer implement?

options.text: Backup and restore, with backups copied to a second Region
options.rationale: Backup and restore costs the least because nothing runs in the recovery Region until a disaster. Copying backups to a second Region every few hours meets a 12-hour RPO, and rebuilding from infrastructure as code and backups fits a 24-hour RTO.

options.text: Pilot light, with a live database replica in a second Region
options.rationale: Pilot light keeps core components such as a database replica running all the time, which costs more than these targets need.

options.text: Warm standby, with a scaled-down copy running in a second Region
options.rationale: Warm standby runs a scaled-down copy of the whole workload, which costs more than a 24-hour RTO requires.

options.text: Multi-site active/active across two Regions
options.rationale: Active/active gives near-zero RTO and RPO at the highest cost, far beyond what the wiki needs.

questions.question:
A company has an order system that must recover from a Regional disaster within 4 hours with no more than 5 minutes of data loss. To keep costs low, the company does not want application servers running in the recovery AWS Region.

Which disaster recovery strategy will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Pilot light: replicate the database continuously, and keep application servers off until failover
options.rationale: Pilot light keeps the core data, such as a cross-Region database replica, continuously up to date, which meets a 5-minute RPO. Application servers are created from AMIs and infrastructure as code only during a failover, which fits a 4-hour RTO at low cost.

options.text: Backup and restore: copy nightly database snapshots to the recovery Region, and rebuild there
options.rationale: Nightly snapshots could lose up to a day of orders, which fails the 5-minute RPO.

options.text: Warm standby: run a scaled-down copy of every tier in the recovery Region
options.rationale: Warm standby meets the targets but keeps application servers running all the time, which the company wants to avoid.

options.text: Multi-site active/active: serve traffic from both Regions at all times
options.rationale: Active/active has the highest cost and runs full capacity in both Regions.

questions.question:
A company has a customer-facing application that must recover from a Regional disaster in under 15 minutes with an RPO of seconds. The company is willing to pay for a smaller, always-running copy of the workload in the recovery AWS Region, but not for full duplicate capacity.

Which disaster recovery strategy will meet these requirements?

options.text: Warm standby
options.rationale: Warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully working copy of the workload in the recovery Region, with data replicated continuously. During a disaster, the copy scales up and takes traffic within minutes.

options.text: Pilot light
options.rationale: Pilot light keeps only core components running, so application servers must be started and scaled during failover, which usually takes longer than 15 minutes.

options.text: Backup and restore
options.rationale: Backup and restore rebuilds everything from backups, which takes hours and loses the data written since the last backup.

options.text: Multi-site active/active
options.rationale: Active/active meets the targets but runs full capacity in both Regions, which the company does not want to pay for.

questions.question:
A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance in us-east-1 and keeps a cross-Region read replica in us-west-2 for disaster recovery. During a Regional outage drill, the database in us-west-2 must start accepting writes.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Promote the read replica in us-west-2 to a standalone DB instance. Point the application to it.
options.rationale: Promoting a read replica stops replication and turns the replica into a standalone DB instance that accepts writes. Applications then connect to the promoted instance's endpoint, often through a DNS record that is updated during the failover.

options.text: Start a Multi-AZ failover on the primary instance.
options.rationale: Multi-AZ failover switches to a standby in the same Region. It does not involve cross-Region read replicas, and it cannot run if the primary Region is down.

options.text: Change the replica's parameter group to set read_only to 0, and then reboot the replica instance.
options.rationale: RDS manages replication on read replicas. Changing a parameter does not turn a replica into a writable primary.

options.text: Restore the latest snapshot of the primary instance in us-west-2. Delete the read replica afterward.
options.rationale: Restoring a snapshot loses data written since the snapshot and takes longer than promoting the replica, which already has current data.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon EC2 instance in us-east-1a with an Amazon EBS data volume that has hourly snapshots. The us-east-1a Availability Zone is impaired, and the company needs the data online on a new instance in us-east-1b.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Create a new volume from the latest snapshot in us-east-1b. Attach it to the new instance.
options.rationale: EBS snapshots are stored regionally, so a volume can be created from a snapshot in any Availability Zone in the Region. The new volume in us-east-1b holds the data as of the last snapshot.

options.text: Detach the volume in us-east-1a, and attach it directly to the new instance in us-east-1b.
options.rationale: An EBS volume can be attached only to instances in its own Availability Zone.

options.text: Copy the snapshot to us-east-1b first, because each EBS snapshot is stored only in the zone of its volume.
options.rationale: Snapshots are already available to every zone in the Region. Snapshot copies are for moving snapshots between Regions or accounts, or for changing encryption.

options.text: Configure EBS Multi-Attach.
options.rationale: Multi-Attach works only for io1 and io2 volumes and only with instances in the same Availability Zone.

questions.question:
A company keeps automated backups for an Amazon RDS database for 35 days, the maximum. A new policy requires monthly backups to be kept for 1 year and then deleted automatically.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan with a monthly rule for the database and a 1-year retention period.
options.rationale: AWS Backup can take monthly snapshots of RDS databases, keep them for the retention period that you set, and delete them automatically. These snapshots are not limited by the 35-day window for automated backups.

options.text: Change the automated backup retention period of the DB instance from 35 days to 365 days.
options.rationale: The maximum retention for RDS automated backups is 35 days, so 365 days is not allowed.

options.text: Ask a CloudOps engineer to take a manual snapshot each month and delete snapshots older than 1 year.
options.rationale: Manual snapshots meet the retention need, but taking and deleting them by hand is effort and easy to forget.

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ for the DB instance.
options.rationale: A Multi-AZ standby is a live copy for failover. It does not keep historical backups.

questions.question:
A company backs up Amazon EC2 instances that run Microsoft SQL Server on Windows. Restores from crash-consistent backups sometimes require database recovery steps. The company needs application-consistent backups without stopping the instances.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable Windows VSS in the AWS Backup plan for the EC2 instances.
options.rationale: With the Windows VSS option enabled, AWS Backup uses the Volume Shadow Copy Service through SSM Agent to quiesce applications such as SQL Server before the snapshot. This creates application-consistent backups without stopping the instance. The instance needs SSM Agent and the required IAM permissions.

options.text: Stop the instances before each backup by using a scheduled AWS Lambda function.
options.rationale: Stopping instances gives consistent backups but causes downtime, which the company wants to avoid.

options.text: Take Amazon EBS snapshots of each volume at different times to spread the I/O load.
options.rationale: Snapshots taken at different times are not consistent with each other, which makes the problem worse.

options.text: Configure fast snapshot restore for the snapshots that AWS Backup creates.
options.rationale: Fast snapshot restore speeds up volume creation. It does not make backups application consistent.

questions.question:
A company completes a business impact analysis for its billing system. The system can lose at most 15 minutes of data and must be back online within 2 hours after a disaster.

Which statement correctly describes these targets?

options.text: The RPO is 15 minutes, and the RTO is 2 hours.
options.rationale: The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as the time since the last recovery point, which is 15 minutes here. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service, which is 2 hours.

options.text: The RTO is 15 minutes, and the RPO is 2 hours.
options.rationale: This reverses the definitions. RTO is about downtime, and RPO is about data loss.

options.text: The RPO and the RTO are both 2 hours and 15 minutes.
options.rationale: RPO and RTO are separate targets. They are not added together.

options.text: The RPO is 2 hours, and the SLA is 15 minutes.
options.rationale: The 2-hour target is the RTO, and an SLA is a service commitment, not a data loss target.

questions.question:
A company must be able to restore the objects in an Amazon S3 bucket to their state at any point in the past 14 days after accidental bulk changes. Versioning is already enabled for the bucket.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Backup continuous backups for the bucket with 14-day retention. Restore to a point in time.
options.rationale: AWS Backup supports continuous backups for Amazon S3, which allow restores to any point in time within a retention period of up to 35 days. The bucket must have versioning enabled, which it already does.

options.text: Write a script that reads all object versions and copies the versions from the chosen time back into place.
options.rationale: This can work, but writing and testing a script that rebuilds a bucket from its versions is a lot of effort and error prone.

options.text: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication.
options.rationale: Replication copies changes as they happen, including the accidental changes, so the replica would not keep the older state.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves noncurrent versions to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 14 days.
options.rationale: Moving old versions to Deep Archive reduces cost but makes them slow to restore, and it does not provide a point-in-time restore.

questions.question:
A company builds its golden AMI manually each month. A CloudOps engineer launches an Amazon EC2 instance; installs patches, the Amazon CloudWatch agent, and security hardening; creates an AMI; and copies the AMI to three AWS Regions. The process takes a day and sometimes misses steps.

Which solution will automate this process with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an EC2 Image Builder pipeline with a recipe, test components, a monthly schedule, and distribution to the three Regions.
options.rationale: EC2 Image Builder automates building, testing, and distributing images. A recipe lists the base image and components such as patching, the CloudWatch agent, and hardening. Test components validate the image, a schedule runs the pipeline monthly, and distribution settings copy the AMI to other Regions and accounts.

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function that launches an instance, runs a script with Run Command, creates an AMI, and copies it to each Region.
options.rationale: This works, but it is custom code that must handle failures, testing, and cleanup, which Image Builder already provides.

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group whose user data installs everything. Create an AMI from the newest instance each month.
options.rationale: Creating AMIs from running instances is not repeatable or tested, and running the install in user data adds boot time to every launch.

options.text: Use AWS CloudFormation to launch an instance each month with cfn-init. Create the AMI manually after the stack completes.
options.rationale: The AMI step is still manual, and there is no built-in testing or multi-Region distribution.

questions.question:
A company has development Amazon EC2 instances that are used only during business hours. The instances must stop at 19:00 and must start at 07:00 on weekdays.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedules that start the AWS-StopEC2Instance and AWS-StartEC2Instance Automation runbooks.
options.rationale: EventBridge Scheduler runs on a cron schedule with no servers to manage, and it can start AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks. The AWS-StopEC2Instance and AWS-StartEC2Instance runbooks already exist, so no custom code is needed.

options.text: Create a cron job on a separate EC2 instance that runs AWS CLI commands to stop and start the development instances.
options.rationale: The separate instance must itself be patched, monitored, and kept running, which adds work.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function for each instance. Run each function from a cron job on an on-premises server.
options.rationale: This needs custom code for each instance and depends on an on-premises server to run the schedule.

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group for the instances. Set the group's capacity to 0 each evening to terminate the instances.
options.rationale: Scaling to 0 terminates the instances instead of stopping them, so development data on local volumes can be lost.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer shares an AMI with another AWS account. The AMI's snapshots are encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key. Users in the other account can see the AMI, but their launches fail with a KMS error.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Update the KMS key policy to allow the other account to use the key. Have that account grant its users access.
options.rationale: To launch an AMI with encrypted snapshots, the other account needs permission to use the KMS key, such as kms:Decrypt, kms:DescribeKey, kms:CreateGrant, and kms:ReEncrypt*. The key policy must allow the other account, and that account's IAM policies must allow its users. The other account can also copy the AMI and re-encrypt it with its own key.

options.text: Re-encrypt the snapshots with the AWS managed key aws/ebs to allow the other account to use the AMI.
options.rationale: Snapshots encrypted with the AWS managed key cannot be shared with other accounts, because the policy of that key cannot be changed.

options.text: Make the AMI public to allow any account to launch it without access to the KMS key.
options.rationale: AMIs with encrypted snapshots cannot be made public, and public images are a security risk.

options.text: Share the AMI with the whole organization instead of sharing it with only the one account.
options.rationale: Sharing with an organization still requires access to the KMS key, so launches would fail in the same way.

questions.question:
A company has a CI pipeline that pushes a new container image to an Amazon ECR repository on every commit. The repository now has thousands of untagged images, and storage costs are rising. The company needs only the last 20 release images and no untagged images older than 7 days.

Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Add an ECR lifecycle policy that expires untagged images after 7 days and keeps the last 20 release images.
options.rationale: ECR lifecycle policies expire images automatically based on rules such as tag status, tag prefix, image count, and image age. One policy can expire untagged images older than 7 days and keep only the 20 newest images with a release tag prefix.

options.text: Add a step to the CI pipeline that lists and deletes old images after each push by using the AWS CLI.
options.rationale: Custom cleanup in the pipeline is code to maintain, and it runs only when the pipeline runs.

options.text: Configure ECR replication to another Region. Delete the source repository once each month.
options.rationale: Replication copies images. Deleting the repository each month would destroy images that are still needed.

options.text: Enable enhanced scanning to have Amazon Inspector delete the old and vulnerable images.
options.rationale: Enhanced scanning finds vulnerabilities. It does not delete images.

questions.question:
A company's security team requires all container images in Amazon ECR to be scanned for vulnerabilities in both operating system packages and programming language packages when the images are pushed. Images also must be rescanned automatically when new CVEs are published.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable enhanced scanning for the registry with continuous scanning, which uses Amazon Inspector.
options.rationale: Enhanced scanning integrates Amazon ECR with Amazon Inspector. It scans images for operating system and programming language package vulnerabilities on push and keeps rescanning them as new vulnerabilities are published.

options.text: Configure basic scanning with scan on push for each repository in the registry.
options.rationale: Basic scanning checks operating system packages when images are pushed or scanned manually. It does not rescan images continuously or cover language packages.

options.text: Run a vulnerability scanner in the CI pipeline before each image is pushed to the registry.
options.rationale: A pipeline scan checks the image once, before it is pushed. It does not rescan stored images when new CVEs appear.

options.text: Configure Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for the Amazon ECS clusters that run the images.
options.rationale: Runtime Monitoring detects threats in running workloads. It does not scan images for known vulnerabilities.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS CloudFormation template that hardcodes Amazon Linux AMI IDs for each AWS Region in a Mappings section. The IDs go out of date, and new stacks launch old, unpatched images.

How should a CloudOps engineer ensure that the template always uses the latest Amazon Linux AMI?

options.text: Use an SSM parameter type that reads the latest AMI ID from the public AWS Systems Manager parameter.
options.rationale: AWS publishes the latest Amazon Linux AMI IDs as public Systems Manager parameters, such as /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64. A template parameter of type AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id> resolves the current ID in each Region when the stack is created or updated.

options.text: Add a Lambda-backed custom resource that searches for the newest image by name in each Region.
options.rationale: A custom resource works, but it is code to maintain, and the public parameters already provide this data.

options.text: Update the Mappings section manually each month with the latest AMI IDs for every Region.
options.rationale: Manual updates are what caused the problem. They are slow and easy to forget.

options.text: Set the ImageId property to latest.
options.rationale: ImageId must be a real AMI ID. Amazon EC2 does not accept latest as a value.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer needs to update a production AWS CloudFormation stack that contains an Amazon RDS DB instance. Before the update runs, the CloudOps engineer must confirm that no resource will be replaced.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Create a change set. Review the Replacement value for each resource before executing it.
options.rationale: A change set shows how an update will change each resource before anything happens, including whether each resource will be replaced (True, False, or Conditional). The engineer can review it and execute it only if it is safe.

options.text: Run drift detection on the stack, and check whether the database shows a status of MODIFIED.
options.rationale: Drift detection compares resources with the current template. It does not preview the changes in a new template.

options.text: Update the stack directly with termination protection enabled.
options.rationale: Termination protection prevents the whole stack from being deleted. It does not stop an update from replacing a resource.

options.text: Delete the stack with a Retain deletion policy. Create a new stack from the updated template.
options.rationale: Deleting and re-creating the stack is risky and unnecessary just to preview changes.

questions.question:
A company's security audit finds that a security group created by an AWS CloudFormation stack allows SSH from 0.0.0.0/0, but the template does not include that rule. A CloudOps engineer suspects that someone changed the security group in the AWS Management Console.

Which CloudFormation feature will confirm this and show the difference?

options.text: Drift detection on the stack
options.rationale: Drift detection compares the current configuration of stack resources with the configuration that the template expects. It reports the security group as MODIFIED and shows the exact property differences, such as the extra ingress rule.

options.text: A change set for the stack
options.rationale: A change set previews the changes from a new template. It does not detect changes made outside CloudFormation.

options.text: A stack policy on the stack
options.rationale: A stack policy limits which resources stack updates can change. It does not detect or block console changes.

options.text: Termination protection on the stack
options.rationale: Termination protection prevents the stack from being deleted. It does not detect changes.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS CloudFormation stack that contains an Amazon RDS DB instance. A final snapshot must be created if the stack is deleted and also if a stack update replaces the DB instance.

Which attributes should a CloudOps engineer set on the DB instance resource to meet these requirements?

options.text: DeletionPolicy: Snapshot and UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot
options.rationale: DeletionPolicy controls what happens when the resource is removed from the stack or the stack is deleted. UpdateReplacePolicy controls what happens to the old resource when an update replaces it. Snapshot on both creates a final DB snapshot in each case.

options.text: DeletionPolicy: Retain and a stack policy that denies Update:*
options.rationale: Retain keeps the instance instead of taking a snapshot, and denying all updates blocks legitimate changes.

options.text: DependsOn the stack's Amazon S3 bucket and UpdatePolicy: Snapshot
options.rationale: DependsOn controls creation order, and UpdatePolicy applies to resources such as Auto Scaling groups. Neither creates snapshots.

options.text: A CreationPolicy with a ResourceSignal and DeletionPolicy: Delete
options.rationale: A CreationPolicy waits for signals during creation, and a Delete policy removes the instance without a snapshot.

questions.question:
A company uses an AWS CloudFormation stack to manage a production web tier and a production database. The company updates the web tier often. Stack updates must never modify or replace the database unless someone explicitly overrides the protection.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Apply a stack policy that denies Update:* on the database resource and allows updates on all other resources.
options.rationale: A stack policy defines which resources stack updates can change. Denying Update:* on the database protects it from modification and replacement, while the rest of the stack can still change. A temporary override policy can be supplied with an update when a database change is really needed.

options.text: Enable termination protection for the stack to prevent updates to the database resource.
options.rationale: Termination protection prevents deleting the stack. It does not stop updates.

options.text: Set a DeletionPolicy of Retain on the database to prevent updates to any of its properties.
options.rationale: DeletionPolicy affects deletion, not updates. An update could still modify or replace the database.

options.text: Create an IAM policy that denies the cloudformation:UpdateStack action for every user in the account.
options.rationale: Denying all stack updates also blocks the frequent web tier changes.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS CloudFormation stack that creates an Auto Scaling group. The group's instances install an application through user data. The stack reports CREATE_COMPLETE before the application is installed, and sometimes the installation fails without the stack noticing.

How should a CloudOps engineer make the stack wait for a successful installation?

options.text: Add a CreationPolicy to the group. Run cfn-signal at the end of the user data script.
options.rationale: A CreationPolicy makes CloudFormation wait for a set number of success signals within a timeout before it marks the resource complete. cfn-signal sends success or failure based on the script's exit code, and a failure or timeout makes the stack roll back.

options.text: Add a DependsOn attribute to the group to wait for the user data script to finish.
options.rationale: DependsOn orders resource creation inside the stack. It cannot see whether a script inside an instance has finished.

options.text: Add a stack output that checks the application URL to make the stack wait for a response.
options.rationale: Outputs are values that the stack returns. They do not test URLs or make the stack wait.

options.text: Increase the stack's timeout to make CloudFormation wait longer before it reports success.
options.rationale: The stack timeout limits how long the stack can take. It does not make CloudFormation wait for the installation.

questions.question:
A company launches Amazon EC2 instances by using an AWS CloudFormation stack. The instances are configured by cfn-init from AWS::CloudFormation::Init metadata. A CloudOps engineer changes a configuration file in the metadata and updates the stack, but the running instances do not get the new file.

What should the CloudOps engineer do so that running instances apply metadata changes automatically?

options.text: Run the cfn-hup daemon on the instances to detect metadata changes and rerun cfn-init.
options.rationale: cfn-hup is a helper daemon that polls the resource metadata for changes. When it detects a change, it runs the actions in its hooks, typically cfn-init, so running instances apply the new configuration without being replaced.

options.text: Add the configuration file to the user data to run it again on every stack update.
options.rationale: User data runs only at first launch by default, so changing it does not update running instances.

options.text: Enable drift detection to make CloudFormation push the new file to the instances.
options.rationale: Drift detection reports differences. It does not change resources or push files.

options.text: Add an UpdatePolicy to the instances to make cfn-init read the metadata on each boot.
options.rationale: UpdatePolicy applies to resources such as Auto Scaling groups during updates. It does not make instances rerun cfn-init.

questions.question:
A company's CloudOps engineers deploy AWS infrastructure with Terraform from their own workstations. Each engineer keeps a local copy of the Terraform state file. Twice, one engineer's apply overwrote changes that another engineer had made. The company must keep one shared state and must prevent two engineers from changing the state at the same time.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure an Amazon S3 backend for the state, with bucket versioning and encryption. Enable state locking for the backend.
options.rationale: The S3 backend keeps one shared state file. Versioning lets the team recover an earlier state, and encryption protects secrets that the state can contain. State locking makes a second operation wait or fail instead of overwriting the state. Current Terraform versions lock with a lock file in the bucket (use_lockfile); locking with an Amazon DynamoDB table is deprecated.

options.text: Commit the state file to the Git repository. Require each engineer to pull the latest commit before each apply.
options.rationale: State files can contain secrets, and Git has no lock, so two engineers can still apply from different copies of the state.

options.text: Store the state file on a shared Amazon EFS file system. Ask the engineers to take turns running terraform apply.
options.rationale: A shared file system gives one copy, but taking turns is a manual process with no lock, so conflicts can still happen.

options.text: Run terraform apply -refresh-only before each apply. Keep a separate copy of the state file on each engineer's workstation.
options.rationale: A refresh-only run updates each local copy from the real resources, but each engineer still has a separate state, and nothing stops two applies at the same time.

questions.question:
An AWS CloudFormation stack update failed, and the rollback also failed because someone deleted one of the stack's resources outside CloudFormation. The stack is now in the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to return the stack to a working state?

options.text: Continue the update rollback, and skip the resource that was deleted outside CloudFormation.
options.rationale: From UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, you can continue the update rollback and list resources to skip, such as one that no longer exists. CloudFormation marks the skipped resources as complete and finishes the rollback to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, after which the stack can be updated again.

options.text: Delete the stack. Create a new stack from the original template with the same name.
options.rationale: Deleting and re-creating the stack is disruptive and could delete production resources that still work.

options.text: Run drift detection on the stack, and then execute the most recent change set again.
options.rationale: Drift detection only reports differences, and a change set cannot be executed while the stack is in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED.

options.text: Update the stack again with the new template, because updates are allowed in this state.
options.rationale: A stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED cannot be updated until its rollback is continued and completes.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS CloudFormation networking stack that exports its VPC ID. Three application stacks read the ID by using Fn::ImportValue. A CloudOps engineer tries to update the networking stack to rename the export, and the update fails.

Why does the update fail?

options.text: An export cannot be changed or removed while another stack imports it.
options.rationale: CloudFormation blocks changes to, and deletion of, an output export that other stacks import. The engineer must first update the importing stacks to stop using the export, and then change it.

options.text: Exports can be renamed only by deleting and re-creating the networking stack.
options.rationale: Re-creating the networking stack is not required, and deleting it would also be blocked while the export is in use.

options.text: Fn::ImportValue works only between stacks that are nested in the same parent.
options.rationale: Fn::ImportValue works between any stacks in the same account and Region. Nested stacks are not required.

options.text: The networking stack needs termination protection before exports can change.
options.rationale: Termination protection prevents stack deletion. It has nothing to do with changing exports.

questions.question:
Several teams at a company copy the same 300 lines of AWS CloudFormation code for a standard load balancer and Auto Scaling setup into their own templates. When the standard changes, each copy must be updated manually, and some copies no longer match the standard.

Which solution will reduce this duplication?

options.text: Move the standard setup into its own template. Use it in each stack as a nested stack.
options.rationale: Nested stacks let a template include another template through an AWS::CloudFormation::Stack resource. The standard setup lives in one template that every team uses as a nested stack, so a change to the standard is made in one place.

options.text: Add the standard setup to a Mappings section that every template copies from a shared file.
options.rationale: Mappings hold static lookup values. They cannot hold resources, and copying a file still duplicates it.

options.text: Use Fn::ImportValue to import the 300 lines of resources from a stack that one team owns.
options.rationale: Fn::ImportValue imports output values, such as IDs. It cannot import resource definitions.

options.text: Enable drift detection for every stack.
options.rationale: Drift detection compares stacks with their own templates. It does not keep templates in sync with each other.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS CloudFormation template that creates an Amazon RDS DB instance. The master password is passed as a plaintext parameter and appears in deployment logs. The password is already stored in AWS Secrets Manager.

How should a CloudOps engineer supply the password without exposing it?

options.text: Use a dynamic reference such as {{resolve:secretsmanager:prod-db:SecretString:password}}.
options.rationale: Dynamic references retrieve values from Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store while the stack operation runs. CloudFormation does not store or display the resolved secret value. Setting ManageMasterUserPassword so that RDS manages the secret in Secrets Manager is another option.

options.text: Store the password in the template's Mappings section, and mark the mapping as encrypted.
options.rationale: Mappings are plain text in the template, and there is no encryption setting for them.

options.text: Pass the password as a parameter with a default value.
options.rationale: Default values are stored in plain text in the template, which spreads the secret further.

options.text: Put the password in an exported stack output, and import it into the DB instance resource.
options.rationale: Outputs are visible to anyone who can describe the stack, so this exposes the password further.

questions.question:
A company created dozens of resources manually in the AWS Management Console over several years. The company now needs to manage these existing resources with AWS CloudFormation without re-creating them.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use the CloudFormation IaC generator to scan the resources, generate a template, and import them into a stack.
options.rationale: The IaC generator scans existing resources in the account and generates a template for the resources that you select. You can then import those resources into a new stack, so CloudFormation manages them without re-creating them.

options.text: Write a new template from scratch, deploy it as a stack, and delete the original resources after testing.
options.rationale: Re-creating resources causes downtime and data migration work, which the company wants to avoid.

options.text: Configure drift detection in the account.
options.rationale: Drift detection works only on resources that are already in a stack. It does not adopt unmanaged resources.

options.text: Use AWS Config to export the resource configurations, and upload the export as a CloudFormation stack.
options.rationale: Config configuration items are not CloudFormation templates, and uploading them would not create a valid stack.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer runs cdk deploy for the first time in a new AWS account and AWS Region. The deployment fails with an error that says that the stack uses assets and that the toolkit stack must be deployed to the environment.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Run cdk bootstrap for that account and Region. Run cdk deploy again.
options.rationale: Bootstrapping deploys the CDKToolkit stack, which creates the S3 bucket, ECR repository, and IAM roles that the CDK uses to upload assets and deploy stacks. Each account and Region must be bootstrapped once before you deploy CDK apps that use assets.

options.text: Run cdk synth to create a template. Deploy it manually in the AWS CloudFormation console.
options.rationale: The synthesized template still references assets that must be uploaded to the bootstrap resources, so a manual deployment would also fail.

options.text: Run cdk diff to see the asset differences. Add the assets to the stack manually.
options.rationale: cdk diff only shows changes. It does not create the resources needed for assets.

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 bucket with the same name as the stack. Run cdk deploy again.
options.rationale: The CDK expects its own bootstrap resources and roles, not a bucket named after the stack.

questions.question:
A company manages infrastructure with the AWS CDK. Before each deployment, a reviewer must see exactly which AWS resources and IAM permissions will change compared with the deployed stack.

Which CDK command should a CloudOps engineer run to meet this requirement?

options.text: cdk diff
options.rationale: cdk diff compares the synthesized template with the deployed stack and lists added, changed, and removed resources. It also highlights security-related changes such as IAM policy statements and security group rules.

options.text: cdk synth
options.rationale: cdk synth generates the CloudFormation template, but it does not compare the template with the deployed stack.

options.text: cdk doctor
options.rationale: cdk doctor checks the local CDK setup for problems. It does not show infrastructure changes.

options.text: cdk bootstrap
options.rationale: cdk bootstrap prepares an environment for deployments. It does not preview changes.

questions.question:
A company keeps AWS CloudFormation templates and parameter files in a GitHub repository. Stacks must update automatically whenever changes are merged into the main branch, without a CI/CD pipeline.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable CloudFormation Git sync for each stack, and link it to the repository and branch.
options.rationale: Git sync connects a stack to a Git repository through an AWS CodeConnections connection. When a commit changes the template or deployment file on the tracked branch, CloudFormation updates the stack automatically.

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for GitHub commits that runs cfn-init on the stack's instances.
options.rationale: cfn-init configures software on instances. It does not update stacks, and GitHub commits do not arrive as EventBridge events by default.

options.text: Set up Amazon S3 Event Notifications on a bucket that GitHub copies the templates into after merges.
options.rationale: GitHub does not copy files to a bucket on its own, and this would still need custom code to update the stacks.

options.text: Configure drift detection for each stack.
options.rationale: Drift detection compares resources with their templates. It does not watch a Git repository.

questions.question:
A company has an Auto Scaling group that fails to launch instances during scale-out. The activity history shows that the subnets do not have enough free IP addresses. The group uses one /28 subnet in each of two Availability Zones.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Add larger subnets to the VPC. Add them to the Auto Scaling group.
options.rationale: A /28 subnet has 16 addresses, and AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet, so only 11 are usable. Adding larger subnets, after adding a secondary CIDR block to the VPC if needed, gives the group room to launch instances.

options.text: Change to a larger instance type that needs fewer IP addresses in total.
options.rationale: Every instance still needs at least one private IP address, so larger instances do not fix the shortage, and they cost more.

options.text: Configure auto-assign public IPv4 addresses for the existing subnets.
options.rationale: Public IPv4 addresses do not replace the private addresses that each instance needs from the subnet.

options.text: Release the five IP addresses that AWS reserves in each subnet.
options.rationale: AWS uses the five reserved addresses for the network address, the VPC router, DNS, future use, and broadcast. They cannot be released.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer's IAM user can create AWS CloudFormation stacks. A stack that launches an Amazon EC2 instance with an instance profile fails with an error that says that the user is not authorized to perform iam:PassRole on the role.

What should be done to resolve this issue while following the principle of least privilege?

options.text: Allow iam:PassRole on that specific role's ARN in the engineer's IAM policy.
options.rationale: Passing a role to a service, such as attaching an instance profile to an EC2 instance, requires iam:PassRole on that role. Allowing it only on the specific role ARN, optionally with an iam:PassedToService condition for ec2.amazonaws.com, follows least privilege.

options.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the engineer's IAM user.
options.rationale: Administrator access fixes the error but grants far more than is needed.

options.text: Add the engineer's IAM user as a principal in the trust policy of the instance profile role.
options.rationale: The trust policy decides who can assume the role. Amazon EC2 assumes it here, and the user needs permission to pass it, not to assume it.

options.text: Remove the instance profile from the template.
options.rationale: Removing the instance profile breaks the application's access to AWS services.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS CloudFormation stack that creates a new VPC. The stack fails with the error The maximum number of VPCs has been reached. The account already has 5 VPCs in the AWS Region, and all of them are in use.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Request a VPC quota increase for the Region through Service Quotas, and retry the stack.
options.rationale: The default quota is 5 VPCs per Region, and it is adjustable. Requesting an increase through Service Quotas lets the stack create the VPC once the increase is approved.

options.text: Delete the default VPC's subnets to stop the VPC from counting toward the quota.
options.rationale: Deleting subnets does not remove the VPC, so it still counts toward the quota.

options.text: Add a DependsOn attribute to create the VPC after the other resources in the stack.
options.rationale: The order in which resources are created does not change the account's VPC quota.

options.text: Change the VPC's CIDR block to a smaller range to fit within the current quota.
options.rationale: The quota counts VPCs, not address space, so a smaller CIDR block does not help.

questions.question:
A company has an Auto Scaling group that uses a single instance type in one Availability Zone. During a large scaling event, the group fails to launch instances. The activity history shows InsufficientInstanceCapacity errors.

Which solution will MOST improve the group's ability to launch instances?

options.text: Configure the group to use several instance types across multiple Availability Zones.
options.rationale: InsufficientInstanceCapacity means that AWS does not have enough capacity of that instance type in that Availability Zone at that moment. Allowing more instance types and more zones gives Auto Scaling other capacity pools to launch from. On-Demand Capacity Reservations can guarantee capacity for planned events.

options.text: Increase the group's maximum capacity to retry more launches at once.
options.rationale: Raising the maximum does not create capacity, so more launches would fail in the same way.

options.text: Request a higher quota for On-Demand Instances of that type through Service Quotas.
options.rationale: This error is about AWS capacity in the zone, not the account's quota. A quota error would say that a limit was exceeded.

options.text: Change the group's health check type from EC2 to ELB to replace failed launches.
options.rationale: The health check type affects how running instances are judged. It does not help instances launch.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS CloudFormation template that creates an Amazon S3 bucket with the BucketName property set to app-logs. The stack fails in the first account where the company deploys it, with an error that the bucket already exists.

What should a CloudOps engineer do so that the template can be deployed in any account and AWS Region?

options.text: Remove the BucketName property.
options.rationale: S3 bucket names in the general purpose namespace are globally unique across all AWS accounts, so a fixed name such as app-logs is almost certainly taken. If BucketName is left out, CloudFormation generates a unique name that other resources can reference with Ref. A name can also be built from the account ID and Region.

options.text: Delete any existing bucket called app-logs in the account. Deploy the stack again.
options.rationale: The existing bucket is probably in another AWS account, so it cannot be deleted from this account.

options.text: Add a DeletionPolicy of Retain to the bucket.
options.rationale: A Retain policy affects what happens on deletion. It does not reserve a name.

options.text: Create the stack with termination protection.
options.rationale: Termination protection prevents the stack from being deleted. It has no effect on bucket names.

questions.question:
A company has a launch template that uses Amazon EBS volumes that are encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key. When the Auto Scaling group launches instances, the instances move to the terminated state almost immediately with the reason Client.InternalError: Client error on launch.

What is the MOST likely cause of this issue?

options.text: The Auto Scaling service-linked role does not have permission to use the KMS key.
options.rationale: Auto Scaling launches instances by using its service-linked role, AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling. If the key policy does not allow that role to use the customer managed key, EBS cannot create the encrypted volumes, and the instances terminate at once with this error. Adding the role to the key policy, or creating a grant, fixes it.

options.text: The launch template does not specify an IAM instance profile for the new instances.
options.rationale: Instances can launch without an instance profile. A missing profile affects the application's AWS access, not the launch.

options.text: The subnet for the Auto Scaling group does not have a route to an internet gateway.
options.rationale: Private subnets without an internet route can still launch instances. Routing does not cause this launch error.

options.text: The KMS key has automatic key rotation enabled, which blocks new EBS volumes.
options.rationale: Key rotation does not block use of the key. Older key material stays available for decryption.

questions.question:
A company uses AWS Organizations. The company's security team must deploy a standard set of IAM roles and an AWS Config rule to every account in the Workloads OU, including accounts that are added later.

Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Create a StackSet with service-managed permissions that targets the OU and has automatic deployment enabled.
options.rationale: With service-managed permissions, StackSets uses Organizations to create the required roles for you. Targeting the OU with automatic deployment enabled deploys stack instances to accounts that join the OU later, and it can remove them from accounts that leave.

options.text: Create a StackSet with self-managed permissions. Add each new account's ID to the StackSet when it joins.
options.rationale: Self-managed permissions require you to create administration and execution roles in every account, and each new account must be added by hand.

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function that runs when an account is created and deploys the stack by assuming a role in it.
options.rationale: Custom code can work, but StackSets provides this behavior natively.

options.text: Ask each account owner to deploy the template from a shared Amazon S3 bucket when their account is created.
options.rationale: Relying on account owners is slow and error prone, and some accounts would be missed.

questions.question:
A company does not use AWS Organizations. A CloudOps engineer needs to deploy an AWS CloudFormation template to 10 accounts by using a StackSet with self-managed permissions. The stack instances fail with an error that the StackSet could not assume a role in the target accounts.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Create the AWSCloudFormationStackSetExecutionRole in each target account. Trust the administrator account.
options.rationale: Self-managed StackSets need an administration role in the administrator account (AWSCloudFormationStackSetAdministrationRole) and an execution role in each target account (AWSCloudFormationStackSetExecutionRole) that trusts it. Without the execution role, StackSets cannot assume a role to create the stack.

options.text: Configure trusted access for StackSets in AWS Organizations.
options.rationale: Trusted access and service-managed permissions require AWS Organizations, which the company does not use.

options.text: Share the template with each target account through AWS RAM, and then retry the stack instances.
options.rationale: StackSets does not need the template to be shared. The failure is about assuming a role.

options.text: Add the target account IDs to the template's Parameters section. Run the operation again.
options.rationale: Target accounts are chosen when you create stack instances, not in template parameters, and this does not create the missing roles.

questions.question:
A company manages most of its AWS infrastructure with Terraform. An Amazon DynamoDB table that holds production data was created manually in the AWS Management Console. The table must now be managed by Terraform without being deleted or re-created.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Write a resource block for the table. Add the table to the Terraform state by using an import block or the terraform import command.
options.rationale: Importing adds an existing resource to the Terraform state, so Terraform manages it from then on without changing it. An import block is reviewed in a plan like any other change, and the terraform import command does the same from the command line. After the import, terraform plan should show no changes when the resource block matches the real table.

options.text: Write a resource block for the table with the same name. Run terraform apply to adopt the existing table by its name.
options.rationale: Without an import, Terraform plans to create a new table with that name, and the apply fails because the table already exists.

options.text: Back up the table to Amazon S3, and delete it. Write a resource block with the same table name, and run terraform apply to re-create it.
options.rationale: Deleting and re-creating the table causes downtime and puts production data at risk, which the requirement rules out.

options.text: Run terraform apply -refresh-only to add the table to the state. Write a resource block for the table after the run.
options.rationale: A refresh-only run updates resources that are already in the state. It does not add a resource that Terraform has never managed.

questions.question:
A company's network team owns a central VPC in a networking account. Application teams in other accounts in the same organization must launch Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon RDS databases into subnets of that VPC. The network team must keep control of routing and network ACLs.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Share the subnets with the application accounts by using AWS Resource Access Manager.
options.rationale: VPC sharing uses AWS RAM to share subnets with other accounts. Participants launch their own resources into the shared subnets, while the owner account keeps control of the VPC, route tables, network ACLs, and gateways.

options.text: Create VPC peering connections between the central VPC and a VPC in each application account.
options.rationale: Peering connects separate VPCs. The application resources would live in their own VPCs, not in the central VPC's subnets.

options.text: Create a cross-account IAM role in the networking account for the application teams to assume.
options.rationale: Assuming a role in the networking account would create the application resources in that account, which mixes ownership and billing.

options.text: Use an AWS CloudFormation StackSet to copy the central VPC into each of the application accounts.
options.rationale: Copying the VPC creates separate VPCs in each account, so the network team would not control a single shared network.

questions.question:
A company has Amazon Route 53 Resolver forwarding rules in a shared services account. The rules send queries for corp.example.com to on-premises DNS servers. Fifty VPCs in other accounts in the organization must use the same rules.

Which solution will meet this requirement in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Share the Resolver rules through AWS RAM. Associate them with the VPCs in each account.
options.rationale: Resolver rules can be shared with other accounts through AWS RAM. The other accounts associate the shared rules with their VPCs, and queries are forwarded through the outbound endpoint in the shared services account, so there is only one set of rules and endpoints to maintain.

options.text: Create an outbound endpoint and identical forwarding rules in every account and every VPC.
options.rationale: Duplicating endpoints and rules in every account adds cost and makes changes harder.

options.text: Create a private hosted zone named corp.example.com. Associate it with all 50 VPCs.
options.rationale: A private hosted zone would answer the queries itself in AWS. It would not forward them to the on-premises DNS servers.

options.text: Change the DHCP options set in each VPC to use the on-premises DNS servers directly.
options.rationale: Pointing VPCs directly at on-premises DNS servers breaks resolution of AWS private names and makes every query depend on the hybrid link.

questions.question:
A company's developers must be able to launch a standard, approved environment from an AWS CloudFormation template on their own. The developers must not have IAM permissions to create the underlying resources, such as VPCs and IAM roles, directly.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Publish the template as an AWS Service Catalog product with a launch constraint role that has the needed permissions.
options.rationale: AWS Service Catalog lets administrators publish approved products in portfolios. A launch constraint names an IAM role that Service Catalog uses to provision the product, so developers need permission only to launch the product, not to create each resource.

options.text: Give the developers the AdministratorAccess policy, and ask them to deploy only the approved template.
options.rationale: Administrator access breaks the requirement that developers cannot create the resources directly.

options.text: Share the template in an Amazon S3 bucket. Let the developers deploy it with their own IAM permissions.
options.rationale: Deploying with their own permissions requires developers to have rights to create VPCs and IAM roles.

options.text: Create a StackSet in the management account that deploys the environment into every developer account daily.
options.rationale: Daily deployments into every account do not let developers launch environments on demand, and they create environments that might not be needed.

questions.question:
A company runs an Amazon ECS service behind an Application Load Balancer. Each new version must run alongside the current version and must be tested before it receives production traffic. The company must be able to roll back quickly.

Which deployment approach will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use an ECS blue/green deployment that tests the new version before it shifts production traffic.
options.rationale: ECS blue/green deployments start the new revision (green) alongside the current one (blue) and can send test traffic to it first. Lifecycle hooks can run validation, production traffic then shifts, and ECS can roll back to blue quickly if CloudWatch alarms fire. ECS supports this natively, and CodeDeploy can also orchestrate it.

options.text: Use an ECS rolling update with a minimum healthy percent of 100 and a maximum percent of 200.
