options.rationale: A rolling update replaces tasks gradually behind the same listener, so there is no separate test traffic path, and rolling back means another rolling deployment.

options.text: Stop the service, update the task definition, and start the service again during a maintenance window.
options.rationale: Stopping the service causes downtime and gives no way to test before release.

options.text: Increase the service's desired count, and register the new task definition with the same target group.
options.rationale: Mixing new tasks into the same target group sends production traffic to them right away, with no validation step or quick rollback.

questions.question:
A company deploys a new version of an AWS Lambda function that handles payments. The company needs 10% of traffic to go to the new version for 10 minutes and the rest to shift automatically if no errors occur. The release must roll back automatically if an Amazon CloudWatch alarm fires.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS CodeDeploy with the LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes configuration and a rollback alarm on the alias.
options.rationale: CodeDeploy shifts traffic between versions on a Lambda alias. The canary configuration sends 10% of traffic to the new version for 10 minutes and then shifts the rest, and a CloudWatch alarm on the deployment triggers an automatic rollback.

options.text: Publish the new version. Update the alias to send all traffic to it after testing it in the console.
options.rationale: Moving all traffic at once is not a canary release, and there is no automatic rollback.

options.text: Create a second function for the new code. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted records to split the traffic.
options.rationale: Route 53 weighted records apply to DNS names, not to direct Lambda invocations, and this setup has no automatic rollback.

options.text: Increase the provisioned concurrency of the new version.
options.rationale: Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts. It does not split or shift traffic between versions.

questions.question:
A company releases a new AMI for a 40-instance Auto Scaling group. The company must replace instances gradually, keep at least 90% of capacity healthy, and pause after the first 25% of instances so that a CloudOps engineer can verify the release.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Start an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 90 and a checkpoint at 25%.
options.rationale: An instance refresh replaces instances in rolling batches and keeps at least the minimum healthy percentage in service. A checkpoint pauses the refresh after a set percentage of instances is replaced, so the team can verify before it continues. Auto rollback can also be enabled.

options.text: Update the launch template, and terminate 10 instances manually every hour until all are new.
options.rationale: Manual terminations are slow and error prone, and there is no built-in pause or health threshold.

options.text: Create a new Auto Scaling group with the new AMI. Delete the old group after it launches.
options.rationale: Deleting the old group after launching a new one does not give a gradual, verified rollout, and it needs traffic switching work.

options.text: Update the launch template, and wait for the group to replace instances during normal scaling.
options.rationale: Normal scaling might never replace some instances, so the fleet would run mixed versions for a long time.

questions.question:
A company deployed a faulty container image to an Amazon ECS service. The new tasks continued to fail their health checks, and the deployment continued to start new tasks for hours until a CloudOps engineer noticed.

What should the CloudOps engineer configure so that Amazon ECS detects failed deployments and returns to the last working version automatically?

options.text: Enable the ECS deployment circuit breaker with the rollback option.
options.rationale: The deployment circuit breaker detects when a rolling deployment cannot reach a steady state, for example when new tasks keep failing health checks. With rollback enabled, ECS returns the service to the last completed deployment automatically.

options.text: Set the service's minimum healthy percent to 0 during deployments.
options.rationale: A minimum healthy percent of 0 lets ECS stop all old tasks during a deployment, which can cause an outage.

options.text: Enable ECS Exec.
options.rationale: ECS Exec helps with debugging inside containers. It does not detect failed deployments or roll back.

options.text: Increase the health check grace period of the service to 2 hours.
options.rationale: A longer grace period makes ECS wait longer before it acts on failed health checks, which makes the problem worse.

questions.question:
A company uses an AWS CloudFormation stack update to change a web application's configuration. CloudFormation must roll back the update automatically if the application's 5XX error alarm goes into the ALARM state during the update or within 15 minutes after the update.

What should a CloudOps engineer configure to meet these requirements?

options.text: Add the alarm as a rollback trigger on the stack with a monitoring time of 15 minutes.
options.rationale: Rollback triggers make CloudFormation monitor CloudWatch alarms during a stack create or update and for a monitoring period afterward of up to 180 minutes. If an alarm goes into ALARM, CloudFormation rolls back the whole operation.

options.text: Add a stack policy that denies updates whenever the 5XX error alarm is in the ALARM state.
options.rationale: Stack policies are static rules about which resources can be updated. They do not react to alarm states.

options.text: Add a CreationPolicy that waits 15 minutes for a signal from the 5XX error alarm on update.
options.rationale: A CreationPolicy waits for signals from instances during creation. CloudWatch alarms do not send these signals.

options.text: Enable termination protection.
options.rationale: Termination protection blocks stack deletion. It does not roll back failed updates.

questions.question:
A company uses an AWS CloudFormation stack to manage a VPC and its subnets. Several application stacks in the same account and AWS Region must use the subnet IDs. Engineers currently copy the IDs into parameter files, and the copies often go out of date.

Which solution will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Export the subnet IDs in the Outputs section of the networking stack. Use Fn::ImportValue in the application stacks.
options.rationale: A cross-stack reference shares values between stacks in the same account and Region. The networking stack exports a value from its Outputs section, and other stacks read it with Fn::ImportValue, so there are no copies to keep up to date.

options.text: Store the subnet IDs in an Amazon S3 object. Update the application stacks to read the object during each deployment.
options.rationale: CloudFormation cannot read values from an S3 object without custom code, and someone must still keep the object up to date.

options.text: Add the VPC and the subnets to every application template. Create a separate network for each application stack.
options.rationale: This creates many separate networks instead of sharing one, which does not meet the requirement to use the existing subnets.

options.text: Use the Mappings section in each application template to hardcode the subnet IDs for each AWS Region and account.
options.rationale: Mappings are still hardcoded copies, so they go out of date in the same way as the parameter files.

questions.question:
A company manages most of its infrastructure with AWS CloudFormation. An Amazon S3 bucket was created manually in the AWS Management Console. The bucket must now be managed by an existing stack without being deleted or re-created.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Add the bucket to the stack's template with a DeletionPolicy attribute. Import the bucket by using a change set of type IMPORT.
options.rationale: A resource import brings an existing resource under stack management. The template must describe the resource and include a DeletionPolicy attribute, and you provide the resource's identifier, which is the bucket name here. A change set of type IMPORT then adds the bucket to the stack without changing it.

options.text: Add the bucket to the stack's template with the same BucketName. Update the stack so that CloudFormation adopts the bucket.
options.rationale: Without an import, CloudFormation tries to create a new bucket with that name, and the update fails because the bucket already exists.

options.text: Empty and delete the bucket. Add a new bucket with the same name to the stack's template, and update the stack.
options.rationale: Deleting the bucket destroys its data, and the requirement is to keep the bucket.

options.text: Run drift detection on the stack. Accept the bucket that drift detection finds as a new resource in the stack.
options.rationale: Drift detection compares resources that are already in the stack with the template. It does not find or adopt resources outside the stack.

questions.question:
A company's developers deploy their own AWS CloudFormation templates. The developers must be able to create and update stacks, but they must not have direct IAM permissions to create the underlying resources. The company must follow the principle of least privilege.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM service role for CloudFormation with the needed permissions. Allow the developers to pass the role when they create stacks.
options.rationale: A CloudFormation service role lets CloudFormation make the calls to create, update, and delete resources, so the developers do not need those permissions themselves. Developers need CloudFormation permissions and iam:PassRole for that one role.

options.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess policy to the developers' IAM roles. Add a permissions boundary that denies all resource creation.
options.rationale: A boundary that denies resource creation would also block the stack operations, because CloudFormation would use the developers' permissions.

options.text: Create an IAM user with the needed permissions. Share the user's access keys with the developers for each deployment.
options.rationale: Shared long-term access keys cannot be traced to one person and are against IAM best practices.

options.text: Add a stack policy to each stack that allows updates. Remove the developers' IAM permissions for CloudFormation actions.
options.rationale: A stack policy protects stack resources from updates. It does not grant permissions, and the developers would no longer be able to use CloudFormation.

questions.question:
A company has thousands of Amazon EC2 instances in 30 accounts and 4 AWS Regions in AWS Organizations. The company must scan instances for missing patches daily and install approved security patches every Sunday, managed from one central configuration.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a patch policy in Quick Setup for Patch Manager that targets the organization and its Regions.
options.rationale: Patch policies, created through Quick Setup, configure Patch Manager scan and install schedules and patch baselines across an organization's accounts and Regions from one place.

options.text: Create a maintenance window and a patch baseline in each account and Region. Register the instances as targets.
options.rationale: This works, but it must be built and maintained in 120 account and Region combinations.

options.text: Add a cron job to each instance's user data that runs the operating system package update command.
options.rationale: Cron jobs on each instance are hard to manage, give no compliance reporting, and do not use approved baselines.

options.text: Build a new AMI each Sunday with the latest patches, and replace every instance in the organization.
options.rationale: Replacing thousands of instances every week is disruptive and not feasible for every workload.

questions.question:
A company uses AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager. Security updates must be installed on production Linux instances only after the updates have been available for 7 days, so that problems can be found in testing first. Patches must then be approved automatically.

How should a CloudOps engineer configure Patch Manager to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a custom patch baseline with a rule that auto-approves security patches 7 days after release.
options.rationale: Patch baseline approval rules can auto-approve patches by classification and severity a set number of days after they are released. A 7-day delay for security patches gives time for testing before production installs them.

options.text: Use the default predefined patch baseline. Schedule the patch installation to run every 7 days.
options.rationale: Running the installation every 7 days does not delay approval. A patch released the day before could still be installed.

options.text: Create a patch group that excludes patches from the last 7 days by listing each one as rejected.
options.rationale: Rejecting each new patch by hand is constant manual work and easy to get wrong.

options.text: Configure Amazon Inspector, and patch only CVEs that Amazon Inspector has reported for at least 7 days.
options.rationale: Inspector finds vulnerabilities but does not control patch approval timing, and this would still need a patching process.

questions.question:
A company's policy requires a specific security agent to be installed and running on every Amazon EC2 instance. Engineers sometimes stop the agent while troubleshooting and forget to start it again.

Which solution will keep the agent in the required state automatically?

options.text: Create a State Manager association that installs and starts the agent on a schedule.
options.rationale: A State Manager association applies a document to targets on a schedule, such as every 30 minutes, and reports compliance. If someone stops the agent, the next run installs or starts it again.

options.text: Run a Run Command document once to install the agent on all of the instances in the fleet.
options.rationale: A one-time command installs the agent once but does not fix it when someone stops it later.

options.text: Add the agent installation to the AMI.
options.rationale: Baking the agent into the AMI covers new instances, but it does not restart the agent on running instances.

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that reports instances where the agent is not running.
options.rationale: Config can report the problem, but reporting alone does not keep the agent running.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer launches Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet that has no NAT gateway or other internet access. The instances use an AMI with SSM Agent preinstalled, but the instances do not appear as managed nodes in AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager.

Which combination of steps will resolve this issue? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Attach an instance profile that includes the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy.
options.rationale: SSM Agent needs AWS credentials with Systems Manager permissions, which the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy provides through an instance profile. Default Host Management Configuration is another way to provide them.

options.text: Create interface VPC endpoints for the Systems Manager services, such as ssm and ssmmessages.
options.rationale: SSM Agent connects outbound to Systems Manager endpoints over HTTPS. Without internet access, interface endpoints for ssm and ssmmessages (and ec2messages for older agent versions) give the agent a private path. The endpoint security group must allow HTTPS from the instances.

options.text: Open inbound port 22 on the instance security group from the Systems Manager service.
options.rationale: Systems Manager does not connect inbound to instances, and it does not use SSH. The agent makes outbound connections.

options.text: Assign an Elastic IP address to each instance to allow Systems Manager to reach it.
options.rationale: Elastic IP addresses do not help in a subnet with no route to an internet gateway, and Systems Manager does not need inbound access.

options.text: Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent to report each instance's status to Fleet Manager.
options.rationale: The CloudWatch agent publishes metrics and logs. Managed node registration depends on SSM Agent, credentials, and network access.

questions.question:
A company runs Terraform from a GitHub Actions workflow to deploy resources to AWS. The workflow uses the access keys of an IAM user, which are stored as repository secrets. The company's security team must remove all long-lived credentials from the workflow.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Create an IAM OIDC identity provider for GitHub. Allow the workflow to assume an IAM role that provides temporary credentials.
options.rationale: With an OIDC identity provider for GitHub, the workflow gets a short-lived token and exchanges it for temporary credentials by assuming an IAM role. A condition on the token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub key in the role's trust policy limits which repositories and branches can assume the role, and no long-lived keys are stored.

options.text: Rotate the IAM user's access keys every 30 days. Update the repository secrets after each rotation of the keys.
options.rationale: Rotation shortens how long each key is valid, but the keys are still long-lived credentials that are stored in GitHub.

options.text: Store the IAM user's access keys in AWS Secrets Manager. Have the workflow read the keys from the secret at the start of each run.
options.rationale: The workflow would still need credentials to read from Secrets Manager, and the access keys would still be long-lived.

options.text: Create a separate IAM user for each workflow. Grant each IAM user only the permissions that its workflow needs.
options.rationale: Separate users improve least privilege, but each user still has long-lived access keys stored in GitHub.

questions.question:
A company needs to patch and run commands on 300 on-premises Linux servers by using the same AWS Systems Manager tools that it uses for its Amazon EC2 instances.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Create a hybrid activation. Install SSM Agent on each server with the activation code and ID.
options.rationale: A hybrid activation creates an activation code and ID that are tied to an IAM service role. Installing SSM Agent with them registers each server as a managed node, so Run Command, Patch Manager, and the other tools work the same way as they do on EC2.

options.text: Attach an EC2 instance profile to each on-premises server to give SSM Agent role credentials.
options.rationale: Instance profiles exist only for EC2 instances. On-premises servers get credentials through a hybrid activation.

options.text: Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent on each server. Send Run Command documents through CloudWatch.
options.rationale: The CloudWatch agent collects metrics and logs. It does not run Systems Manager commands.

options.text: Open inbound port 443 on each server to allow Systems Manager to push commands to the servers.
options.rationale: SSM Agent makes outbound HTTPS connections to Systems Manager. Systems Manager does not push commands through inbound ports.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer needs to run a shell script once on 500 Linux Amazon EC2 instances that are tagged Role=Web to change a local log configuration. The output of every run must be kept for later review, and SSH access is not allowed.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Run Command with AWS-RunShellScript. Target the Role=Web tag. Send output to an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.rationale: Run Command runs a document on many managed nodes at once, selected by tag, with rate controls and no SSH. Command output can be written to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs for review.

options.text: Create an EC2 Image Builder pipeline that adds the script to a new AMI. Replace all of the instances.
options.rationale: Building a new AMI and replacing instances is far more work than running one script once.

options.text: Add the script to each instance's user data, and reboot the instances.
options.rationale: User data runs only on first boot by default, so a reboot does not run it again, and the output is not kept centrally.

options.text: Use EC2 Instance Connect to open a session to each instance, and save the output in a document.
options.rationale: Instance Connect uses SSH, which is not allowed, and connecting to 500 instances by hand is slow.

questions.question:
A company's security team needs a report of which software packages and versions are installed on every Amazon EC2 instance across 20 accounts. The report must be queryable with SQL and must stay up to date automatically.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable AWS Systems Manager Inventory. Use a resource data sync to an Amazon S3 bucket that Amazon Athena can query.
options.rationale: Inventory collects metadata such as installed applications and versions from managed nodes. A resource data sync gathers inventory from many accounts and Regions into one S3 bucket, where Amazon Athena can query it with SQL.

options.text: Run a script on each instance every day that emails its package list to the security team.
options.rationale: Daily emails from each instance are hard to combine and query, and the script must be maintained.

options.text: Enable AWS Config recording for EC2 instances, and download each configuration item as a CSV file.
options.rationale: Downloading configuration items by hand does not give an automatic, SQL-queryable report across accounts, and software data comes from Systems Manager anyway.

options.text: Configure AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon EC2, and search the trail for package install API calls.
options.rationale: Installing a package inside an operating system is not an AWS API call, so CloudTrail does not record it.

questions.question:
A company has an application with 80 configuration values for each of three environments: dev, test, and prod. Developers store the values in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as one long flat list of parameter names, and loading the right set for an environment is error prone. Some of the values are secrets.

How should a CloudOps engineer organize the parameters?

options.text: Use a path hierarchy such as /app/prod/db-url. Use SecureString for the secret values.
options.rationale: Hierarchical names group parameters by application and environment, and GetParametersByPath loads every parameter under /app/prod/ in one call. IAM policies can grant access by path, and SecureString encrypts the secret values with AWS KMS.

options.text: Store all values for each environment in one String parameter as a large JSON document.
options.rationale: One large document is hard to update safely and can exceed the 4 KB size limit of standard parameters. The secrets would also be stored as plain text.

options.text: Store each value as a separate secret in AWS Secrets Manager with the environment in a tag.
options.rationale: Secrets Manager suits secrets that need rotation, but storing 240 ordinary configuration values there costs more and is not needed.

options.text: Put all values in environment variables in the AMI.
options.rationale: Values in an AMI are hard to change, are visible to anyone on the instance, and need a new AMI for each change.

questions.question:
A company has users who upload images and PDF files to the uploads/ prefix of an Amazon S3 bucket. An AWS Lambda function must create a thumbnail for every .jpg file within seconds of upload. Other files must not invoke the function.

Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Add an S3 event notification for object creation with prefix uploads/ and suffix .jpg that invokes the function.
options.rationale: S3 Event Notifications can invoke a Lambda function directly when objects are created, with prefix and suffix filters so that only .jpg files under uploads/ trigger it. Events usually arrive within seconds.

options.text: Schedule the function every minute to list the bucket. Create thumbnails for any new .jpg files.
options.rationale: Polling the bucket every minute is slower, costs more as the bucket grows, and must track which files were already processed.

options.text: Enable S3 Inventory each day. Invoke the function for each .jpg file listed in the report.
options.rationale: S3 Inventory reports are produced daily or weekly, which is far too slow.

options.text: Configure AWS CloudTrail data events. Invoke the function from a metric filter on PutObject calls.
options.rationale: Metric filters create metrics and cannot pass object details to a function, so this is slow and indirect.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon S3 bucket. When objects are created in the bucket, three teams must each process them: one with an AWS Lambda function, one with an AWS Step Functions workflow, and one through an Amazon SQS queue. The third team needs only objects larger than 1 GB.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure Amazon EventBridge notifications for the bucket.
options.rationale: When EventBridge notifications are enabled, Amazon S3 sends the bucket's events to the default event bus, where many rules can use them.

options.text: Create Amazon EventBridge rules for each team, with a size filter in the pattern for the team that needs it.
options.rationale: EventBridge rules can match fields in the event, such as the object size with a numeric filter, and each rule can send to targets such as Lambda, Step Functions, and SQS. Each team gets its own routing without code.

options.text: Create three S3 Event Notifications with the same event type and prefix, one for each target.
options.rationale: S3 Event Notifications cannot have overlapping configurations for the same event type and prefix, and they cannot filter by object size.

options.text: Write a Lambda function that receives each S3 event and forwards it to the other two targets.
options.rationale: A forwarding function is custom code to maintain and a single point of failure.

options.text: Configure S3 Replication to three buckets, one for each team. Configure events on each copy.
options.rationale: Replicating every object three times adds storage cost and delay just to send events to three teams.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS Lambda function that is invoked by Amazon S3 object creation events on a bucket. The function resizes each image and writes the result back to the same bucket. After deployment, invocations and costs grow out of control.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve the root cause of this issue?

options.text: Write the resized images to a different bucket, or use a prefix filter that excludes the output prefix.
options.rationale: Each resized image written to the same bucket creates a new event, which invokes the function again in a loop. Writing output to a separate bucket, or triggering only on an input prefix that the output never uses, breaks the loop. Lambda recursive loop detection can stop some loops, but the design still needs fixing.

options.text: Increase the function's reserved concurrency to keep up with the number of events.
options.rationale: More concurrency lets the loop grow even faster and raises costs.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning to send only one event notification for each object key that is written.
options.rationale: Versioning does not reduce events. Every write still creates a new event.

options.text: Add a dead-letter queue to the function to move the extra invocations into the queue.
options.rationale: A dead-letter queue holds failed asynchronous invocations. These invocations succeed, so the loop continues.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS Lambda function that processes messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue. The function's timeout is 5 minutes, and the queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds. Some messages are processed several times, and a few malformed messages fail repeatedly.

Which combination of steps will resolve these issues? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set the queue's visibility timeout to at least six times the function's timeout.
options.rationale: If the visibility timeout is shorter than the processing time, messages become visible again while the function is still working on them, so they are processed again. AWS recommends a visibility timeout of at least six times the function timeout for Lambda event source mappings.

options.text: Add a dead-letter queue with a redrive policy that sets a maxReceiveCount.
options.rationale: A redrive policy moves a message to a dead-letter queue after it has been received maxReceiveCount times without being deleted. Malformed messages stop retrying and can be examined separately.

options.text: Change the function's timeout to 30 seconds to match the visibility timeout.
options.rationale: A shorter function timeout could cut off valid processing that needs more than 30 seconds.

options.text: Enable long polling for the queue by setting a receive wait time of 20 seconds.
options.rationale: Long polling reduces empty receives and cost. It does not stop duplicates or failing messages.

options.text: Increase the queue's message retention period from 4 days to 14 days.
options.rationale: Longer retention keeps failing messages around even longer.

questions.question:
A company has a monthly database maintenance process with five steps: take a snapshot, run an AWS Lambda function to verify the snapshot, wait for a DBA to approve, apply a parameter change, and send a report. Each step must retry on failure, and the process must wait up to 24 hours for the approval.

Which solution will orchestrate this process with the LEAST custom code?

options.text: Build an AWS Step Functions state machine with retries and a callback task that waits for an approval token.
options.rationale: Step Functions coordinates multi-step workflows with built-in retries and error handling. A task that uses the waitForTaskToken pattern pauses until an approver returns the token, and standard workflows can run for up to a year, so a 24-hour wait is fine.

options.text: Chain five Lambda functions that call each other directly, and sleep inside the approval function.
options.rationale: Lambda functions time out after 15 minutes, so a function cannot sleep for 24 hours, and chained calls make retries hard to manage.

options.text: Run a cron job on an Amazon EC2 instance that calls each step in order and polls a file for the approval.
options.rationale: A server-based script must be patched and monitored, and it needs its own retry logic.

options.text: Create five Amazon EventBridge rules that each start the next step when the previous one writes a log.
options.rationale: Chaining rules through log messages is fragile and hard to follow, and it gives no clear way to wait for approval.

questions.question:
A company uses AWS DevOps Agent to investigate incidents. When an investigation completes, the company must create a ticket in its internal ticketing system through an HTTP API and must post a summary to a chat channel automatically.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for DevOps Agent investigation events that targets an API destination and the chat function.
options.rationale: AWS DevOps Agent publishes investigation events to Amazon EventBridge for custom automation. A rule that matches completed investigations can call the ticketing system through an API destination and invoke the function that posts to chat, with no polling.

options.text: Have an engineer copy each finished investigation from the DevOps Agent web app into the ticketing system.
options.rationale: Manual copying is slow and depends on someone remembering to do it.

options.text: Poll the DevOps Agent API every 5 minutes from an Amazon EC2 instance, and create tickets for any new results.
options.rationale: Polling from a server is custom code and infrastructure to maintain, and EventBridge already delivers the events.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on a DevOps Agent metric that opens a ticket whenever an investigation ends.
options.rationale: An alarm watches metric values. It cannot carry investigation details to create a ticket.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer edits AWS CloudFormation templates in Kiro. Kiro must run cfn-lint and fix simple problems automatically every time a template file is saved, without being asked each time.

Which Kiro feature should the CloudOps engineer configure?

options.text: An agent hook that is triggered when a template file is saved
options.rationale: Agent hooks run an agent action automatically when an event happens in the IDE, such as saving a file that matches a pattern. A hook on template saves can run cfn-lint and fix simple findings without a manual prompt.

options.text: A steering file that lists all of the cfn-lint rules for the project
options.rationale: Steering files give Kiro persistent guidance, but they do not run anything when a file is saved.

options.text: A spec that describes how the templates should be linted
options.rationale: Specs plan the requirements, design, and tasks for a feature. They do not react to file events.

options.text: An MCP server that stores the most recent lint results
options.rationale: MCP servers connect Kiro to external tools and data. Storing results does not run the linter on each save.

questions.question:
A company's finance team needs every new Amazon EC2 instance to be tagged with the IAM identity of the person who launched it, within minutes of launch, no matter how the instance was launched. AWS CloudTrail is enabled in the account.

Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches the RunInstances event from AWS API Call via CloudTrail.
options.rationale: EventBridge receives CloudTrail management events as AWS API Call via CloudTrail events. A rule on ec2:RunInstances matches every launch, whether it comes from the console, the CLI, an SDK, or infrastructure as code.

options.text: Target an AWS Lambda function that reads userIdentity from the event and tags the new instances.
options.rationale: The event's userIdentity field shows who made the call, and responseElements lists the new instance IDs. A Lambda function can call CreateTags with that identity.

options.text: Require every user to add an Owner tag in the console launch wizard before launching an instance.
options.rationale: Relying on users is not reliable, and it does not cover launches from the CLI, SDKs, or automation.

options.text: Run an AWS Config rule once a day that tags instances with the name of the account's root user.
options.rationale: The root user is not the person who launched the instance, and a daily rule does not tag within minutes.

options.text: Add a user data script to the launch template that tags each instance with its instance profile.
options.rationale: The instance profile identifies the instance's role, not the person who launched it, and not every launch uses this template.

questions.question:
A company runs version 1 of an application in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Version 2 is deployed to a second Auto Scaling group with its own target group. The company must shift 10%, then 50%, then 100% of traffic to version 2 and must be able to switch back instantly if needed, without DNS changes.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use weighted target groups in the ALB listener rule. Change the weights at each step.
options.rationale: An ALB listener rule can forward to several target groups with weights. Changing the weights moves traffic between versions within seconds, with no DNS caching delays, and setting the old group back to 100% rolls back instantly.

options.text: Create an Amazon Route 53 weighted record for each group. Change the record weights at each step.
options.rationale: Weighted DNS records can split traffic, but the scenario rules out DNS changes, and clients that cache DNS make shifts and rollbacks slow.

options.text: Register the version 2 instances in the version 1 target group. Remove old instances gradually.
options.rationale: Mixing both versions in one target group gives no control over the share of traffic and no instant rollback.

options.text: Run an instance refresh on the version 1 group with checkpoints at 10% and 50% of the instances.
options.rationale: An instance refresh replaces instances in one group. Rolling back means another refresh, which is not instant.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer deletes an AWS CloudFormation stack for a retired application. The deletion fails with DELETE_FAILED because the stack's Amazon S3 bucket is not empty. The data in the bucket is no longer needed.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Empty the bucket, and then delete the stack again.
options.rationale: CloudFormation cannot delete an S3 bucket that still contains objects. After the objects, and all object versions if versioning is on, are deleted, the stack deletion can finish. If the data were still needed, the bucket could be retained when the stack is deleted.

options.text: Enable termination protection on the stack. Delete the stack again.
options.rationale: Termination protection prevents a stack from being deleted, which is the opposite of what is needed.

options.text: Add a DeletionPolicy of Delete to the bucket only.
options.rationale: Delete is already the default policy, and it still cannot delete a bucket that has objects in it.

options.text: Run drift detection, and then execute a change set.
options.rationale: Drift detection and change sets do not remove objects from the bucket.

questions.question:
A company uses AWS CodeDeploy in-place deployments to release new versions of an application to 10 Amazon EC2 instances. At least 9 instances must stay in service at all times during a deployment.

Which deployment configuration should a CloudOps engineer choose to meet this requirement?

options.text: CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime
options.rationale: OneAtATime deploys to one instance at a time, so 9 of the 10 instances stay in service throughout the deployment.

options.text: CodeDeployDefault.HalfAtATime
options.rationale: HalfAtATime deploys to up to half of the instances at once, which leaves only 5 in service.

options.text: CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce
options.rationale: AllAtOnce deploys to every instance at the same time, which can take the whole application out of service.

options.text: A custom configuration with 50% minimum healthy hosts
options.rationale: A 50% minimum healthy hosts setting allows 5 instances to be out of service at once.

questions.question:
A company must patch its production Amazon EC2 Linux instances only on Saturdays between 02:00 and 05:00. New patching tasks must not start during the last hour of that period. All instances are managed by AWS Systems Manager.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a Systems Manager maintenance window with a 3-hour duration and a 1-hour cutoff. Register the instances as targets and AWS-RunPatchBaseline as a task.
options.rationale: A maintenance window defines a schedule, a duration, and a cutoff, which is the number of hours before the end of the window when Systems Manager stops starting new tasks. AWS-RunPatchBaseline is the Patch Manager document that scans for and installs patches.

options.text: Create a cron job on each instance that runs the package manager's update command at 02:00 on Saturdays. Send the output of each run to Amazon S3.
options.rationale: Cron jobs must be set up and maintained on every instance, and they do not stop new work before the end of the period.

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that checks for missing patches. Add an automatic remediation action that installs patches as soon as an instance is noncompliant.
options.rationale: Remediation runs when the rule finds noncompliance, which can be at any time, not only during the allowed period.

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that runs at 02:00 on Saturdays. Invoke an AWS Lambda function that connects to each instance over SSH to install patches.
options.rationale: This needs custom code and inbound SSH access, which Systems Manager makes unnecessary.

questions.question:
A company has a script that refreshes currency exchange rates from a partner API and writes them to an Amazon DynamoDB table every 15 minutes. The script runs as a cron job on a dedicated t3.micro Amazon EC2 instance that must be patched and sometimes stops. The script finishes in under 1 minute.

Which solution will run the script with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Move the script to an AWS Lambda function. Invoke it every 15 minutes with Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.
options.rationale: Lambda runs short tasks with no servers to patch, and EventBridge Scheduler invokes it at a fixed rate with retries. A task that finishes in under 1 minute fits well within the 15-minute Lambda limit.

options.text: Move the cron job to a larger instance. Add an Auto Scaling group to keep one instance running.
options.rationale: This keeps a server to patch and adds cost, which is the overhead the team wants to remove.

options.text: Move the script into an Amazon ECS service that runs one task all the time and sleeps 15 minutes in a loop.
options.rationale: A task that runs all the time and sleeps wastes resources and still needs its own scheduling logic.

options.text: Configure DynamoDB Streams. Run the script whenever an item in the table is written or changed.
options.rationale: Streams trigger on table changes, not on a schedule, so the rates would not be refreshed every 15 minutes.

questions.question:
A company manages its production infrastructure with AWS CloudFormation. The company requires a review of the exact resource changes before any stack update is applied. The company also must identify each day any manual changes that were made outside CloudFormation.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a change set for each update. Review the change set before executing it.
options.rationale: A change set shows how a stack update will change each resource, including replacements, before anything changes. You execute the change set only after the review.

options.text: Deploy the cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check AWS Config managed rule.
options.rationale: This managed rule runs drift detection on the stacks and marks a stack as noncompliant when its resources differ from the template. It runs on a periodic schedule, so manual changes are found each day.

options.text: Enable termination protection on each stack. Review the stack events after each update.
options.rationale: Termination protection stops a stack from being deleted. Stack events show what already happened, not what will change.

options.text: Apply a stack policy that denies all updates. Remove the policy during each planned update.
options.rationale: A stack policy can block updates to resources, but it does not show which changes an update will make.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail Insights on the account's trail to detect manual resource changes.
options.rationale: CloudTrail Insights detects unusual rates of API calls. It does not compare resources with a template.

questions.question:
A company uses Amazon S3 events to invoke an AWS Lambda function asynchronously. When the function continues to fail after its retries, the event is lost. Failed events must be sent to an Amazon SQS queue along with error details, and successful results must be sent to an Amazon EventBridge event bus.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure Lambda destinations: on failure to the SQS queue, and on success to the event bus.
options.rationale: For asynchronous invocations, Lambda destinations send a record of each invocation to a target based on the result. The on-failure record includes the original event and error details, and on-success records can go to an EventBridge event bus, with no code changes.

options.text: Add a try and catch block to the function code that writes every event to both targets before returning.
options.rationale: Code inside the function cannot capture failures such as timeouts that stop the function, and it adds logic to maintain.

options.text: Set the function's reserved concurrency to 1 to process events one at a time without failures.
options.rationale: Lower concurrency does not prevent failures, and it slows processing.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning to replay failed events from the previous versions of the objects.
options.rationale: Object versions are not events, and versioning does not keep a record of failed invocations.

questions.question:
A company requires IAM users to sign in with MFA before they can do anything other than manage their own MFA device. Some users sign in without MFA and can still stop Amazon EC2 instances.

Which IAM policy approach will enforce this requirement?

options.text: Attach a policy that denies all but MFA self-management actions when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false.
options.rationale: A Deny statement with a condition such as BoolIfExists aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent false blocks every action except the ones a user needs to set up MFA. After the user signs in with MFA, the condition no longer matches, and the user's other permissions apply.

options.text: Attach a policy that allows all actions only when the aws:SecureTransport condition key is set to true.
options.rationale: aws:SecureTransport checks whether a request used TLS. It has nothing to do with MFA.

options.text: Enable an account password policy that requires users to change their passwords every 30 days.
options.rationale: A password policy controls password strength and rotation. It does not require MFA.

options.text: Attach a policy that denies all actions whenever the aws:RequestedRegion condition key does not equal us-east-1.
options.rationale: aws:RequestedRegion restricts Regions. It does not check whether the user signed in with MFA.

questions.question:
A company has an application on an Amazon EC2 instance that reads objects from an Amazon S3 bucket. The developers stored an IAM user's access keys in the application's configuration file. A security review flags this as a risk.

Which solution will remove this risk in the MOST secure manner?

options.text: Attach an IAM role with read access to the bucket through an instance profile. Delete the keys.
options.rationale: An instance profile gives the application temporary credentials that rotate automatically through the instance metadata service. The SDK picks them up with no keys in files, and the long-lived keys can be deleted.

options.text: Encrypt the configuration file with AWS KMS.
options.rationale: The application still has to decrypt and use long-lived keys, so the keys can still leak and never expire.

options.text: Move the access keys into environment variables on the instance. Remove them from the file.
options.rationale: Environment variables still hold long-lived keys that can leak through logs or process listings.

options.text: Rotate the access keys every 90 days. Store the new keys in the same configuration file.
options.rationale: Rotation limits how long a key is exposed, but the keys are still long-lived and stored on the instance.

questions.question:
A company's third-party monitoring vendor needs read-only access to the company's AWS account. The vendor serves many customers and calls the company's account from the vendor's own AWS account.

How should a CloudOps engineer grant access in the MOST secure manner?

options.text: Create an IAM role that trusts the vendor's account. Require a unique external ID in the trust policy.
options.rationale: A cross-account role lets the vendor use temporary credentials from its own account. Requiring a unique external ID in the trust policy (the sts:ExternalId condition) protects against the confused deputy problem, where another of the vendor's customers could trick the vendor into accessing your account.

options.text: Create an IAM user for the vendor with read-only permissions. Send the access keys by email.
options.rationale: Long-lived access keys sent by email can leak and must be rotated by hand, and they are not needed for cross-account access.

options.text: Share the company account's root credentials with the vendor.
options.rationale: Root credentials must never be shared. They have unrestricted access to the account.

options.text: Add the vendor's account to the company's Amazon S3 bucket policies. Allow all read actions on all buckets.
options.rationale: Bucket policies cover only Amazon S3, and monitoring needs read access across many services.

questions.question:
A company has 25 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations and 2,000 employees in Microsoft Entra ID. Employees must sign in with their corporate credentials and get access to accounts based on their Entra ID groups. The company must stop using IAM users.

Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Connect IAM Identity Center to Entra ID with SAML and SCIM, and assign permission sets to groups.
options.rationale: IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on to all accounts in the organization. SAML federates sign-in with Entra ID, SCIM provisions users and groups automatically, and permission sets that are assigned to groups create the roles in each account.

options.text: Create an IAM user in every account for each employee, and sync their passwords from Entra ID every night.
options.rationale: This keeps thousands of IAM users with long-lived credentials, which the company wants to stop.

options.text: Create a SAML identity provider and roles in each of the 25 accounts, and map groups in each one.
options.rationale: Per-account SAML federation works, but it must be built and maintained in 25 accounts, which is more overhead.

options.text: Create one IAM user per team in the management account. Share the passwords with each team.
options.rationale: Shared credentials break accountability and least privilege.

questions.question:
A company stores sensitive data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The bucket must be accessible only through a specific gateway VPC endpoint in the company's VPC, even by users who have IAM permissions to the bucket.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies all S3 actions when aws:SourceVpce does not equal the endpoint ID.
options.rationale: A Deny statement with a StringNotEquals condition on aws:SourceVpce blocks every request that does not arrive through that endpoint. An explicit deny overrides any allow, so even users with IAM permissions cannot reach the bucket from anywhere else.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows access only when aws:SourceIp matches the VPC's CIDR block.
options.rationale: aws:SourceIp does not contain private VPC addresses for requests that arrive through a VPC endpoint, so this condition would not work as intended.

options.text: Attach a security group to the bucket that allows inbound HTTPS only from the gateway VPC endpoint.
options.rationale: S3 buckets do not have security groups.

options.text: Add a route in the VPC route table that sends all traffic for the bucket to a NAT gateway.
options.rationale: A NAT gateway sends traffic to the public S3 endpoint, which does not limit access to the VPC endpoint.

questions.question:
A company must keep all workloads in eu-central-1 and eu-west-1 for data residency. Users in member accounts must not be able to create resources in other AWS Regions, but global services such as IAM and Amazon Route 53 must continue to work.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Attach an SCP that denies requests to other Regions by using aws:RequestedRegion, with global services exempted.
options.rationale: An SCP that denies aws:RequestedRegion values other than the two approved Regions sets a guardrail for every principal in member accounts. Exempting global services such as IAM, AWS Organizations, Route 53, CloudFront, and AWS Support keeps them working, because their requests go to us-east-1.

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to each IAM user and role that allows actions only in eu-central-1 and eu-west-1.
options.rationale: IAM policies on each identity are easy to miss or change, and new roles would not be covered automatically.

options.text: Configure AWS Config in all other Regions with a rule that deletes any new resources that it finds.
options.rationale: Deleting resources after they are created is reactive, and data might already be stored in the wrong Region.

options.text: Opt out of every other Region for each member account from the account settings in the management account.
options.rationale: Only opt-in Regions can be disabled. Regions that are enabled by default cannot be disabled, so this cannot block them.

questions.question:
A company allows developers to create IAM roles for their AWS Lambda functions. The company's security team must ensure that any role a developer creates can never have more than a defined set of permissions, even if the developer attaches AdministratorAccess to the role.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Require a permissions boundary on every role that developers create, enforced with an IAM condition key.
options.rationale: A permissions boundary sets the maximum permissions that identity-based policies can grant to a role. If the developers' own policy allows iam:CreateRole only when the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition matches the approved boundary, every role they create is capped, even with AdministratorAccess attached.

options.text: Attach an SCP to the account that denies the developers access to the iam:CreateRole action.
options.rationale: Denying role creation stops developers from doing their work, which is not the goal.

options.text: Enable IAM Access Analyzer to delete any role with too many permissions automatically every day.
options.rationale: Access Analyzer reports findings. It does not delete roles or cap their permissions.

options.text: Ask developers to use only AWS managed policies when they attach policies to their new roles.
options.rationale: AWS managed policies include AdministratorAccess, and a request to developers is not an enforced control.

questions.question:
A company has hundreds of projects that share one AWS account. Engineers must be able to start and stop only the Amazon EC2 instances that belong to their own project. New projects are added every week, and the company's security team does not want to update IAM policies for each new project.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Tag instances and roles with Project. Allow actions only when the resource and principal Project tags match.
options.rationale: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) uses tags in policy conditions. One policy that compares aws:ResourceTag/Project with aws:PrincipalTag/Project works for every project, including new ones, as long as resources and roles are tagged correctly. Engineers must not be allowed to change the Project tag.

options.text: Create an IAM policy for each project that lists the instance IDs of that project's instances. Update it weekly.
options.rationale: Per-project policies with instance IDs must change whenever instances or projects change, which is the work the team wants to avoid.

options.text: Create a separate VPC for each project. Allow the engineers to manage instances only inside their own VPC.
options.rationale: IAM does not easily scope EC2 start and stop actions by VPC, and a VPC for each project adds network overhead.

options.text: Create an IAM group for each project. Add a new group with its own policy every week for each new project.
options.rationale: A new group and policy every week is the manual work the team wants to avoid.

questions.question:
A company's security review finds that the root user of an AWS account has active access keys and no MFA device. Administrators sign in through AWS IAM Identity Center for their daily work.

Which combination of steps follows AWS best practices? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Delete the access keys for the root user.
options.rationale: Root user access keys grant unrestricted access to the account and should not exist. Delete them, and use roles for programmatic access.

options.text: Configure MFA for the root user.
options.rationale: MFA protects the most powerful identity in the account from a stolen password. In AWS Organizations, centralized root access management can also remove root credentials from member accounts.

options.text: Rotate the root user's access keys every 90 days.
options.rationale: Rotation shortens how long a key is valid, but the root user should have no access keys at all.

options.text: Store the root user's access keys in AWS Secrets Manager.
options.rationale: Storing the keys more safely still leaves long-lived root credentials that should not exist.

options.text: Attach a permissions boundary to the root user.
options.rationale: Permissions boundaries apply to IAM users and roles. They cannot limit the root user.

questions.question:
A company has an application role that sometimes receives AccessDenied errors from AWS KMS when it reads encrypted objects from Amazon S3. A CloudOps engineer needs to find which KMS key, which API action, and which principal were involved in each failure.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Search AWS CloudTrail for kms.amazonaws.com events with errorCode AccessDenied, and review their details.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records KMS API calls, including failed ones, with the errorCode, the action (such as Decrypt), the key ARN, and the userIdentity of the caller. CloudTrail Lake or CloudWatch Logs Insights can filter these events quickly.

options.text: Enable S3 server access logging, and wait for the next failure to see the error in the logs.
options.rationale: Server access logs show S3 requests, but they do not show the KMS call details or the key that denied access.

options.text: Run the IAM policy simulator against every KMS key in the account with every possible KMS action.
options.rationale: Simulating every key and action is slow and would not show what actually failed.

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs for the application's subnets, and look for rejected traffic going to AWS KMS.
options.rationale: Flow logs show network traffic. AccessDenied is a permissions error, not a network problem.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer needs to attach a new IAM policy to a production role. Before attaching the policy, the CloudOps engineer must confirm that the role will be allowed to call s3:PutObject on one bucket and denied on all other buckets. The check must account for the SCPs and permissions boundary that apply to the role.

Which tool should the CloudOps engineer use?

options.text: The IAM policy simulator
options.rationale: The IAM policy simulator tests identity-based policies, permissions boundaries, resource-based policies, and SCPs against chosen actions and resources. It shows whether each request would be allowed or denied without making real requests.

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor checks
options.rationale: Trusted Advisor checks for best practices, such as unrestricted security groups. It does not evaluate specific policy decisions.

options.text: Amazon Inspector findings
options.rationale: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities and network exposure. It does not test IAM policies.

options.text: AWS Config rule evaluations
options.rationale: Config evaluates resource configurations against rules. It does not simulate API authorization.

questions.question:
A company's security team must be notified whenever an Amazon S3 bucket, AWS KMS key, IAM role, or AWS Lambda function in any of the organization's accounts is shared with a principal outside the organization.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an organization external access analyzer in IAM Access Analyzer. Route findings to Amazon SNS with Amazon EventBridge.
options.rationale: An external access analyzer that uses the organization as its zone of trust analyzes resource-based policies and reports findings for resources shared outside the organization. Findings are sent to EventBridge, so a rule can notify the team through Amazon SNS.

options.text: Write a Lambda function that reads every resource policy each hour and compares the principals with the organization.
options.rationale: This is custom code that must understand complex policy logic for many resource types.

options.text: Configure Amazon GuardDuty in every account, and alert on findings that show data being read from S3 buckets.
options.rationale: GuardDuty detects threats from activity. It does not analyze resource policies for external sharing.

options.text: Use AWS Trusted Advisor to check bucket permissions weekly, and email the results to the security team.
options.rationale: The Trusted Advisor check covers only S3 bucket permissions, and a weekly email is not timely.

questions.question:
A company must find IAM roles that have not been used for 90 days, and permissions inside roles that are never used, so that the company can remove them and enforce least privilege across all of its accounts.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Create an unused access analyzer in IAM Access Analyzer with a 90-day tracking period.
options.rationale: An unused access analyzer reports unused roles, unused access keys and passwords, and unused service and action permissions, based on a tracking period that you choose. It can cover the whole organization and gives findings that you can act on.

options.text: Create an external access analyzer in IAM Access Analyzer with the account as the zone of trust.
options.rationale: External access analyzers find resources shared outside the zone of trust. They do not report unused permissions.

options.text: Search the AWS CloudTrail event history in each account for roles that have no events in 90 days.
options.rationale: Event history keeps only 90 days of management events for each Region, and analyzing it by hand across all accounts is slow and incomplete.

options.text: Configure AWS Config. Use a managed rule that deletes IAM roles that are older than 90 days.
options.rationale: A role's age does not show whether it is used, and deleting roles automatically could break workloads.

questions.question:
A company has a new application role with broad permissions. The application has run in a test account for 30 days with AWS CloudTrail enabled. The company needs a least-privilege policy based on what the application actually used.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate a policy from the role's CloudTrail activity. Review it.
options.rationale: Access Analyzer policy generation reviews the role's CloudTrail activity for a chosen period and creates a policy with the services and actions that the role actually used. The team reviews and refines the policy before attaching it.

options.text: Use the IAM policy simulator to generate a policy that allows every action the role has access to.
options.rationale: The simulator tests existing policies. It does not generate policies, and allowing every action is not least privilege.

options.text: Attach the ReadOnlyAccess managed policy. Add actions back when the application fails.
options.rationale: Fixing failures one at a time in production causes outages and slow progress.

options.text: Use AWS Config to record the role's permissions. Copy the recorded policy to production.
options.rationale: Config records the current broad policy, so copying it does not reduce the permissions.

questions.question:
A user in a member account has an IAM policy that allows ec2:RunInstances on all resources. When the user tries to launch a p4d.24xlarge Amazon EC2 instance, the request fails with an explicit deny, but launches of t3 instances work. No permissions boundary is attached to the user.

What is the MOST likely cause of this issue?

options.text: An SCP that applies to the account denies ec2:RunInstances for certain instance types.
options.rationale: An explicit deny that the user's own policy does not explain often comes from a service control policy. SCPs can deny actions with conditions such as ec2:InstanceType, and an explicit deny overrides the IAM allow. Decoding the authorization message shows which kind of policy denied the request.

options.text: The user's IAM policy is missing the ec2:DescribeInstanceTypes action for large types.
options.rationale: Describe permissions are not needed to launch a specific instance type, and a missing permission would cause an implicit deny, not an explicit deny.

options.text: The account has an On-Demand Instance quota that is too low for the p4d instance family.
options.rationale: A quota problem returns a limit exceeded error, not an access denied error.

options.text: The p4d.24xlarge instance type requires the user to sign in with the AWS account root user.
options.rationale: Launching instances never requires the root user.

questions.question:
An Amazon EC2 API call fails with an error that includes an encoded authorization failure message. A CloudOps engineer needs to see which policy statement denied the request.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Run aws sts decode-authorization-message with the encoded message.
options.rationale: STS DecodeAuthorizationMessage turns the encoded message into readable details about the request, including the matched statements and whether the deny was explicit. The caller needs the sts:DecodeAuthorizationMessage permission.

options.text: Run aws iam simulate-custom-policy with the encoded message text.
options.rationale: The policy simulator tests policies that you give it. It does not decode authorization messages.

options.text: Base64 decode the message locally to read the policy statement.
options.rationale: The message is encrypted, not just encoded, so it cannot be read with a simple Base64 decode.

options.text: Paste the encoded message into the AWS CloudTrail console to decode it.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records the failed call, but it does not decode this message.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon S3 bucket in account A. The bucket's objects are encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key in account A. A role in account B has an IAM policy that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket, and the bucket policy allows the role. Downloads from account B continue to fail with AccessDenied.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Allow the account B role to use kms:Decrypt in the key policy. Allow kms:Decrypt in the role's IAM policy.
options.rationale: To read objects encrypted with SSE-KMS, the caller needs permission to use the key. Across accounts, the key policy in account A must allow the account B role (or account B), and the role's IAM policy in account B must also allow kms:Decrypt on the key ARN.

options.text: Change the bucket's default encryption to SSE-S3 for new objects, and leave the existing objects encrypted as they are.
options.rationale: Existing objects stay encrypted with the KMS key, so reads of them would still fail.

options.text: Enable S3 Object Ownership with the bucket owner preferred setting.
options.rationale: Object Ownership controls who owns uploaded objects. It does not grant KMS permissions.

options.text: Add the account B role to the bucket's ACL with full control, in addition to the existing bucket policy.
options.rationale: ACLs grant S3 permissions only, and S3 access is already allowed. The missing piece is the KMS key permission.

questions.question:
A company attaches an SCP to the organization root that denies stopping AWS CloudTrail trails. During a test, a user in the management account can still stop a trail.

Why can the user stop the trail?

options.text: SCPs do not affect users and roles in the management account.
options.rationale: Service control policies never restrict the management account, even when they are attached to the organization root. Sensitive actions there must be controlled with IAM policies, and workloads should run in member accounts.

options.text: SCPs apply only to the root users of the member accounts.
options.rationale: SCPs apply to all IAM users and roles in member accounts, including the root user of those accounts.

options.text: SCPs take 24 hours to apply after they are attached to the root.
options.rationale: SCPs take effect quickly after they are attached. There is no 24-hour delay.

options.text: SCPs apply only to resources created after the SCP is attached.
options.rationale: SCPs restrict actions on all resources, no matter when the resources were created.

questions.question:
A company's security team must manage Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub CSPM, and IAM Access Analyzer for all accounts from a dedicated security account instead of the management account.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Register the security account as the delegated administrator for each service in Organizations.
options.rationale: Many security services support a delegated administrator. Registering the security account as the delegated administrator lets it enable and manage the service for all member accounts, so the security team does not need to work in the management account.

options.text: Move the security account to the root OU.
options.rationale: OU placement does not grant administrative powers over other accounts.

options.text: Create IAM users in the management account for the security team. Use them for each service.
options.rationale: This keeps the team working in the management account, which AWS recommends limiting to essential tasks.

options.text: Share the management account's root credentials with the security team for these three services.
options.rationale: Root credentials must never be shared.

questions.question:
A company is setting up a new multi-account environment. New accounts must be created with a standard baseline, central logging, and preventive and detective guardrails that are applied automatically.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Set up AWS Control Tower. Create accounts through Account Factory in governed OUs.
options.rationale: Control Tower sets up a landing zone with log archive and audit accounts, and Account Factory creates new accounts with a standard baseline. Controls are applied to OUs as preventive SCPs, detective AWS Config rules, and proactive CloudFormation hooks.

options.text: Create accounts with the Organizations API. Run a script that configures each new account.
options.rationale: Scripts can work, but they are custom tooling to build and maintain.

options.text: Create accounts manually, and ask each account owner to follow a written security checklist.
options.rationale: Manual setup and checklists are inconsistent, and they do not enforce guardrails.

options.text: Create one account for every workload. Use IAM policies as the only guardrails.
options.rationale: IAM policies alone can be changed by account administrators, and they give no organization-wide guardrails or central logging.

questions.question:
A company's finance team requires every new Amazon EC2 instance to have a CostCenter tag with one of five approved values. Launches that do not include a valid tag must be blocked in all accounts in the organization.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a tag policy that defines CostCenter and its allowed values, with enforcement for EC2 instances.
options.rationale: Tag policies standardize tag keys and values across the organization. With enforcement enabled for a resource type, a request that sets the tag to a value that is not allowed is blocked.

options.text: Create an SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances when aws:RequestTag/CostCenter is missing.
options.rationale: Tag policies do not block resources that are created without the tag. An SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances when the aws:RequestTag/CostCenter key is null makes the tag required at launch.

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that deletes instances without a CostCenter tag once a day.
options.rationale: Deleting instances after they launch is disruptive, and it does not block the launch.

options.text: Ask each team to add the CostCenter tag in the console when they launch instances.
options.rationale: A request to teams is not enforced, and it does not cover the CLI or automation.

options.text: Enable cost allocation tags in the Billing console for the CostCenter tag key only.
options.rationale: Cost allocation tags make tags appear in billing reports. They do not require or validate tags.

questions.question:
A company stores shared reports in an Amazon S3 bucket. Applications in every account in the company's organization in AWS Organizations must be able to read the reports, and no one outside the organization can have access. New accounts are added often.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject when aws:PrincipalOrgID matches the organization ID.
options.rationale: The aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key checks that the caller belongs to the organization, so new accounts are covered automatically and no account list is needed. Roles in other accounts still need IAM permissions to read the bucket. Resource control policies (RCPs) can enforce a similar boundary across many resources.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that lists the ID of every member account. Update it for each new account.
options.rationale: An account list works, but someone must update it every time an account is added, which is the overhead the company wants to avoid.

options.text: Create an IAM role in the bucket's account. Have the applications in each account assume it.
options.rationale: A shared role adds setup in every account and changes how each application reaches the reports.

options.text: Disable S3 Block Public Access. Allow s3:GetObject for all principals in the bucket policy.
options.rationale: This makes the bucket public, so anyone on the internet could read the reports.

questions.question:
A company uses a bastion host with SSH keys to administer Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The company's security team must remove the bastion host and all inbound SSH rules. The security team also needs a record of each session.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with an instance profile on each instance. Send session logs to Amazon S3.
options.rationale: Session Manager needs no open inbound ports, no bastion hosts, and no SSH keys. Access is controlled through IAM, and session logs can go to Amazon S3 or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The instances need an instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy.

options.text: Move the bastion host to a public subnet. Restrict inbound SSH to the office IP range, and log each SSH command.
options.rationale: This keeps the bastion host and the inbound SSH rules, which the security team must remove.

options.text: Use Amazon EC2 Instance Connect to push temporary SSH keys. Keep inbound port 22 open to the VPC CIDR block.
options.rationale: Instance Connect avoids long-term keys, but it still uses SSH and an inbound rule on port 22.

options.text: Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to the VPC. Allow inbound SSH from the on-premises network to the instances.
options.rationale: A VPN changes the network path, but the inbound SSH rules and SSH keys remain.

questions.question:
A company's engineers sign in to AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center. The engineers now need to run AWS CLI commands against several accounts, and they must not create IAM access keys.

What should the engineers do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure an AWS CLI profile for IAM Identity Center. Run aws sso login to get temporary credentials.
options.rationale: The AWS CLI supports IAM Identity Center profiles. aws sso login opens a browser sign-in, and the CLI then gets short-lived credentials for the chosen account and permission set, so no access keys are needed.

options.text: Create an IAM user with access keys in each account. Add the keys to the AWS CLI configuration file.
options.rationale: This creates long-lived access keys, which the engineers must avoid.

options.text: Copy the session cookie from the AWS access portal into the AWS CLI configuration on each workstation.
options.rationale: Session cookies are not CLI credentials, and copying them is insecure.

options.text: Ask an administrator to share the management account's access keys with all of the engineers' profiles.
options.rationale: Sharing access keys breaks least privilege and accountability.

questions.question:
A company uses AWS Organizations. The company's security team must ensure that no one in any member account, including account administrators, can stop AWS CloudTrail logging or delete a trail.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Attach an SCP to the member accounts' OUs that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail.
options.rationale: SCPs set the maximum permissions for every principal in member accounts, including administrators and the root user, and account administrators cannot remove them. An organization trail also helps, because member accounts cannot change it.

options.text: Attach an IAM policy that denies those actions to every IAM user and role in each of the member accounts.
options.rationale: Administrators in each account could detach or edit the policy, and new roles would not be covered automatically.

options.text: Enable CloudTrail log file integrity validation.
options.rationale: Validation proves whether log files changed after delivery. It does not stop anyone from disabling logging.

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that reports when CloudTrail logging is stopped in any member account.
options.rationale: Config can detect and report the change, but it does not prevent it.

questions.question:
