A company's AWS Trusted Advisor dashboard shows a red security check for security groups that allow unrestricted access (0.0.0.0/0) to port 22 on several production instances. Administrators use SSH only for occasional troubleshooting.

Which solution will resolve the finding and keep administrative access in the MOST secure manner?

options.text: Remove the SSH rules. Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager for administrative access.
options.rationale: Session Manager gives shell access through SSM Agent with no inbound ports and no SSH keys, and sessions are controlled by IAM and can be logged. Removing the open SSH rules removes the exposure that Trusted Advisor flagged.

options.text: Change the SSH rules to allow 0.0.0.0/0 on port 2222 instead of port 22 on the instances.
options.rationale: Moving SSH to another port still leaves it open to the whole internet.

options.text: Keep the SSH rules. Enable Amazon GuardDuty to detect brute force SSH attempts.
options.rationale: GuardDuty detects attacks, but the open port remains exposed.

options.text: Keep the SSH rules. Suppress the AWS Trusted Advisor check for these security groups.
options.rationale: Hiding the finding does not fix the exposure.

questions.question:
AWS notifies a company that an IAM user's access key was found in a public GitHub repository. The AWS Trusted Advisor Exposed Access Keys check is also red for the key.

What should a CloudOps engineer do FIRST?

options.text: Deactivate the exposed access key, and replace it with a new key or a role for the workload.
options.rationale: An exposed key must be treated as compromised. Deactivating it stops further use right away. The team should then replace it, preferably with temporary credentials from a role, review CloudTrail for misuse, and delete the old key.

options.text: Make the GitHub repository private to stop others from seeing the access key from now on.
options.rationale: The key has already been seen and may already be in use by attackers. Hiding the repository does not revoke it.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail Insights to report unusual API activity from the key in the future.
options.rationale: Detecting unusual activity later does not stop an attacker who already has the key.

options.text: Add the key to an IAM policy that denies it only for requests that come from outside the VPC.
options.rationale: IAM policies cannot target a single access key in this way, and the key would still be valid.

questions.question:
A company must receive a notification and must start remediation automatically whenever the status of an AWS Trusted Advisor security check changes to red in its account.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for Trusted Advisor check status changes in us-east-1 with Amazon SNS and AWS Lambda targets.
options.rationale: Trusted Advisor sends check status change events to EventBridge in the us-east-1 Region. A rule that matches red security checks can notify the team through Amazon SNS and invoke a Lambda function or an Automation runbook to remediate.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that watches the Trusted Advisor console page, and refresh the page every 5 minutes.
options.rationale: CloudWatch alarms watch metrics, not web pages.

options.text: Configure AWS Config in us-east-1. Create an AWS Config rule for each of the Trusted Advisor security checks.
options.rationale: Config rules evaluate resource configurations. They do not receive Trusted Advisor check results.

options.text: Export the Trusted Advisor report to Amazon S3 weekly, and run an AWS Lambda function that compares the reports.
options.rationale: Weekly comparisons are slow and are custom code to maintain.

questions.question:
A company uses AWS Organizations. An auditor requires 40 accounts to be continuously evaluated against a common set of controls based on the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, with results for each account.

Which solution will meet this requirement in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Deploy an AWS Config conformance pack based on the CIS template to all accounts from the delegated administrator.
options.rationale: A conformance pack is a collection of AWS Config rules and remediation actions that is deployed as one unit. Sample templates exist for frameworks such as CIS, and organization conformance packs deploy them to all member accounts and report compliance by account.

options.text: Write custom AWS Lambda functions for each CIS control, and run them in every account of the organization once a week.
options.rationale: Custom functions for every control are a lot of code to build and maintain, and weekly runs are not continuous.

options.text: Run Amazon Inspector in every account, and export the vulnerability findings to the auditor each month.
options.rationale: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities and network exposure. It does not evaluate CIS account configuration controls.

options.text: Configure AWS CloudTrail in every account, and ask the auditor to read through the trail logs for each of the controls.
options.rationale: Logs alone do not evaluate controls. The auditor would have to analyze configurations by hand.

questions.question:
A company uses AWS Config in 30 accounts and 3 AWS Regions. The company's compliance team needs a single view of noncompliant resources across all of those accounts and Regions.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Create an AWS Config aggregator for the organization in a central account.
options.rationale: An aggregator collects AWS Config configuration and compliance data from multiple accounts and Regions, or from a whole organization, into one account. The team can view and query noncompliant resources in one place.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard in each account that shows Config compliance data.
options.rationale: Per-account dashboards do not give a single cross-account view.

options.text: Copy every Config snapshot to one Amazon S3 bucket, and read the files manually each week.
options.rationale: Reading snapshot files by hand is slow and does not scale.

options.text: Create a Config rule in the central account that evaluates resources in all accounts.
options.rationale: Config rules evaluate resources in their own account and Region. An aggregator is needed to combine the results.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS Config managed rule that marks security groups that allow SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 as noncompliant. The company's security team needs these SSH rules removed automatically within minutes of detection.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Add an automatic remediation action to the Config rule that runs the AWS-DisablePublicAccessForSecurityGroup runbook.
options.rationale: Config rules can have remediation actions that run Systems Manager Automation runbooks. With automatic remediation enabled, Config runs the runbook, such as AWS-DisablePublicAccessForSecurityGroup, on each noncompliant security group by using an IAM role that you provide.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function that runs every hour, lists every security group in every Region, and removes any open SSH rules.
options.rationale: A scheduled function is custom code and runs only hourly, so open rules could exist for up to an hour.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty to remove the open SSH rules when it detects SSH brute force activity.
options.rationale: GuardDuty detects threats. It does not change security groups by itself.

options.text: Email the noncompliant resources to the security team each day to fix them manually.
options.rationale: Manual fixes are slow, and open SSH rules would stay in place for up to a day.

questions.question:
A company's policy requires every Amazon EBS volume to have a DataClass tag and to be encrypted. The company needs one AWS Config rule that checks both conditions together, but no managed rule does this.

What should a CloudOps engineer create to meet this requirement?

options.text: An AWS Config custom rule that uses AWS CloudFormation Guard or an AWS Lambda function
options.rationale: When no managed rule fits, a custom rule can evaluate configuration items with a policy written in CloudFormation Guard, or with a Lambda function for more complex logic. One rule can check both the tag and the encryption setting.

options.text: An AWS CloudTrail Insights selector for all of the EBS volume creation events
options.rationale: CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API activity rates. It does not evaluate resource configurations.

options.text: An AWS Trusted Advisor custom check that covers each of the EBS volumes
options.rationale: Trusted Advisor does not support custom checks of this kind.

options.text: An Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the VolumeQueueLength metric for each volume
options.rationale: VolumeQueueLength measures pending I/O. It says nothing about tags or encryption.

questions.question:
A company must be able to determine how each of its security groups was configured at any point in time. The company also must evaluate each configuration change against company rules.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable AWS Config to record security groups. Create AWS Config rules, and review the resource timeline for each security group.
options.rationale: AWS Config records how resources are configured and how they change over time, and the resource timeline shows each past configuration. AWS Config rules evaluate each change against the company's desired settings. CloudTrail shows who made the API call, while AWS Config shows the resulting configuration.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail Insights on the account's trail. Review the Insights events that are recorded for each security group.
options.rationale: CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API call rates. It does not keep the configuration of a security group at each point in time.

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs for each network interface. Run Amazon Athena queries against the logs to review accepted connections.
options.rationale: Flow logs show traffic that the security groups allowed or rejected, not the rules that were configured.

options.text: Review the AWS Trusted Advisor security checks each week. Export the results of each check to an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.rationale: Trusted Advisor checks show current best-practice results. They do not provide a history of each configuration change.

questions.question:
A company has 2,000 Amazon S3 buckets across many accounts. The company's security team needs to find which buckets contain personally identifiable information (PII), such as passport numbers and credit card numbers, and must continue to check as the data changes.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure Amazon Macie with automated sensitive data discovery for the organization.
options.rationale: Macie uses managed and custom data identifiers to find sensitive data, such as PII and financial data, in Amazon S3. Automated sensitive data discovery samples objects across buckets continuously and keeps a sensitivity score for each bucket, across the organization.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection to inspect every object for sensitive data.
options.rationale: GuardDuty S3 Protection detects suspicious access to S3. It does not inspect object contents for sensitive data.

options.text: Run Amazon Athena queries over every bucket each week to search for PII patterns.
options.rationale: Athena works only on data that you define tables for, and weekly custom queries across 2,000 buckets are a lot of work.

options.text: Use S3 Inventory reports to list object names that contain the words passport or card.
options.rationale: Object names do not show what the objects contain.

questions.question:
A company must continuously scan its Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon ECR container images for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. New resources must be included automatically.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable Amazon Inspector in the account. Review the findings for the EC2 instances and the container images.
options.rationale: Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability management service. It automatically discovers EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions, and it continually scans them for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the account. Review the threat findings for the EC2 instances and the container images.
options.rationale: GuardDuty detects active threats from logs and runtime activity. It does not inventory software vulnerabilities.

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie in the account. Review the sensitive data findings for the EC2 instances and the container images.
options.rationale: Macie finds sensitive data in Amazon S3. It does not scan instances or container images.

options.text: Enable AWS Config in the account. Review the compliance results for the EC2 instances and the container images.
options.rationale: AWS Config evaluates resource configuration. It does not scan installed software for known vulnerabilities.

questions.question:
A company is implementing a data classification scheme. Every Amazon S3 bucket must be labeled Public, Internal, or Confidential, and only the security team can read Confidential buckets. The company also must detect buckets that have no label.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Tag each bucket with a DataClassification key, and find missing tags with the AWS Config required-tags rule.
options.rationale: Tags are a common way to label resources with their classification. The AWS Config required-tags managed rule reports buckets that are missing the DataClassification key, so missing labels are found continuously.

options.text: Use bucket policies or tag-based conditions that let only the security team's roles read Confidential buckets.
options.rationale: Access controls based on the classification, such as a bucket policy or a condition on aws:ResourceTag/DataClassification, make sure that only the security team's roles can read Confidential data. Encryption with a customer managed KMS key adds another layer.

options.text: Record each bucket's classification in a spreadsheet, and review it with the security team every quarter.
options.rationale: A spreadsheet is not linked to the resources and goes out of date quickly.

options.text: Encrypt Confidential buckets with SSE-S3 to allow only the security team to decrypt the objects.
options.rationale: S3 manages SSE-S3 keys for every authorized user, so SSE-S3 does not limit who can read the objects.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning for Confidential buckets to stop other users from reading the objects.
options.rationale: Versioning keeps object versions. It does not restrict who can read objects.

questions.question:
A company's security team must receive an email notification whenever the root user of the company's AWS account is used. An AWS CloudTrail trail already delivers events to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Create a metric filter on the log group that matches root user activity. Create an alarm on the metric that notifies an Amazon SNS topic.
options.rationale: A metric filter on CloudTrail logs can match events where userIdentity.type is Root. An alarm on the resulting metric then notifies an SNS topic with an email subscription. AWS security standards recommend this exact control for root user use.

options.text: Enable AWS Config with the root-account-mfa-enabled managed rule. Send each rule compliance change to an Amazon SNS topic.
options.rationale: This rule checks whether the root user has MFA. It does not report when the root user is used.

options.text: Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer. Send each new analyzer finding to an Amazon SNS topic.
options.rationale: Access Analyzer finds resources that are shared outside the zone of trust. It does not report root user activity.

options.text: Review the AWS Trusted Advisor security checks each week. Send the summary to the security team's email address.
options.rationale: A weekly manual review does not notify the team whenever the root user is used.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that was created without encryption. A new policy requires all databases to be encrypted at rest with a customer managed AWS KMS key.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Take a snapshot, copy it with encryption using the KMS key, and restore a new DB instance from the copy.
options.rationale: Encryption cannot be enabled for an existing unencrypted RDS DB instance. Copying a snapshot with encryption and restoring it creates an encrypted instance. The application then moves to the new endpoint, so the change needs a planned cutover. An RDS blue/green deployment is a newer way to encrypt an unencrypted DB instance.

options.text: Modify the DB instance. Enable encryption with the KMS key. Apply the change immediately.
options.rationale: RDS does not support enabling encryption for an existing unencrypted DB instance.

options.text: Create an encrypted read replica of the unencrypted DB instance. Promote that read replica to primary.
options.rationale: RDS cannot create an encrypted read replica from an unencrypted DB instance.

options.text: Enable default Amazon EBS encryption in the Region.
options.rationale: EBS encryption by default applies to EBS volumes that you create. It does not change RDS storage.

questions.question:
A company needs every new Amazon EBS volume in an AWS Region to be encrypted automatically. The company also has an unencrypted data volume, attached to a running instance, that must be encrypted.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable EBS encryption by default for the account in the Region.
options.rationale: EBS encryption by default is a Regional account setting. After it is enabled, all new volumes and snapshot copies in the Region are encrypted with the default KMS key or a key that you choose.

options.text: Snapshot the volume, create an encrypted volume from it, and swap the volumes.
options.rationale: An existing volume cannot be encrypted in place. Creating an encrypted volume from a snapshot, and then attaching it in place of the old volume, encrypts the data. The switch needs a short planned stop for the data volume.

options.text: Run the modify-volume command with the encrypted option on the existing volume.
options.rationale: Elastic Volumes can change size, type, and performance, but it cannot encrypt an existing volume.

options.text: Attach an IAM policy that denies the creation of unencrypted EBS volumes only.
options.rationale: A deny policy blocks unencrypted volumes, but it does not encrypt anything automatically, and it does nothing for the existing volume.

options.text: Enable Amazon S3 default encryption for the bucket that stores the EBS snapshots.
options.rationale: EBS snapshots are not stored in a bucket that you manage, so S3 bucket settings do not apply.

questions.question:
A company has a data pipeline that writes millions of small objects every hour to an Amazon S3 bucket that uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. The pipeline receives ThrottlingException errors from AWS KMS, and KMS request costs are high.

Which solution will reduce the KMS requests with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure S3 Bucket Keys for the bucket's SSE-KMS encryption setting.
options.rationale: With S3 Bucket Keys, S3 uses a short-lived bucket-level key from AWS KMS to create data keys for objects, instead of calling KMS for every object. This can reduce KMS requests and costs by up to 99%.

options.text: Switch the bucket to dual-layer encryption with DSSE-KMS for every object.
options.rationale: Dual-layer encryption adds a second layer of encryption and increases KMS use instead of reducing it.

options.text: Create a second KMS key, and split the objects across the two keys at random.
options.rationale: Splitting traffic across keys needs application changes and does not reduce the total number of KMS requests, because request quotas are shared across keys in the account and Region.

options.text: Request a higher limit for the S3 PUT request rate on the bucket's prefixes.
options.rationale: The errors come from AWS KMS, not from S3 request rates.

questions.question:
A company's compliance standard requires the key material of a customer managed AWS KMS key to be rotated every 180 days. The key was created with key material that AWS KMS generated.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Enable automatic key rotation for the key with a rotation period of 180 days.
options.rationale: Automatic rotation for customer managed keys supports a custom rotation period from 90 to 2,560 days. KMS creates new key material on that schedule and keeps the older material to decrypt existing data, so nothing needs to be re-encrypted. On-demand rotation is also available.

options.text: Create a new key every 180 days, and re-encrypt all of the data with the new key manually.
options.rationale: Manual rotation with re-encryption is a lot of work and is not needed for keys with KMS-generated key material.

options.text: Enable automatic rotation for the AWS managed key that the service uses by default.
options.rationale: AWS managed keys rotate every year on a schedule that you cannot change.

options.text: Schedule the key for deletion every 180 days.
options.rationale: Deleting a key makes all data encrypted under it unrecoverable.

questions.question:
A company has an application that encrypts data in us-east-1 with an AWS KMS key and replicates the encrypted data to eu-west-1 for disaster recovery. The application in eu-west-1 must decrypt the data locally without calling the KMS key in us-east-1.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Use a KMS multi-Region primary key in us-east-1 and a replica key in eu-west-1.
options.rationale: Multi-Region keys are related keys in different Regions that share the same key ID and key material. Data encrypted with the primary key in us-east-1 can be decrypted with the replica key in eu-west-1 without any cross-Region KMS calls.

options.text: Create a new single-Region key in eu-west-1. Use it to decrypt the replicated data.
options.rationale: A different key cannot decrypt data that was encrypted under the original key.

options.text: Export the key material from us-east-1, and import it into the AWS managed key in eu-west-1.
options.rationale: AWS KMS does not let you export key material that it generated, and AWS managed keys cannot import key material.

options.text: Share the us-east-1 key with eu-west-1 by using AWS RAM.
options.rationale: KMS keys are not shared across Regions through AWS RAM.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer schedules a customer managed AWS KMS key for deletion with a 30-day waiting period because the company believes that the key is unused. The company must be alerted if anything tries to use the key during the waiting period.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Create a metric filter and alarm on AWS CloudTrail logs for requests that fail because the key is pending deletion.
options.rationale: During the waiting period, the key cannot be used, and requests that try to use it fail and are recorded in CloudTrail. A metric filter on those events in CloudWatch Logs, with an alarm, alerts the team so that it can cancel the deletion if the key is still needed.

options.text: Enable automatic key rotation to write a new entry in AWS CloudTrail each time that the key is used.
options.rationale: Rotation creates new key material. It does not alert anyone about attempted use.

options.text: Disable the key instead, and wait for the users of the key to open a support ticket with the team.
options.rationale: Disabling a key first is a safer test, but waiting for tickets is not an alert and may come too late.

options.text: Shorten the waiting period to 7 days to find any problems with the deletion sooner.
options.rationale: A shorter waiting period gives less time to find problems before the key, and any data encrypted under it, is lost for good.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon S3 bucket with default encryption that uses SSE-KMS with a specific customer managed key. Some applications upload objects with an explicit header that requests SSE-S3, which overrides the default. The company's security team requires every object to be encrypted with that KMS key.

Which solution will enforce this requirement?

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies PutObject requests whose encryption headers do not specify the required KMS key.
options.rationale: A bucket policy can deny PutObject requests unless the encryption headers name SSE-KMS and the required key, by using condition keys such as s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id. Uploads that ask for SSE-S3 or for a different key are rejected.

options.text: Enable S3 Bucket Keys to make all objects use the bucket-level key no matter which headers are sent.
options.rationale: S3 Bucket Keys reduce KMS request costs. They do not override an explicit request for SSE-S3.

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode to prevent objects from being uploaded with SSE-S3.
options.rationale: Object Lock protects object versions from deletion. It does not control encryption settings.

options.text: Rely on the bucket's default encryption setting, because it always overrides any headers that applications send.
options.rationale: Default encryption applies only when a request does not specify encryption. An explicit header overrides it.

questions.question:
A company runs a public website behind an Application Load Balancer that has only an HTTP listener on port 80. The company must serve all traffic over HTTPS with a free certificate that renews automatically. Users who type http:// must be sent to HTTPS.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Request a public ACM certificate with DNS validation. Add an HTTPS listener on port 443 that uses it.
options.rationale: Public ACM certificates are free, and ACM renews DNS-validated certificates automatically as long as the validation CNAME record stays in place. An HTTPS listener on the ALB terminates TLS with the certificate.

options.text: Change the port 80 listener's default action to redirect requests to HTTPS on port 443.
options.rationale: A listener rule with a redirect action returns an HTTP 301 response to the HTTPS URL, so users who type http:// are moved to HTTPS.

options.text: Install a self-signed certificate on each Amazon EC2 instance. Keep the ALB listener on port 80.
options.rationale: Browsers do not trust self-signed certificates, and the ALB would still serve plain HTTP to users.

options.text: Import a certificate bought from a third-party CA into ACM, and renew it manually every year.
options.rationale: Imported certificates cost money from the CA and are not renewed automatically by ACM.

options.text: Add a rule to the ALB security group that blocks inbound port 80 traffic from the internet.
options.rationale: Security groups cannot block traffic from the internet with a deny rule, and blocking port 80 would break users who type http:// instead of redirecting them.

questions.question:
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) sends a company a notice that a DNS-validated public certificate used by an Amazon CloudFront distribution is not eligible for automatic renewal. Someone recently cleaned up old records in the domain's Amazon Route 53 hosted zone.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Re-create the ACM validation CNAME record in the hosted zone.
options.rationale: ACM renews DNS-validated certificates automatically only while the CNAME validation record is present and resolvable. Restoring the record lets ACM validate the domain again and renew the certificate before it expires.

options.text: Request a new certificate with email validation. Attach it to the distribution each year.
options.rationale: Email validation requires someone to approve each renewal, which adds manual work and risk.

options.text: Export the certificate from ACM, and import it again.
options.rationale: Re-importing does not extend a certificate's expiration date, and ACM does not renew imported certificates.

options.text: Move the certificate to the Region of the CloudFront origin.
options.rationale: Certificates for CloudFront must be in us-east-1, regardless of where the origin is.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer requested an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for www.example.com in eu-west-1 and needs to use the certificate with an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The certificate does not appear in the certificate list in the CloudFront console.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Request or import the certificate in the us-east-1 Region, and select it in CloudFront.
options.rationale: CloudFront can use only ACM certificates that are in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, us-east-1. The certificate must be requested or imported there.

options.text: Wait 24 hours for the certificate to replicate from eu-west-1 to all CloudFront locations.
options.rationale: ACM certificates do not replicate between Regions.

options.text: Attach the certificate to an ALB in eu-west-1. Set that ALB as the CloudFront origin.
options.rationale: A certificate on the origin load balancer secures traffic from CloudFront to the origin. It does not serve the viewer-facing domain on CloudFront.

options.text: Share the certificate with the CloudFront service principal by using AWS Resource Access Manager.
options.rationale: ACM certificates are not shared with CloudFront through AWS RAM.

questions.question:
An auditor finds that clients can download objects from a company's Amazon S3 bucket over plain HTTP. The company requires all requests to the bucket to use TLS.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies all S3 actions when aws:SecureTransport is false.
options.rationale: aws:SecureTransport is false for requests made over HTTP. A Deny statement with that condition rejects every unencrypted request, so clients must use HTTPS.

options.text: Enable default encryption with SSE-KMS to encrypt all requests in transit.
options.rationale: Server-side encryption protects data at rest. It does not stop requests from using plain HTTP.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to route requests over encrypted connections.
options.rationale: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers. It does not block HTTP requests.

options.text: Enable S3 Block Public Access to reject HTTP requests from the internet.
options.rationale: Block Public Access controls public permissions. It does not decide whether authorized requests use TLS.

questions.question:
A company requires every connection to its Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance to use TLS. Some older clients still connect without TLS.

How should a CloudOps engineer enforce this requirement?

options.text: Set the rds.force_ssl parameter to 1 in the DB parameter group. Update the clients.
options.rationale: The rds.force_ssl parameter makes the database reject connections that do not use SSL/TLS. Clients must be updated to connect with TLS and to trust the RDS certificate authority before the change, or they will fail to connect.

options.text: Configure encryption at rest for the DB instance by restoring it from an encrypted snapshot copy.
options.rationale: Encryption at rest protects stored data. It does not force connections to use TLS.

options.text: Add a security group rule that allows only port 443 to the DB instance from the application.
options.rationale: PostgreSQL listens on its own port, usually 5432. A port 443 rule does not control whether database connections use TLS.

options.text: Configure IAM database authentication.
options.rationale: IAM authentication changes how users authenticate. It does not force other clients to use TLS.

questions.question:
A company imports certificates from a third-party certificate authority into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for several load balancers. ACM does not renew imported certificates, and one of the certificates expired last month and caused an outage.

Which solution will warn the company at least 30 days before an imported certificate expires?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the ACM DaysToExpiry metric, or an Amazon EventBridge rule for expiration events.
options.rationale: ACM publishes the DaysToExpiry metric for certificates and sends approaching expiration events to EventBridge, starting 45 days before expiration by default. An alarm or rule can notify the team in time to renew the certificate and import it again. The acm-certificate-expiration-check Config rule is another option.

options.text: Enable automatic renewal for each imported certificate in the ACM console settings.
options.rationale: ACM cannot renew imported certificates. They must be renewed with the issuing CA and imported again.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for ACM to log each expiration in the trail.
options.rationale: Expiration is not an API call, so CloudTrail does not record it.

options.text: Create an Amazon Route 53 health check for each of the domains to fail on the day that the certificate expires.
options.rationale: A health check that fails on the expiration day gives no warning in advance.

questions.question:
A company's security standard requires an Application Load Balancer to accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 with strong ciphers. A scan shows that the HTTPS listener still accepts TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Change the HTTPS listener's security policy to one that allows only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
options.rationale: The listener's security policy, such as ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06, sets which TLS versions and ciphers the load balancer negotiates. Choosing a policy that allows only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 stops the older protocols.

options.text: Import a new certificate into ACM that was issued with the TLS 1.3 protocol enabled for it.
options.rationale: Certificates are not tied to a TLS version. The protocol versions come from the listener's security policy.

options.text: Add a security group rule that blocks clients that try to connect with TLS 1.0 or 1.1.
options.rationale: Security groups filter by IP address, port, and protocol. They cannot see TLS versions.

options.text: Configure AWS WAF with a rule that blocks TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 requests at the listener.
options.rationale: AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests after TLS is negotiated, so it cannot control which TLS versions the listener accepts.

questions.question:
A company has an application that keeps the master password for an Amazon RDS for MySQL database in a configuration file. The password must be stored securely and rotated every 30 days without custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure manner?

options.text: Let RDS manage the master user password in AWS Secrets Manager. Set the rotation schedule to 30 days.
options.rationale: When RDS manages the master user password, it stores the password in Secrets Manager and rotates it with managed rotation, with no Lambda function to write. The application reads the current value from Secrets Manager. The default rotation period is 7 days, and it can be changed.

options.text: Store the password as a SecureString in Parameter Store. Enable its automatic rotation feature.
options.rationale: Parameter Store does not rotate SecureString parameters automatically.

options.text: Store the password in an encrypted Amazon S3 object. Replace it every 30 days by using a scheduled AWS Lambda script.
options.rationale: This is custom code, and the database password would still have to be changed and kept in sync correctly.

options.text: Store the password in an AWS Lambda environment variable. Update the variable manually each month.
options.rationale: Manual updates are error prone, and environment variables are not a secure secret store.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS Secrets Manager rotation function that runs in private subnets so that the function can reach an Amazon RDS database. Rotation fails, and the function's logs show timeouts when the function calls the Secrets Manager API. The subnets have no NAT gateway.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager that allows HTTPS from the function's security group.
options.rationale: A function in private subnets without a NAT gateway has no path to the public Secrets Manager endpoint. An interface VPC endpoint gives it a private path, and the endpoint's security group must allow inbound HTTPS from the function.

options.text: Move the rotation function out of the VPC to reach both Secrets Manager and the database.
options.rationale: Outside the VPC, the function could reach Secrets Manager but not the private database.

options.text: Increase the rotation function's timeout from 30 seconds to 15 minutes to give the API call time to finish.
options.rationale: The calls time out because there is no network path, so a longer timeout only delays the failure.

options.text: Attach the SecretsManagerReadWrite policy to the database's IAM role to complete the rotation.
options.rationale: This is a network problem, not a permissions problem, and the database does not call Secrets Manager.

questions.question:
A company has a secret in AWS Secrets Manager in account A that stores API credentials. An application role in account B must read the secret. The secret is encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager.

Which solution will allow the role in account B to read the secret?

options.text: Encrypt the secret with a customer managed key. Allow account B in the key policy and the secret policy.
options.rationale: Cross-account access to a secret needs a resource policy on the secret that allows the role, a customer managed KMS key whose key policy allows account B to decrypt, and an IAM policy in account B that allows GetSecretValue and kms:Decrypt. The policy of the AWS managed key cannot be changed to allow another account.

options.text: Add a resource policy to the secret that allows account B to read it. Keep using the aws/secretsmanager key.
options.rationale: The resource policy alone is not enough, because account B cannot use the AWS managed key.

options.text: Share the secret with account B by using AWS RAM. Keep using the aws/secretsmanager key for it.
options.rationale: Secrets Manager uses resource policies, not AWS RAM, for cross-account access, and account B still could not use the AWS managed key.

options.text: Replicate the secret to account B by using Secrets Manager replication to a Region in that account.
options.rationale: Replication copies a secret to other Regions in the same account, not to another account.

questions.question:
A company has a multi-Region application that reads database credentials from AWS Secrets Manager in us-east-1. During a disaster recovery test in us-west-2, the application cannot start because it cannot reach the secret.

Which solution will make the secret available in us-west-2 and keep it in sync with rotations?

options.text: Replicate the secret to us-west-2 with Secrets Manager multi-Region secret replication.
options.rationale: Secrets Manager can replicate a secret to other Regions. Replicas stay in sync when the primary secret's value changes, including through rotation, and the application can read the replica locally during a Regional outage.

options.text: Create a new secret in us-west-2 manually. Copy the value each time the secret rotates.
options.rationale: Manual copies drift out of sync after each rotation.

options.text: Store a copy of the secret value in Parameter Store in us-west-2 as a String parameter.
options.rationale: A String parameter stores the credentials in plain text, and it does not stay in sync with rotations.

options.text: Grant the us-west-2 application access to the us-east-1 secret's AWS KMS key in that Region.
options.rationale: The secret itself would still exist only in us-east-1, which might be unavailable during a disaster.

questions.question:
A company has an application that needs a third-party license key that never rotates, along with 30 other configuration values. The license key must be encrypted at rest at the lowest cost.

Where should a CloudOps engineer store the license key?

options.text: In Parameter Store as a SecureString standard parameter
options.rationale: SecureString parameters are encrypted with AWS KMS, and standard parameters have no storage charge. They suit secrets that do not need automatic rotation, such as a fixed license key.

options.text: In AWS Secrets Manager with a 30-day automatic rotation schedule
options.rationale: Secrets Manager charges for each secret every month and is built for rotation, which this key does not need.

options.text: In a plaintext String parameter in Parameter Store
options.rationale: A String parameter is not encrypted, so the license key would be stored in plain text.

options.text: In the application's source code repository
options.rationale: Secrets in source code can leak through the repository and its history.

questions.question:
Amazon GuardDuty reports a CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS finding for a company's Amazon EC2 instance. For future findings of this type, the company's security team needs the instance isolated automatically and its disks preserved for forensics.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use an Amazon EventBridge rule on the finding type to start automation that isolates the instance and snapshots its volumes.
options.rationale: GuardDuty sends findings to EventBridge. A rule that matches the finding type can start a Systems Manager Automation runbook or a Lambda function that replaces the instance's security groups with an isolation security group and creates EBS snapshots for forensics.

options.text: Enable GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 to terminate the instance as soon as malware is found.
options.rationale: Malware Protection scans EBS volumes and reports findings. It does not terminate instances, and terminating would destroy evidence.

options.text: Create a suppression rule for the finding type to stop the instance from sending cryptocurrency DNS queries.
options.rationale: Suppression rules hide findings from view. They do not stop the activity, and they would hide a real threat.

options.text: Add a GuardDuty trusted IP list that contains the instance's IP address to block its traffic.
options.rationale: Trusted IP lists tell GuardDuty not to generate findings for those addresses. They do not block traffic.

questions.question:
A company runs an approved vulnerability scanner from a fixed Amazon EC2 instance. Every day, Amazon GuardDuty generates many Recon:EC2/Portscan findings for this scanner, which hides real findings.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Create a GuardDuty suppression rule that matches the finding type and the scanner instance.
options.rationale: Suppression rules automatically archive new findings that match criteria such as the finding type and the instance ID. The expected scanner findings no longer appear in the active list, while other findings are unaffected.

options.text: Disable GuardDuty in the account during the hours of each day when the scanner is running.
options.rationale: Turning off GuardDuty leaves the account unmonitored for real threats during those hours.

options.text: Archive each Portscan finding manually from the GuardDuty console after the security team reviews it.
options.rationale: Archiving findings by hand every day is repetitive work that suppression rules automate.

options.text: Add the scanner's IP address to a GuardDuty threat list.
options.rationale: Threat lists contain known malicious IP addresses and would generate more findings, not fewer.

questions.question:
A company must detect threats in its AWS account, such as Amazon EC2 instances that communicate with known malicious IP addresses and unusual API activity. The solution must analyze existing AWS logs and must not require agents on the instances.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the account. Send the findings to the security team through Amazon EventBridge.
options.rationale: GuardDuty is a threat detection service that analyzes data sources such as CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs. It uses threat intelligence and machine learning, and its foundational detection needs no agents.

options.text: Enable Amazon Inspector in the account. Send the findings to the security team through Amazon EventBridge.
options.rationale: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities and network exposure. It does not detect active threats such as communication with malicious IP addresses.

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie in the account. Send the findings to the security team through Amazon EventBridge.
options.rationale: Macie finds sensitive data in Amazon S3. It does not monitor instance traffic or API activity.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events. Run a weekly Amazon Athena query to find unusual activity in the events.
options.rationale: This needs custom queries and a weekly review. It would not use threat intelligence to identify malicious IP addresses.

questions.question:
A company uses Amazon Inspector agent-based scanning for the Amazon EC2 instances in an account. Several instances show no vulnerability findings and are listed as unmanaged. SSM Agent is installed on these instances, but the instances have no instance profile.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Attach an instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the instances.
options.rationale: For agent-based scanning, an instance must be managed by Systems Manager: SSM Agent must be running, and the instance needs permission. AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore provides that permission. With hybrid or agentless scanning enabled, Inspector can also scan unmanaged instances by using EBS snapshots.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring to send vulnerability data to Amazon Inspector.
options.rationale: Runtime Monitoring detects threats in running workloads for GuardDuty. It does not supply package inventories to Inspector.

options.text: Enable AWS Config recording for the instances to allow Amazon Inspector to read their package list.
options.rationale: Inspector does not use Config data to find software vulnerabilities.

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs for the instances to allow Amazon Inspector to find old software packages.
options.rationale: Flow logs record network traffic metadata. They do not show installed software versions.

questions.question:
A company's security team needs all accounts in the organization evaluated against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard. The same standards and controls must be enabled in every account and AWS Region and must be managed from one place.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Security Hub CSPM central configuration from the delegated administrator with a configuration policy.
options.rationale: Central configuration lets the delegated administrator create configuration policies that enable Security Hub CSPM, standards, and controls for chosen accounts, OUs, and Regions. New accounts get the same settings automatically.

options.text: Configure AWS Security Hub CSPM in each account and Region manually. Enable the standard in each one.
options.rationale: Configuring every account and Region by hand is slow and drifts over time.

options.text: Deploy a separate AWS Config rule for each control in the standard by using a StackSet for every account.
options.rationale: Rebuilding the standard as separate Config rules is a large effort that Security Hub CSPM already provides.

options.text: Configure Amazon Inspector in every account.
options.rationale: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities. It does not evaluate the best practices controls.

questions.question:
AWS Security Hub CSPM generates findings for a control whose risk a company has accepted for its development accounts only. These findings must be marked as suppressed automatically in development accounts, while the same findings stay active in production accounts.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an automation rule that matches the control in development accounts and sets the status to SUPPRESSED.
options.rationale: Automation rules update findings as Security Hub receives them, based on criteria such as the control ID and the account ID. Setting the workflow status to SUPPRESSED for development accounts hides the accepted findings there, while production findings stay active.

options.text: Disable the control in every account and Region in the organization, including the production accounts.
options.rationale: Disabling the control everywhere removes the check from production too.

options.text: Archive each finding in the development accounts manually after it appears in the Security Hub console.
options.rationale: Manual handling is repetitive and easy to forget.

options.text: Disable Security Hub CSPM in the development accounts.
options.rationale: Turning off Security Hub CSPM removes all of the other checks in those accounts.

questions.question:
A company's security team receives separate findings from Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, and AWS Security Hub CSPM. The security team needs these signals correlated to show which resources face the highest risk.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable AWS Security Hub, which correlates the signals into exposures and prioritizes risks.
options.rationale: AWS Security Hub correlates signals from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and Security Hub CSPM and identifies exposures, such as a reachable resource with an exploitable vulnerability. It prioritizes risks so that the team can act on the most important issues first.

options.text: Export all findings to Amazon S3, and write Amazon Athena queries that join them by resource ID.
options.rationale: Custom queries can join findings, but building and maintaining risk correlation logic is a large effort.

options.text: Enable AWS Config aggregators.
options.rationale: Config aggregators combine configuration and compliance data. They do not correlate security findings from these services.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that shows the finding counts for each service side by side.
options.rationale: Counts side by side do not show which specific resources combine several risks.

questions.question:
A company needs to test a new customer-facing web application for exploitable vulnerabilities before each major release. The company has no penetration testing staff and needs on-demand tests that take the application's design and code into account.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Security Agent to run on-demand penetration tests against the application.
options.rationale: AWS Security Agent performs on-demand penetration testing that uses context from the application's design documents, source code, and infrastructure as code. It reports exploitable vulnerabilities with guidance for fixing them, and it also offers design and code security reviews.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty for the account to test the application for attacks.
options.rationale: GuardDuty detects threats from activity in the account. It does not attack your application to find vulnerabilities.

options.text: Enable Amazon Inspector to perform penetration tests on the web application.
options.rationale: Inspector scans for known software vulnerabilities and network reachability. It does not perform penetration tests of application logic.

options.text: Enable AWS Shield Advanced to simulate attacks against the application.
options.rationale: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS attacks. It does not test applications for vulnerabilities.

questions.question:
A company's administrators use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to access Amazon EC2 instances. Auditors require a record of every command typed in each session, and the session data must be encrypted with a key that the company controls.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure Session Manager preferences to send session logs to Amazon S3 or Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
options.rationale: Session Manager can upload or stream session output, including the commands that are run, to an S3 bucket or a CloudWatch Logs log group for auditing.

options.text: Configure AWS KMS encryption of session data with a customer managed key in the preferences.
options.rationale: Session Manager preferences can require that session data is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, in addition to the TLS encryption that protects data in transit.

options.text: Open port 22 on the instances to capture session commands by using VPC Flow Logs.
options.rationale: Session Manager does not use SSH, and flow logs record only traffic metadata, not commands.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events to record every command that is typed in a session.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records the StartSession API call and who started it, but not the commands typed inside the session.

options.text: Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent to capture the keyboard input of each session.
options.rationale: The CloudWatch agent collects metrics and log files. It is not the way to record session activity.

questions.question:
A company has Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet that cannot download operating system updates from the internet. A NAT gateway was created in the same private subnet, and the private subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to that NAT gateway.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Create the NAT gateway in a public subnet that routes to an internet gateway. Point the private route at it.
options.rationale: A public zonal NAT gateway must be in a public subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. A NAT gateway inside the private subnet has no path to the internet, so its traffic goes nowhere. A regional NAT gateway is another option that does not need a public subnet.

options.text: Assign an Elastic IP address to each instance in the private subnet.
options.rationale: Instances in a subnet without a route to an internet gateway cannot use public IP addresses to reach the internet, and the design is meant to keep them private.

options.text: Add an inbound rule to the instance security group that allows all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on every port.
options.rationale: Security groups are stateful, so return traffic for outbound requests is already allowed. Opening inbound access adds risk and does not create a route.

options.text: Change the private subnet's route for 0.0.0.0/0 to the VPC's local route instead of to the NAT gateway.
options.rationale: The local route covers only traffic within the VPC's CIDR range. It cannot send traffic to the internet.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer launches a web server on an Amazon EC2 instance in a subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. The instance's security group allows HTTP from 0.0.0.0/0. Users still cannot reach the server from the internet.

What is the MOST likely cause of this issue?

options.text: The instance does not have a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP address.
options.rationale: An instance needs a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP address to be reached from the internet through an internet gateway. If auto-assign public IP is disabled for the subnet, the instance has only a private address.

options.text: The subnet's default network ACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic.
options.rationale: The default network ACL allows all traffic, so it would not block the users.

options.text: The VPC does not have a NAT gateway for inbound traffic from the internet.
options.rationale: NAT gateways are for outbound connections from private subnets. They do not accept inbound connections from the internet.

options.text: The security group needs an outbound rule that allows the HTTP responses.
options.rationale: Security groups are stateful, so responses to allowed inbound requests are allowed automatically.

questions.question:
A company has a custom network ACL on a public subnet. The network ACL allows inbound TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and outbound TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0, and it denies all other traffic. Clients cannot load pages from a web server in the subnet, and their connections time out.

What should a CloudOps engineer change to resolve this issue?

options.text: Allow outbound TCP 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0 in the network ACL for return traffic.
options.rationale: Network ACLs are stateless, so return traffic must be allowed explicitly. Responses from the server go to the client's ephemeral port, typically in the range 1024-65535, which the outbound rules currently deny.

options.text: Allow inbound TCP 1024-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0 in the instance's security group.
options.rationale: Security groups are stateful and already allow responses. The block is in the stateless network ACL.

options.text: Add an outbound rule for TCP 443 to the instance's security group for responses.
options.rationale: Security groups track connections, so responses to allowed inbound traffic do not need outbound rules.

options.text: Move the deny rule for all traffic to the lowest rule number.
options.rationale: Rules are evaluated from the lowest number up, so a deny-all rule at the top would block all traffic, including HTTPS.

questions.question:
A company has a three-tier application with web, app, and database tiers. The app tier runs in an Auto Scaling group whose instance IP addresses change often. The database security group must allow MySQL traffic only from the app tier instances.

How should a CloudOps engineer configure the database security group?

options.text: Add an inbound rule for port 3306 with the app tier's security group as the source.
options.rationale: A security group rule can use another security group as its source. Any instance that has the app tier's security group is allowed, whatever its IP address, so scaling events need no rule changes.

options.text: Add an inbound rule for port 3306 with the app subnet's CIDR blocks as the source.
options.rationale: CIDR blocks allow every resource in those subnets, not only the app tier, and they need updates if the subnets change.

options.text: Add a network ACL rule that allows port 3306 from each app instance's current IP address.
options.rationale: Per-instance IP rules break whenever instances are replaced, and network ACLs have a small rule limit.

options.text: Add an inbound rule for port 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0, and rely on the private subnets.
options.rationale: 0.0.0.0/0 allows any source that can route to the database, which is far broader than required.

questions.question:
A company has a VPC with IPv6 enabled. Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet must reach IPv6 software repositories on the internet, but inbound IPv6 connections from the internet must not reach the instances.

What should a CloudOps engineer configure to meet these requirements?

options.text: An egress-only internet gateway with a ::/0 route from the private subnet
options.rationale: An egress-only internet gateway allows outbound IPv6 traffic and the responses to it, but it blocks connections that start from the internet. It is the IPv6 equivalent of outbound-only access through a NAT gateway.

options.text: A NAT gateway with an IPv6 route from the private subnet to ::/0
options.rationale: NAT gateways translate IPv4 addresses (and support NAT64 to reach IPv4 services). They are not used for IPv6-to-IPv6 egress.

options.text: An internet gateway with a ::/0 route and a network ACL that blocks inbound
options.rationale: An internet gateway allows inbound IPv6 connections. A stateless network ACL that blocks inbound traffic would also block the responses unless it is carefully tuned, which is fragile.

options.text: A gateway VPC endpoint for the repositories with an IPv6 prefix list
options.rationale: Gateway VPC endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, not for general internet repositories.

questions.question:
A company has a VPC with private subnets in three Availability Zones. All of the subnets route through a single NAT gateway in one Availability Zone. When that Availability Zone had an outage, instances in the other two Availability Zones lost internet access.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to prevent this issue?

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone. Route each private subnet to its own zone's gateway.
options.rationale: A zonal NAT gateway runs in one Availability Zone, so it is lost with that zone. One NAT gateway per zone, with each private route table pointing to the gateway in the same zone, keeps the other zones online and avoids cross-zone data charges. NAT gateways now also offer a regional availability mode that spans zones automatically.

options.text: Add a second Elastic IP address to the existing NAT gateway.
options.rationale: Elastic IP addresses do not move a NAT gateway out of its Availability Zone.

options.text: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance in an Auto Scaling group that has a desired capacity of one.
options.rationale: A NAT instance is a server to patch and scale, and it is still a single point of failure while it is being replaced.

options.text: Add an internet gateway route to the private subnets for use when the NAT gateway is unavailable.
options.rationale: An internet gateway route makes the subnets public, and instances without public IP addresses still could not use it.

questions.question:
A company has a VPC with the CIDR block 10.0.0.0/24 that has run out of IP addresses. The company cannot re-create the VPC because many resources depend on it.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Associate a secondary IPv4 CIDR block with the VPC. Create new subnets in it.
options.rationale: You can add secondary IPv4 CIDR blocks to an existing VPC, within the allowed ranges, and create new subnets in them. Existing resources keep working, and new resources use the new subnets.

options.text: Change the VPC's primary CIDR block from /24 to /16 by editing the VPC settings.
options.rationale: A VPC's primary CIDR block cannot be changed after the VPC is created.

options.text: Resize the existing subnets to larger CIDR blocks while the instances keep running.
options.rationale: A subnet's CIDR block cannot be changed after the subnet is created.

options.text: Delete the five reserved addresses in each subnet.
options.rationale: AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet, and they cannot be released.

questions.question:
A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. Requests to example.com/api must go to one group of instances, and requests to example.com/images must go to a different group of instances. All requests must use the same domain name and HTTPS.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use one Application Load Balancer with two target groups. Add listener rules with path conditions that route each path to its target group.
options.rationale: An Application Load Balancer works at the application layer. A listener rule with a path-pattern condition can send each URL path to its own target group behind one domain name and one HTTPS listener.

options.text: Use one Network Load Balancer with two target groups. Configure the TCP listener to choose a target group based on the URL path.
options.rationale: A Network Load Balancer works at the transport layer and cannot read the URL path.

options.text: Use two Application Load Balancers. Create an Amazon Route 53 weighted record that splits the traffic between the load balancers.
options.rationale: Weighted records split traffic by percentage. DNS cannot route by URL path.

options.text: Use one target group for all instances. Run a reverse proxy on every instance that forwards requests to the correct group of instances.
options.rationale: This adds software to manage on every instance for a feature that the load balancer provides.

questions.question:
A company's partner accepts API calls only from a fixed list of IP addresses. The company's application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets that use a NAT gateway for outbound traffic.

Which IP address should the company give to the partner?

options.text: The Elastic IP address that is associated with the NAT gateway
options.rationale: Traffic from the private subnets leaves through the NAT gateway, which replaces the source address with its Elastic IP address. The partner sees only that address, so allowlisting it covers every instance behind the NAT gateway.

options.text: The private IP addresses that are assigned to each application instance
options.rationale: Private addresses are not routable on the internet, and the partner never sees them.

options.text: The public IP address of the VPC's internet gateway
options.rationale: An internet gateway does not have its own public IP address. It translates addresses that belong to resources.

options.text: The CIDR block of the private subnets in the VPC
options.rationale: Private CIDR blocks are not visible on the internet.

questions.question:
A company has applications in private subnets that upload large amounts of data to Amazon S3 in the same AWS Region through a NAT gateway. NAT gateway data processing charges are high. The company's security team also requires this path to reach only the company's own buckets.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3. Associate it with the private subnets' route tables.
options.rationale: A gateway endpoint for S3 adds a route that uses the S3 prefix list, so traffic to S3 in the Region bypasses the NAT gateway. Gateway endpoints have no hourly or data processing charge.

options.text: Attach an endpoint policy that allows access only to the company's bucket ARNs.
options.rationale: Endpoint policies control which actions and resources can be reached through the endpoint. Allowing only the company's bucket ARNs stops data from being sent to other buckets through this path.

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for S3 in each subnet to remove all charges for S3 traffic.
options.rationale: Interface endpoints for S3 have hourly and data processing charges. They are useful for on-premises access, but the gateway endpoint is the cheaper fix here.

options.text: Move the NAT gateway to a larger size to process data at a lower price per GB.
options.rationale: NAT gateways do not have sizes, and data processing is charged per GB.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to make uploads bypass the NAT gateway automatically.
options.rationale: Transfer Acceleration uses edge locations and still sends traffic from private subnets through the NAT gateway, and it adds charges.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer creates an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon SQS with private DNS enabled. Amazon EC2 instances in the VPC still resolve sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com to public IP addresses, and their requests go through the NAT gateway.

What should the CloudOps engineer check FIRST?

options.text: Verify that the VPC has both the enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames attributes enabled.
options.rationale: Private DNS for interface endpoints relies on the Amazon-provided DNS resolver and a private hosted zone that AWS manages. Both enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames must be true on the VPC for the service name to resolve to the endpoint's private addresses.

options.text: Verify that the endpoint's security group allows inbound UDP port 53 from the instance subnets.
options.rationale: DNS queries go to the VPC resolver, not to the endpoint, so the endpoint does not need to allow port 53. It needs to allow HTTPS from clients.

options.text: Verify that the SQS queue policy allows access only from the endpoint's private IP addresses.
options.rationale: A queue policy controls access, but it does not change how the name resolves.

options.text: Verify that a gateway VPC endpoint for SQS is attached to each of the private subnets' route tables.
options.rationale: Gateway endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB.

questions.question:
A SaaS company must offer a TCP service to 200 customer VPCs in other AWS accounts. Many customer VPCs use CIDR blocks that overlap with the company's VPC. Customers must not get access to any other resources in the company's VPC.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Put the service behind a Network Load Balancer, and share it as a PrivateLink endpoint service.
options.rationale: AWS PrivateLink exposes a service behind a Network Load Balancer as an endpoint service. Customers create interface endpoints in their own VPCs, traffic flows only to the service, and overlapping CIDR blocks do not matter because there is no routing between the VPCs.

options.text: Create a VPC peering connection with each customer VPC. Add routes to the service subnet.
options.rationale: VPC peering does not work with overlapping CIDR blocks, and peering gives broader network access than one service.

options.text: Attach every customer VPC to a shared transit gateway. Add routes to the service subnet.
options.rationale: Transit Gateway routing also fails with overlapping CIDR blocks, and it exposes more of the network.

options.text: Give the service a public IP address, and ask customers to reach it through their NAT gateways.
options.rationale: Public exposure sends traffic over the internet and opens the service to anyone who can reach it.

questions.question:
A company has VPC A peered with VPC B, and VPC B peered with VPC C. Instances in VPC A cannot reach instances in VPC C, even though all route tables have routes for the peering connections that they use.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to allow traffic between VPC A and VPC C?

options.text: Create a peering connection between VPC A and VPC C. Add routes in both VPCs.
options.rationale: VPC peering is not transitive, so traffic cannot pass through VPC B to reach VPC C. A direct peering connection between A and C, with routes on both sides and matching security group rules, connects them. For many VPCs, a transit gateway is easier to manage.

options.text: Add a route in VPC A that sends VPC C's CIDR block to the A-to-B peering connection.
options.rationale: VPC B does not forward traffic between peering connections, so this route does not work.

options.text: Enable DNS resolution for the existing peering connections in both of the directions.
options.rationale: DNS resolution settings help resolve private hostnames. They do not make peering transitive.

options.text: Allow VPC C's CIDR block in the security groups of the instances in VPC A and VPC B.
options.rationale: Security groups allow traffic only when a route exists, and there is no route from A to C.

questions.question:
A company connects 30 VPCs to a transit gateway. Production VPCs must not be able to reach development VPCs, but every VPC must be able to reach a shared services VPC.

How should a CloudOps engineer configure the transit gateway to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use separate TGW route tables for production and development that both propagate the shared VPC.
options.rationale: Transit gateway route tables control which attachments can reach each other. Production attachments associate with a production route table and development attachments with a development route table. Each of these tables has routes to the shared services VPC but not to the other environment, and the shared services table has routes to both.

options.text: Use one TGW route table for every attachment, and block the traffic with network ACLs in each of the VPCs.
options.rationale: A single route table lets every VPC reach every other VPC, and maintaining network ACLs in 30 VPCs is error prone.

options.text: Create a separate transit gateway for each VPC, and peer every transit gateway with each other.
options.rationale: Thirty transit gateways and a full mesh of peering connections add cost and complexity.

options.text: Disable default route table association, and leave the attachments without any route tables.
options.rationale: Attachments without route tables cannot route traffic at all, so no VPC could reach the shared services VPC.

questions.question:
A company's on-premises servers connect to a VPC through AWS Direct Connect with a private virtual interface. The servers must upload data to Amazon S3 privately, without traversing the public internet.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for S3. Have the servers use its endpoint-specific DNS names.
options.rationale: Interface endpoints for S3 have private IP addresses in the VPC, so on-premises servers can reach them over Direct Connect or VPN. The servers use the endpoint-specific DNS names, or Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints with private DNS, to send S3 requests through the endpoint.

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3. Add a route to it in each of the on-premises router tables.
options.rationale: Gateway endpoints work only for traffic that starts inside the VPC. They cannot be reached from on-premises networks.

options.text: Route the on-premises traffic through a NAT gateway in the VPC to reach the public S3 endpoint.
options.rationale: VPCs do not support edge-to-edge routing, so on-premises traffic cannot use the VPC's NAT gateway to reach the internet.

options.text: Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration. Send the uploads to the accelerate endpoint over the link.
options.rationale: Transfer Acceleration sends traffic over the internet to edge locations, not over the private link.

questions.question:
A company uses AWS Site-to-Site VPN with static routing, and only one of the two tunnels is configured on its customer gateway device. During AWS maintenance on that tunnel, the company lost connectivity.

Which solution will provide automatic failover between the tunnels?

options.text: Configure both tunnels on the customer gateway. Use BGP dynamic routing for failover.
options.rationale: Each Site-to-Site VPN connection has two tunnels that terminate on different AWS endpoints for redundancy. Configuring both tunnels and using BGP lets traffic move to the healthy tunnel automatically during maintenance or a failure.

options.text: Create a second customer gateway in AWS that points to the same IP address of the device.
options.rationale: A second customer gateway resource with the same IP address does not add a tunnel on the device, so the single-tunnel problem remains.

options.text: Replace the VPN with a VPC peering connection to the on-premises network for redundancy.
options.rationale: VPC peering connects VPCs only. It cannot connect to an on-premises network.

options.text: Enable acceleration for the VPN.
options.rationale: Accelerated VPN improves performance through AWS Global Accelerator. It does not keep a tunnel up during maintenance.

questions.question:
A company has a login page behind an Application Load Balancer. The page receives credential stuffing attacks in which single IP addresses send thousands of requests per minute. Normal users send fewer than 20 login requests in 5 minutes.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to mitigate these attacks?

options.text: Add an AWS WAF rate-based rule, scoped down to the login path, that blocks IPs over a limit.
options.rationale: A rate-based rule counts requests from each IP address over a time window and blocks addresses that exceed the limit. A scope-down statement limits the count to the login path, so normal browsing is not affected. The AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention rule group adds more protection.

options.text: Add a security group rule on the ALB that denies the attacking IP addresses as they appear.
options.rationale: Security groups do not support deny rules, and tracking attacker IP addresses by hand cannot keep up.

options.text: Enable AWS Shield Standard for the ALB to block each of the credential stuffing attempts.
options.rationale: Shield Standard protects against common network and transport layer DDoS attacks. It does not inspect login requests.

options.text: Increase the ALB idle timeout to limit how many connections attackers can open each minute.
options.rationale: A longer idle timeout keeps connections open longer, which does not limit requests.

questions.question:
A company plans to add the AWS Managed Rules core rule set to the AWS WAF web ACL of a production application. The company is concerned that some of the rules might block legitimate traffic.

How should a CloudOps engineer roll out the rule group safely?

options.text: Add the rule group with its action overridden to Count, review the logs, and then switch to Block.
options.rationale: Overriding rule actions to Count lets AWS WAF record which requests would match without blocking them. After reviewing WAF logs and sampled requests, the team can exclude or scope down noisy rules and then enable blocking.

options.text: Add the rule group in Block mode during a weekend. Remove it if users complain on Monday.
options.rationale: Blocking first risks an outage, and waiting for complaints means that real users were affected.

options.text: Add the rule group to a web ACL that is not associated with any resource, and then wait for one week.
options.rationale: A web ACL that is not associated with a resource sees no traffic, so it provides no data.

options.text: Add the rule group. Change the web ACL's default action from Allow to Block at the same time.
options.rationale: Changing the default action to Block would block all traffic that no rule allows, which is a much bigger change.

questions.question:
A company enables AWS WAF for its application. Some customers now receive HTTP 403 errors when they submit a support form that contains code samples. A CloudOps engineer needs to find which rule blocks these requests.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Enable web ACL logging, and look for the terminatingRuleId in the logs for the blocked requests.
