options.rationale: Web ACL logs record each inspected request, the action taken, and the terminatingRuleId of the rule that blocked it. Logs can go to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or Data Firehose. Sampled requests in the console also help.

options.text: Configure ALB access logs, and look for the WAF rule name inside the user agent field of each request.
options.rationale: ALB access logs do not record which WAF rule matched, and the user agent is set by the client.

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs for the ALB subnets, and look for rejected packets from the customers.
options.rationale: The requests are blocked at layer 7 with an HTTP 403 response, so flow logs would show accepted traffic.

options.text: Configure AWS CloudTrail data events for AWS WAF.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records WAF configuration API calls, not the web requests that AWS WAF inspects.

questions.question:
A company's public website has been hit by large DDoS attacks that caused scaling costs to spike. The company needs 24/7 access to the AWS Shield Response Team during attacks and protection against scaling charges caused by DDoS attacks.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Add the website's resources as protected resources.
options.rationale: Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation for protected resources such as CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, Global Accelerator accelerators, and Route 53 hosted zones. It includes access to the Shield Response Team and cost protection for scaling charges caused by DDoS attacks.

options.text: Rely on AWS Shield Standard, which includes the Shield Response Team at no extra cost.
options.rationale: Shield Standard protects all AWS customers against common attacks at no cost, but it does not include the Shield Response Team or cost protection.

options.text: Add AWS WAF rate-based rules, which include cost protection for DDoS scaling charges.
options.rationale: Rate-based rules help with application layer floods, but AWS WAF does not provide DDoS cost protection.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty. Use its findings to request credits for DDoS scaling charges.
options.rationale: GuardDuty detects threats in your account. It is not a DDoS protection service, and it does not provide credits.

questions.question:
A company must restrict outbound internet traffic from its private subnets to an approved list of domain names, such as updates.example.com, and block everything else. The traffic currently leaves through a NAT gateway.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group. Route egress traffic through it.
options.rationale: Network Firewall supports stateful domain list rules that inspect the TLS SNI and HTTP Host header to allow or deny traffic by domain name. Routing the private subnets' egress through firewall endpoints before the NAT gateway enforces the allow list.

options.text: Add security group outbound rules that allow the approved domain names and deny all of the other traffic.
options.rationale: Security groups work with IP addresses, CIDR blocks, prefix lists, and other security groups. They cannot filter by domain name, and they have no deny rules.

options.text: Add network ACL rules that allow the approved domain names and deny all other outbound traffic.
options.rationale: Network ACLs filter by IP address and port only.

options.text: Create an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone for each approved domain.
options.rationale: Private hosted zones answer for the names that they contain. They do not stop queries for other names or connections to other IP addresses.

questions.question:
A company's security team must stop Amazon EC2 instances in every VPC in the account from resolving domain names that are known to be used for malware and botnet command and control. The company does not want to maintain domain lists manually.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with AWS managed domain lists associated with each VPC.
options.rationale: DNS Firewall filters DNS queries that go through Route 53 Resolver in your VPCs. AWS managed domain lists, such as lists of malware and botnet domains, are kept up to date by AWS, and a rule group can block or alert on queries that match them.

options.text: Add a network ACL rule that denies outbound traffic on port 53 from every subnet in each VPC.
options.rationale: Blocking all DNS traffic would break every name lookup, not only the malicious ones.

options.text: Configure Amazon GuardDuty.
options.rationale: GuardDuty detects DNS activity linked to threats and reports findings, but it does not block queries.

options.text: Create a private hosted zone named com that returns 0.0.0.0 for every malicious domain name.
options.rationale: A hosted zone named com would break resolution of every .com domain, and keeping it current by hand is the work the team wants to avoid.

questions.question:
A company's bill shows high Regional data transfer charges. Application instances in us-east-1a send most of their internet traffic to a NAT gateway in us-east-1b and read from database replicas in other Availability Zones. The company must keep its Multi-AZ design.

Which solution will MOST reduce these data transfer charges?

options.text: Route each zone's traffic to a NAT gateway in the same zone, and prefer same-zone database replicas.
options.rationale: Data transfer between Availability Zones in the same Region is charged in each direction. Sending each zone's internet-bound traffic through a NAT gateway in the same zone, and reading from replicas in the same zone where possible, removes most cross-zone charges while keeping the Multi-AZ design.

options.text: Move all instances and databases into one Availability Zone to remove all cross-zone traffic.
options.rationale: One zone removes the charges but breaks the Multi-AZ requirement, so the application would fail if that zone fails.

options.text: Enable cross-zone load balancing on every load balancer to spread traffic across zones.
options.rationale: Cross-zone load balancing spreads traffic across zones, which can increase cross-zone data transfer.

options.text: Replace the NAT gateway with an internet gateway route in the private subnets of us-east-1a.
options.rationale: An internet gateway route would make the subnets public, and instances without public IP addresses still could not use it.

questions.question:
A company's VPC costs increased after AWS began to charge for all public IPv4 addresses. The company has many Elastic IP addresses that are not associated with any resource. The company also has many instances with public IP addresses that are reached only through a load balancer.

Which combination of steps will reduce these costs? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Release the Elastic IP addresses that are not associated with any resource.
options.rationale: AWS charges for every public IPv4 address, whether it is in use or idle. Releasing Elastic IP addresses that are not associated with anything removes their charge. IPAM public IP insights can help find them.

options.text: Move instances behind the load balancer to private subnets without public IPs.
options.rationale: Instances that are reached only through a load balancer do not need public addresses. Placing them in private subnets, with NAT for outbound access if needed, removes their public IPv4 charges and reduces exposure.

options.text: Replace each public IPv4 address with a second Elastic IP address on the instance.
options.rationale: Elastic IP addresses are also public IPv4 addresses and are charged the same way.

options.text: Enable auto-assign public IPv4 addresses for every subnet in the VPC by default.
options.rationale: Auto-assigning public addresses adds more public IPv4 addresses and more cost.

options.text: Move the load balancer into private subnets.
options.rationale: An internet-facing load balancer must be in public subnets with public addresses to receive internet traffic, so this would take the site offline.

questions.question:
A media company serves large video files directly from an Amazon S3 bucket to viewers around the world. Data transfer out from Amazon S3 to the internet is the largest item on the bill, and many viewers request the same files.

Which solution will reduce data transfer costs?

options.text: Serve the files through an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as its origin.
options.rationale: Data transfer from Amazon S3 to CloudFront is free, and CloudFront serves repeated requests from edge caches. CloudFront data transfer out pricing is usually lower than S3 data transfer to the internet, so caching popular files reduces cost and improves performance.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to send downloads through the AWS edge network.
options.rationale: Transfer Acceleration adds a per-GB charge on top of normal data transfer, so it increases cost.

options.text: Move the files to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval to lower the cost of each download.
options.rationale: Glacier Instant Retrieval lowers storage cost but adds retrieval charges, and data transfer out is still charged.

options.text: Create S3 Replication copies in three Regions. Let viewers pick the nearest one.
options.rationale: Extra copies add storage and replication costs, and downloads still incur S3 data transfer out charges.

questions.question:
A company uses a single NAT instance that a CloudOps engineer must patch and manage. The NAT instance has become a bottleneck and a single point of failure for private subnets in two Availability Zones.

Which solution will resolve these issues with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone. Update each private route table to use the NAT gateway in its Availability Zone.
options.rationale: AWS recommends NAT gateways over NAT instances because they provide better availability and bandwidth and AWS manages them. One NAT gateway in each Availability Zone keeps each zone independent.

options.text: Launch a larger NAT instance in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum size of 1. Use a script to update the route tables after each replacement.
options.rationale: A NAT instance still needs patching, and a script must manage failover. Bandwidth depends on the instance type.

options.text: Launch a second NAT instance in the other Availability Zone. Use a script to move the routes when a health check of an instance fails.
options.rationale: Two NAT instances remove the single point of failure, but the company must still patch them and maintain the failover script.

options.text: Create an internet gateway for the private subnets. Update each private route table to send internet traffic to the internet gateway.
options.rationale: Routing to an internet gateway makes the subnets public and does not work for instances without public IP addresses.

questions.question:
A company created an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone named internal.example.com in account A and associated the zone with a VPC in account A. Instances in a VPC in account B must resolve the zone's records, but their queries return NXDOMAIN.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Authorize the association in account A. Associate the zone with the VPC from account B.
options.rationale: A private hosted zone can be associated with a VPC in another account. An administrator in account A creates a VPC association authorization, and an administrator in account B then associates the VPC with the zone. The VPC must have DNS resolution and DNS hostnames enabled.

options.text: Share the private hosted zone with account B by using AWS RAM, and accept the share in account B.
options.rationale: Private hosted zones themselves are not shared through AWS RAM, so cross-account association uses an association authorization. Route 53 Profiles, which can be shared through AWS RAM, are another way to apply DNS settings at scale.

options.text: Create a public hosted zone with the same name.
options.rationale: A public zone would expose the internal records to the internet.

options.text: Create a VPC peering connection between the VPCs.
options.rationale: Peering does not make a private hosted zone available to the other VPC. The zone must be associated with that VPC.

questions.question:
A company has applications in a VPC that must resolve hostnames in the on-premises domain corp.local, which only the on-premises DNS servers know. The VPC is connected to the data center through AWS Direct Connect.

What should a CloudOps engineer configure to meet this requirement?

options.text: A Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for corp.local to the on-premises DNS servers
options.rationale: An outbound endpoint lets Route 53 Resolver send queries out of the VPC. A forwarding rule for corp.local sends matching queries to the on-premises DNS servers over Direct Connect, while all other queries are still resolved by Route 53 Resolver.

options.text: An Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint that the on-premises DNS servers are able to forward queries to
options.rationale: Inbound endpoints handle the opposite direction: they let on-premises servers resolve names in AWS.

options.text: A private hosted zone named corp.local with a copy of each on-premises DNS record in it
options.rationale: Copying records by hand goes out of date and duplicates the on-premises DNS data.

options.text: A DHCP options set that points the VPC only at the on-premises DNS server IP addresses
options.rationale: Sending all queries to on-premises servers breaks resolution of AWS private names and makes every lookup depend on the hybrid link.

questions.question:
A company's on-premises servers must resolve records in an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone named aws.example.com that is associated with a VPC. The data center connects to the VPC through an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Create a Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC. Forward aws.example.com from on-premises DNS to it.
options.rationale: An inbound endpoint gives Route 53 Resolver IP addresses in the VPC that on-premises DNS servers can reach over the VPN. A conditional forwarder for aws.example.com on the on-premises servers sends those queries to the endpoint, which answers from the private hosted zone.

options.text: Create a Resolver outbound endpoint in the VPC. Associate a forwarding rule for aws.example.com.
options.rationale: Outbound endpoints send queries from the VPC to other DNS servers, which is the opposite direction.

options.text: Change the private hosted zone into a public hosted zone.
options.rationale: A private hosted zone cannot be converted into a public zone, and publishing internal records is a security risk.

options.text: Point the on-premises servers directly at the Amazon DNS server address at the base of the VPC CIDR block plus two.
options.rationale: The Amazon-provided DNS server cannot be reached from outside the VPC, so on-premises servers cannot query it directly.

questions.question:
A company runs the same application in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1. Users around the world must be sent to the AWS Region that gives them the fastest response, and traffic must avoid any Region that becomes unhealthy.

Which Amazon Route 53 configuration will meet these requirements?

options.text: Latency-based records for each Region, with health checks associated
options.rationale: Latency-based routing answers with the Region that has the lowest measured network latency for the user. With health checks, Route 53 skips an unhealthy Region and answers with the next best one.

options.text: Geolocation records for each continent, with a default record for others
options.rationale: Geolocation routes by the user's location, not by measured latency, so some users might not get the fastest Region.

options.text: Weighted records with equal weights for each Region and no health checks
options.rationale: Equal weights spread users across Regions regardless of latency, and without health checks a failed Region keeps receiving traffic.

options.text: A simple record with all three load balancer addresses as its values
options.rationale: A simple record with several values returns them in random order, with no latency awareness or health checks.

questions.question:
A company has a licensing agreement that requires users in Germany to be served by an application stack in eu-central-1. All other users must be served by a stack in us-east-1. Users whose location cannot be determined must still be served.

Which Amazon Route 53 configuration will meet these requirements?

options.text: Geolocation routing with a Germany record for eu-central-1 and a Default record for us-east-1
options.rationale: Geolocation routing answers based on where the DNS query comes from. A record for Germany sends those users to eu-central-1, and the Default record covers every other location, including queries whose location cannot be determined.

options.text: Latency-based routing with one record for eu-central-1 and one record for us-east-1
options.rationale: Latency routing would send some users outside Germany to eu-central-1, and some German users could go elsewhere, which breaks the licensing rule.

options.text: Geoproximity routing with a large positive bias on the eu-central-1 record and none on us-east-1
options.rationale: Geoproximity shifts traffic by distance and bias, so the boundary would not match the borders of Germany.

options.text: Geolocation routing with only a Germany record that points to eu-central-1
options.rationale: Without a Default record, Route 53 returns no answer for users outside Germany or for unknown locations.

questions.question:
A company is migrating a website from an on-premises server to an Application Load Balancer on AWS. The company must send 10% of users to AWS first, increase the share gradually, and move users back if errors appear.

Which Amazon Route 53 routing policy will meet these requirements?

options.text: Weighted routing
options.rationale: Weighted routing splits DNS responses between records in proportion to their weights, such as 90 and 10. Changing the weights shifts traffic gradually, and setting the AWS record's weight to 0 moves users back. A low TTL makes changes take effect faster.

options.text: Failover routing
options.rationale: Failover routing sends all traffic to the primary while it is healthy, so it cannot send a percentage of users.

options.text: Multivalue answer routing
options.rationale: Multivalue answer returns several healthy records for clients to choose from. It does not control the share of traffic.

options.text: IP-based routing
options.rationale: IP-based routing sends users based on their source IP ranges, not by percentage.

questions.question:
A company has a small internal service that runs on 6 Amazon EC2 instances without a load balancer. DNS must return up to 8 healthy instance IP addresses at random so that clients spread their requests. Unhealthy instances must not be returned.

Which Amazon Route 53 configuration will meet these requirements?

options.text: Multivalue answer records for each instance, each with its own health check
options.rationale: Multivalue answer routing returns up to 8 healthy records, chosen at random, for each query. A health check on each record removes unhealthy instances from the responses. It does not replace a load balancer, but it improves availability for simple cases.

options.text: A simple record that lists all 6 instance IP addresses as values of the same record
options.rationale: A simple record returns all of its values without health checks, so clients can still receive the addresses of failed instances.

options.text: Failover records, with one primary record and five secondary records
options.rationale: Failover routing supports one primary and one secondary record, and it does not spread traffic across instances.

options.text: Latency-based records for each instance in the same AWS Region
options.rationale: Latency routing chooses between Regions. Records in the same Region do not spread traffic in a useful way.

questions.question:
A company needs both example.com (the zone apex) and www.example.com to point to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). A CloudOps engineer tries to create a CNAME record for example.com, and Amazon Route 53 rejects the record.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Create an alias A record for example.com that targets the ALB.
options.rationale: DNS does not allow a CNAME record at the zone apex. A Route 53 alias record can point the apex to AWS resources such as an ALB, a CloudFront distribution, or an S3 website endpoint. It follows IP address changes automatically, and queries to alias records for AWS resources have no charge.

options.text: Create an A record for example.com with the ALB's current IP addresses.
options.rationale: ALB IP addresses change over time, so a static A record would break.

options.text: Create an MX record for example.com that points to the ALB's DNS name.
options.rationale: MX records direct email delivery. They do not route web traffic.

options.text: Create a TXT record for example.com that contains the ALB's DNS name.
options.rationale: TXT records hold text values, such as verification strings. Browsers do not use them to find a website.

questions.question:
A company's security team must log every DNS query that public resolvers send to Amazon Route 53 for the company's public hosted zone. A CloudOps engineer tries to set up query logging to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group in eu-west-1, but the log group cannot be selected.

What should the CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Create the log group in us-east-1. Add a resource policy that allows Route 53 to write to it.
options.rationale: Query logging for public hosted zones sends logs to CloudWatch Logs in the US East (N. Virginia) Region. The log group must be in us-east-1, and a CloudWatch Logs resource policy must allow Route 53 to publish to it.

options.text: Enable Resolver query logging for the VPC in eu-west-1 to capture public zone queries.
options.rationale: Resolver query logging records queries made from inside your VPCs. It does not capture queries from public resolvers on the internet.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for Route 53 to record every public DNS query in the trail.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records Route 53 API calls, such as record changes, not DNS queries.

options.text: Change the hosted zone to a private hosted zone to allow query logging in any AWS Region.
options.rationale: Changing the zone type would make the domain unreachable from the internet.

questions.question:
A company will move a website to a new IP address next week. The current A record has a TTL of 86,400 seconds. Users must reach the new address within minutes after the change.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Lower the TTL to 60 seconds at least a day before the change, and update the record during the cutover.
options.rationale: Resolvers cache a record for its TTL. Lowering the TTL in advance, by at least as long as the old TTL, makes sure that cached copies expire quickly. After the cutover, the TTL can be raised again.

options.text: Keep the TTL at 86,400 seconds, and ask each public DNS resolver to flush its cache after the cutover is done.
options.rationale: You cannot flush the caches of public resolvers that you do not control.

options.text: Raise the TTL to 172,800 seconds before the change.
options.rationale: A longer TTL keeps the old address cached for even longer.

options.text: Delete the record during the cutover. Create a new record with the same name a day later.
options.rationale: Deleting the record causes failed lookups for a full day.

questions.question:
A company serves a static website from an Amazon S3 bucket through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Users can also download files directly from the bucket's URL, which bypasses CloudFront and its AWS WAF rules. The bucket uses SSE-KMS encryption.

How should a CloudOps engineer make the files reachable only through CloudFront?

options.text: Use origin access control. Allow only the distribution's ARN in the bucket policy and key policy.
options.rationale: Origin access control (OAC) lets CloudFront sign its requests to the S3 origin. A bucket policy that allows the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal only when AWS:SourceArn is the distribution's ARN blocks direct access. OAC supports SSE-KMS, so the key policy must also allow the distribution.

options.text: Configure S3 static website hosting. Allow public read access only for the CloudFront edge IP ranges.
options.rationale: Public read access, even if it is scoped to IP ranges, keeps the bucket publicly reachable and is hard to maintain.

options.text: Use an origin access identity. Disable Block Public Access.
options.rationale: Origin access identity is the legacy method and does not support SSE-KMS, and disabling Block Public Access is unnecessary and risky.

options.text: Add a CloudFront geo restriction that blocks every country except the countries where the users live.
options.rationale: Geo restriction applies to requests that go through CloudFront. It does not stop direct requests to the bucket.

questions.question:
A training company sells video courses. Each course has hundreds of video files under one path in Amazon CloudFront. Only paying customers can watch the videos, and customers must not be able to share links that work indefinitely.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Use CloudFront signed cookies with an expiration time for the course path.
options.rationale: Signed cookies grant access to many files, such as everything under one path, with one set of cookies. The policy can set an expiration time, so shared access stops working after it expires.

options.text: Use CloudFront signed URLs for each of the hundreds of files in a course.
options.rationale: Signed URLs work, but the application would have to create a signed URL for every file, which is more effort when a course has hundreds of files.

options.text: Make the Amazon S3 bucket public, and change the object names every few days.
options.rationale: A public bucket can be accessed by anyone who finds an object name, and renaming files does not control access.

options.text: Enable CloudFront geo restriction for the countries of paying customers.
options.rationale: Geo restriction controls access by country, not by whether a user has paid.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon CloudFront distribution that serves images from an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1. The company replicates the bucket to us-west-2. CloudFront must serve images from us-west-2 automatically if the primary bucket returns errors.

What should a CloudOps engineer configure to meet this requirement?

options.text: An origin group with the primary bucket, the secondary bucket, and failover status codes
options.rationale: An origin group has a primary and a secondary origin. When the primary returns one of the configured status codes, such as 500, 502, 503, or 504, or the connection fails, CloudFront retries the request against the secondary origin automatically.

options.text: Two distributions, and an Amazon Route 53 failover record that points to the second one when needed
options.rationale: Two distributions with DNS failover are more complex and slower, because DNS changes depend on health checks and caching.

options.text: A Lambda@Edge function that copies each failed image from us-west-2 into us-east-1 on demand
options.rationale: Copying files on demand is custom code, and the primary bucket would still be failing.

options.text: A longer default TTL
options.rationale: Caching helps only for images that are already cached. New or expired requests would still fail.

questions.question:
A company has a multiplayer game that uses UDP and runs on Network Load Balancers in two AWS Regions. Players need static IP addresses that they can allowlist in their firewalls, lower latency over long distances, and failover between Regions within seconds.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups for the NLBs in both Regions.
options.rationale: Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IP addresses, carries traffic over the AWS global network from the nearest edge location, and supports TCP and UDP. Health checks move traffic to healthy endpoint groups within seconds, without DNS caching delays.

options.text: Use an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the NLBs with caching disabled.
options.rationale: CloudFront delivers HTTP and HTTPS content. It does not proxy arbitrary UDP traffic, so it cannot front a UDP game.

options.text: Use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing with health checks for the two NLBs.
options.rationale: DNS-based routing gives no static IP addresses that cover both Regions, and failover is slowed by DNS caching.

options.text: Use Elastic IP addresses on the NLBs, and ask players to switch addresses during a failure.
options.rationale: Asking players to switch addresses by hand is not automatic failover.

questions.question:
A company uses an Application Load Balancer (ALB) as the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has AWS WAF rules. Users can bypass CloudFront by calling the ALB's DNS name directly. The ALB must accept only requests that come through this distribution.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Allow inbound traffic on the ALB security group only from the CloudFront managed prefix list.
options.rationale: The AWS-managed prefix list com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing contains the IP ranges that CloudFront uses to reach origins. Allowing only that prefix list blocks direct requests from other sources.

options.text: Have CloudFront add a secret custom header. Add an ALB listener rule that requires it.
options.rationale: The prefix list covers every CloudFront distribution, including distributions that other customers own. A secret header that only your distribution adds, checked by an ALB listener rule, makes sure that requests come through your distribution. CloudFront VPC origins, which keep the ALB in private subnets, are another option.

options.text: Enable access logs for the ALB, and block direct callers manually when they show up in the logs.
options.rationale: Blocking callers by hand after the fact is slow and does not prevent the bypass.

options.text: Configure cross-zone load balancing.
options.rationale: Cross-zone load balancing spreads traffic across targets. It does not restrict who can reach the ALB.

options.text: Add a CloudFront geo restriction that blocks the countries where most direct requests come from.
options.rationale: Geo restriction applies only to requests that come through CloudFront, so it does not affect direct calls to the ALB.

questions.question:
A company needs to redirect old URL paths to new paths and add security headers to every Amazon CloudFront response. The logic is simple, and the company needs the lowest cost.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: CloudFront Functions on the viewer request and viewer response events
options.rationale: CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at edge locations on viewer request and viewer response events, with sub-millisecond startup and very high scale, at a lower price than Lambda@Edge. Redirects and header changes are typical uses. A response headers policy can also add security headers without code.

options.text: Lambda@Edge functions on the origin request and origin response events
options.rationale: Lambda@Edge suits heavier logic, such as network calls, but it costs more, so it is not the cheapest choice for simple logic.

options.text: An AWS Lambda function behind an ALB that the distribution uses as its origin
options.rationale: Sending every request to an origin function adds latency and cost and removes the benefit of edge caching.

options.text: An AWS WAF rule group that rewrites URLs and adds the response headers
options.rationale: AWS WAF filters requests. It does not rewrite URLs or add response headers to responses.

questions.question:
A company's video service delivers content through Amazon CloudFront. Because of distribution rights, the service must not serve content to viewers in three specific countries.

Which solution will meet this requirement in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Enable CloudFront geographic restrictions with a block list of those countries.
options.rationale: CloudFront geographic restrictions use a GeoIP database to allow or block viewers by country. A block list returns HTTP 403 to viewers in the listed countries, with no code.

options.text: Create an Amazon Route 53 geolocation record that returns no answer for those three countries.
options.rationale: DNS location is based on the resolver, not the viewer, and users could still reach the distribution through other resolvers.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies requests from the IP ranges of those three countries.
options.rationale: Requests to the bucket come from CloudFront, not from viewers, and country IP ranges change often.

options.text: Write a Lambda@Edge function that looks up each viewer's country in a third-party API.
options.rationale: A custom function adds latency and cost, and CloudFront already provides country-based restrictions.

questions.question:
A company uses Amazon Route 53 health checks for a public web server. The health checks always report unhealthy, but the site works for users. The server's security group allows HTTPS only from the company's office and from a list of partner IP addresses.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Allow inbound HTTPS from the Route 53 health checker IP ranges in the security group.
options.rationale: Route 53 health checkers send requests from AWS IP ranges on the internet, so the security group must allow them. The ranges are published in ip-ranges.json under the ROUTE53_HEALTHCHECKS service, and an AWS-managed prefix list for Route 53 health checks is also available.

options.text: Change the health check to use the server's private IP address to keep the check inside the VPC.
options.rationale: Health checkers run on the internet and cannot reach private IP addresses.

options.text: Enable string matching in the health check to ignore connection timeouts from the server.
options.rationale: String matching checks the response body. It cannot help when the request never reaches the server.

options.text: Increase the health check failure threshold to 10 to report healthy more often.
options.rationale: A higher threshold only delays the unhealthy status. Every check still fails.

questions.question:
Users cannot connect to a company's application on an Amazon EC2 instance. VPC Flow Logs for the instance's network interface show the inbound request from a user as ACCEPT and show the instance's response to the user's ephemeral port as REJECT.

What is the MOST likely cause of this issue?

options.text: The subnet's network ACL denies the outbound response traffic.
options.rationale: Security groups are stateful: if an inbound request is accepted, its response is allowed automatically. A rejected response therefore points to the stateless network ACL, which must allow outbound traffic to the client's ephemeral ports.

options.text: The instance's security group denies the inbound request traffic.
options.rationale: The flow log shows the inbound request as ACCEPT, so it was not denied.

options.text: The instance's security group denies the outbound response traffic.
options.rationale: Because security groups are stateful, an accepted inbound request means that its response is allowed, whatever the outbound rules say.

options.text: The route table has no route back to the user's IP address range.
options.rationale: A missing route would not appear as a REJECT record for the response. Flow logs show REJECT when a security group or network ACL denies traffic.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer must find which instances in private subnets send the most traffic to the internet through a NAT gateway. VPC flow logs on the NAT gateway's network interface show only the NAT gateway's own IP address as the source of the internet traffic.

Which solution will identify the original source instances with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use a custom flow log format with pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr, publish to Amazon S3, and query with Amazon Athena.
options.rationale: The pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr fields show the original packet-level addresses of traffic that passes through an intermediate device such as a NAT gateway. Publishing flow logs to Amazon S3 and querying them with Athena makes it easy to rank instances by bytes sent.

options.text: Enable ALB access logs for the NAT gateway, and sort the requests by the client IP field in each log.
options.rationale: NAT gateways are not load balancers and have no access logs.

options.text: Install packet capture software on the NAT gateway, and analyze the captures each day.
options.rationale: NAT gateways are managed by AWS, so you cannot install software on them.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for the NAT gateway to record each connection.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records API calls, not network connections.

questions.question:
A company has an application on an Amazon EC2 instance in VPC A that cannot connect to a database on port 5432 on an instance in VPC B. The VPCs are connected through a transit gateway, and the path involves several route tables, security groups, and network ACLs.

Which tool will MOST quickly identify the component that blocks the path?

options.text: VPC Reachability Analyzer
options.rationale: Reachability Analyzer analyzes the network configuration between a source and a destination without sending packets. It reports whether the destination is reachable and, if it is not, which component blocks the path, such as a missing transit gateway route, a security group rule, or a network ACL rule.

options.text: Amazon Inspector network reachability findings
options.rationale: Inspector network reachability findings show which ports on instances are exposed to networks such as the internet. They do not trace a specific path between two resources to show what blocks it.

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
options.rationale: Trusted Advisor checks for best practices. It does not analyze a specific network path.

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics
options.rationale: Synthetics canaries can show that a connection fails, but not which configuration component causes the failure.

questions.question:
Users report that some of a company's API calls through an Application Load Balancer take more than 10 seconds. A CloudOps engineer must determine whether the time is spent in the load balancer or in the backend targets for each slow request.

Which data source should the CloudOps engineer use?

options.text: ALB access logs, comparing the request, target, and response processing time fields
options.rationale: Each ALB access log entry records request_processing_time, target_processing_time, and response_processing_time. A large target_processing_time shows that the backend was slow, while large values in the other fields point to the load balancer or the client connection. The TargetResponseTime metric shows the same trend in aggregate.

options.text: VPC Flow Logs for the ALB network interfaces, comparing the start and end time of each record
options.rationale: Flow logs aggregate traffic over capture windows and do not show HTTP request timings.

options.text: AWS CloudTrail management events for Elastic Load Balancing, comparing the event times of each call
options.rationale: CloudTrail records API calls that manage the load balancer, not client requests.

options.text: The ALB's HealthyHostCount metric, comparing the number of healthy targets during each request
options.rationale: HealthyHostCount shows how many targets are healthy. It does not show the latency of individual requests.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of a product catalog. The cache hit ratio is 15%. The cache key includes a session cookie, tracking query strings such as utm_source, and the User-Agent header. The catalog content does not depend on any of these values.

Which solution will MOST improve the cache hit ratio?

options.text: Use a cache policy that leaves cookies, the tracking query strings, and User-Agent out of the cache key.
options.rationale: Every value in the cache key creates a separate cached object, so including cookies, tracking parameters, and User-Agent splits the cache into many copies of the same content. A cache policy that includes only values that change the response raises the hit ratio. An origin request policy can still forward values that the origin needs without adding them to the cache key.

options.text: Lower the minimum TTL in the cache policy to 0 seconds to refresh objects more often.
options.rationale: A lower TTL makes objects expire sooner, which lowers the hit ratio.

options.text: Enable Origin Shield in a Region far from the origin to share one cache across more edge locations.
options.rationale: Origin Shield can help, but it should be placed in the Region closest to the origin, and it does not fix a fragmented cache key.

options.text: Add more origins to an origin group to spread cache misses across several origin servers.
options.rationale: Origin groups are for failover. They do not change how often CloudFront finds objects in its cache.

questions.question:
A company deploys updates to main.js in the Amazon S3 origin of an Amazon CloudFront distribution. After a deployment, many users still receive the old version for up to 24 hours, which is the file's TTL. Users must get new versions right after each deployment from now on.

Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a CloudFront invalidation for /main.js right after the current deployment.
options.rationale: An invalidation removes the cached object from edge caches, so the next request fetches the new file from the origin. It fixes the current deployment, and invalidation paths beyond the monthly free allowance are charged.

options.text: Use versioned file names, such as main.3f2a1c.js. Update the HTML references.
options.rationale: Versioned file names give each release a new URL that is not in any cache, so users get the new file at once while long TTLs stay in place. This is the recommended long-term approach.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning for the origin bucket to make CloudFront fetch the newest version.
options.rationale: S3 Versioning keeps object versions in the bucket. CloudFront still serves its cached copy until the TTL expires.

options.text: Increase the default TTL to 7 days to make CloudFront check the origin less often.
options.rationale: A longer TTL makes stale content last even longer.

options.text: Enable CloudFront standard logging to remove stale objects from the edge locations.
options.rationale: Logging records requests. It does not remove anything from the cache.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses a custom origin, origin.example.com, over HTTPS. After the origin team replaced the origin's certificate with a self-signed certificate, CloudFront started to return HTTP 502 errors.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Install a certificate on the origin from a trusted CA that covers origin.example.com.
options.rationale: CloudFront validates the origin's certificate when it connects over HTTPS. A self-signed certificate, or one whose name does not match the origin domain, makes the TLS handshake fail, and CloudFront returns 502 Bad Gateway. A certificate from a trusted CA that covers the origin name fixes the problem.

options.text: Increase the origin response timeout in the distribution settings from 30 to 60 seconds.
options.rationale: The timeout setting affects slow responses, which cause 504 errors. Here the TLS handshake fails before any response.

options.text: Invalidate all paths in the distribution to make CloudFront fetch new copies of objects.
options.rationale: Invalidations clear cached objects. They do not fix the connection to the origin.

options.text: Change the viewer protocol policy to allow HTTP and remove the need for viewer certificates.
options.rationale: The viewer protocol policy controls the viewer side. The failure is on the connection from CloudFront to the origin.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of an Application Load Balancer. The distribution returns HTTP 504 errors for a reporting endpoint. The origin needs about 45 seconds to generate each report. Other endpoints work normally.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Increase the origin response timeout for the origin to more than 45 seconds.
options.rationale: CloudFront waits for the origin response timeout, 30 seconds by default, before it gives up and returns 504 Gateway Timeout. Raising the timeout above 45 seconds (values above 120 seconds need a quota increase) lets the report finish. Making the report asynchronous is a better long-term fix.

options.text: Lower the distribution's default TTL to refresh the reports more often.
options.rationale: TTL affects caching of successful responses. It does not let slow requests finish.

options.text: Add a geo restriction to allow only users near the origin to call the endpoint.
options.rationale: Distance to the origin is not the cause. The origin itself takes 45 seconds.

options.text: Replace the ALB origin with an Amazon S3 bucket that serves the reporting endpoint.
options.rationale: S3 cannot run the report generation logic.

questions.question:
A company serves static images through Amazon CloudFront. The images always show Miss in the X-Cache response header. The origin sends Cache-Control: no-store on every response, and the cache policy uses the origin's cache headers with a minimum TTL of 0.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to make CloudFront cache the images?

options.text: Change the origin to send Cache-Control: max-age for images, or set a minimum TTL in the cache policy.
options.rationale: With a minimum TTL of 0, CloudFront follows the origin's Cache-Control headers, and no-store tells it not to cache. Sending a max-age value for images from the origin, or raising the minimum TTL in the cache policy, lets CloudFront cache them.

options.text: Enable automatic compression in the cache policy to make the images small enough to cache.
options.rationale: Compression reduces object size. It does not override caching directives.

options.text: Add the images' query strings to the cache key to give each image request its own cache entry.
options.rationale: Adding values to the cache key splits the cache further, and it does not change the no-store directive.

options.text: Enable HTTP/3 for the distribution to serve the image requests from the edge caches.
options.rationale: HTTP/3 changes the protocol between viewers and CloudFront. It does not affect caching rules.

questions.question:
A company runs Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate in private subnets that have no NAT gateway. The tasks fail to start with an error that says that they cannot pull the container image from Amazon ECR.

Which combination of VPC endpoints is required for the tasks to pull images? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Interface VPC endpoints for com.amazonaws.region.ecr.api and ecr.dkr
options.rationale: Pulling an image calls the ECR API (ecr.api) for authentication and metadata and the Docker registry endpoint (ecr.dkr) for the image itself. Without internet access, the tasks need interface endpoints for both.

options.text: A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, where ECR stores image layers
options.rationale: ECR stores image layers in Amazon S3, so a gateway endpoint for S3 on the private route tables is also needed. If the tasks send logs to CloudWatch Logs, a logs interface endpoint is needed too.

options.text: A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon DynamoDB, where ECR stores image manifests
options.rationale: ECR does not store manifests in DynamoDB, and no DynamoDB endpoint is needed to pull images.

options.text: An interface VPC endpoint for AWS Systems Manager, which ECS uses to pull
options.rationale: Systems Manager endpoints are not used to pull container images.

options.text: An interface VPC endpoint for Amazon EC2, which Fargate uses for images
options.rationale: Fargate does not need an EC2 endpoint to pull images from ECR.

questions.question:
A company has an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection that uses BGP, and both tunnels show UP. On-premises hosts cannot reach instances in the VPC's private subnets. The on-premises router receives the VPC CIDR block through BGP correctly.

What should a CloudOps engineer check to resolve this issue?

options.text: Verify that route propagation from the virtual private gateway is enabled in the subnets' route tables.
options.rationale: The tunnels are up and the on-premises side has the VPC routes, so the missing piece is the return path. Turning on route propagation for the virtual private gateway in the private subnets' route tables adds the on-premises prefixes learned through BGP. Security groups and network ACLs must also allow the traffic.

options.text: Verify that the VPN connection uses static routing instead of BGP.
options.rationale: BGP is working, and switching to static routing would not add routes to the VPC route tables.

options.text: Verify that the customer gateway has an Elastic IP address that is attached to an Amazon EC2 instance in the VPC.
options.rationale: The customer gateway is the on-premises device. It is not an Elastic IP address on an AWS instance.

options.text: Verify that an internet gateway is attached to the VPC.
options.rationale: VPN traffic uses the virtual private gateway, not an internet gateway.

questions.question:
A company has VPC A and VPC B attached to a transit gateway. Both attachments are associated with the same transit gateway route table, which has propagated routes for both VPC CIDR blocks. Instances in VPC A still cannot reach VPC B.

What is the MOST likely cause of this issue?

options.text: VPC A's subnet route tables have no route that sends VPC B's CIDR block to the transit gateway.
options.rationale: The transit gateway route table handles routing between attachments, but each VPC's own subnet route tables must also send traffic for the other VPC's CIDR block to the transit gateway. VPC B also needs a return route.

options.text: Transit gateways do not support traffic between two VPCs that are attached to the same route table.
options.rationale: Attachments that share a route table with routes to each other can communicate. This is a common design.

options.text: VPC A and VPC B must be peered with each other in addition to being attached to the transit gateway.
options.rationale: Peering is not needed when both VPCs route through the transit gateway.

options.text: The transit gateway needs an internet gateway attachment to route traffic between the two VPCs.
options.rationale: Transit gateways route between attachments directly. Internet gateways are attached to VPCs, not to transit gateways.

questions.question:
A company runs a TCP-based application on Amazon EC2 instances. A partner must allowlist the application's IP addresses in its firewall, so each Availability Zone needs a static IP address. The application must handle millions of requests each second.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use a Network Load Balancer. Associate an Elastic IP address with the load balancer in each Availability Zone.
options.rationale: A Network Load Balancer works at the transport layer and handles millions of requests per second. An internet-facing Network Load Balancer can have one Elastic IP address for each Availability Zone, which gives the partner static addresses.

options.text: Use an Application Load Balancer. Give the partner the IP addresses that its DNS name currently resolves to.
options.rationale: The IP addresses of an Application Load Balancer can change over time, so they are not safe to allowlist.

options.text: Use an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Give the partner the published IP ranges for all CloudFront edge locations.
options.rationale: CloudFront IP ranges are shared, very large, and change over time, so this does not give the partner a small static list.

options.text: Use an Amazon Route 53 simple record. Point the record to the public IP address of each EC2 instance.
options.rationale: This exposes each instance directly, gives no load balancing, and the addresses change when instances are replaced.

questions.question:
A global streaming company hosts its application on AWS. The company needs to know when internet problems, such as an ISP outage in a specific city, affect its users' latency and availability, and which users are affected.

Which service should a CloudOps engineer use to meet these requirements?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch Internet Monitor
options.rationale: Internet Monitor uses AWS's view of global internet traffic to measure performance and availability between your application and its users, broken down by city, network (ASN), and Region. It creates health events when internet issues affect your users and can suggest changes, such as serving users from different Regions.

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch Network Flow Monitor
options.rationale: Network Flow Monitor measures traffic between workloads inside AWS, not the internet path to end users.

options.text: AWS Health Dashboard
options.rationale: The Health Dashboard reports events that affect AWS services and your resources, not problems with third-party ISPs.

options.text: VPC Flow Logs
options.rationale: Flow logs record traffic metadata for VPC network interfaces. They do not measure user experience across the internet.

questions.question:
A company connects its data center to a VPC by using an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet. The company transfers large datasets every day and needs a dedicated private connection that does not use the internet.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Order an AWS Direct Connect connection. Create a private virtual interface to the VPC's virtual private gateway.
options.rationale: Direct Connect links the data center to an AWS Direct Connect location over a dedicated Ethernet fiber-optic connection, bypassing internet service providers. A private virtual interface gives access to the VPC.

options.text: Add a second Site-to-Site VPN connection. Configure both connections to use the same customer gateway device.
options.rationale: A second VPN connection adds resilience, but the traffic still travels over the internet.

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator. Send the data center's traffic to the accelerator's static IP addresses.
options.rationale: Global Accelerator improves paths for internet users to AWS endpoints. The data center's traffic still starts on the internet.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the VPC. Send the data center's traffic to the distribution.
options.rationale: CloudFront delivers content to viewers. It is not a private connection from a data center to a VPC.

questions.question:
A company's remote employees connect to an AWS Client VPN endpoint successfully, but they cannot reach application servers in a private subnet of the associated VPC. The servers' security group allows traffic from the Client VPN endpoint's security group.

What should a CloudOps engineer check FIRST?

options.text: Verify that an authorization rule allows the users' group to access the private subnet's CIDR range.
options.rationale: Client VPN authorization rules control which networks connected users can reach. Without a rule that allows the users, or their Active Directory or SAML group, to reach the subnet's CIDR range, connections succeed but traffic to that network is dropped. The Client VPN route table also needs a route to the destination.

options.text: Verify that each employee's laptop has a public IP address that is registered in the VPC's route tables.
options.rationale: Client VPN assigns client addresses from its own CIDR range. Employees' public IP addresses do not go into VPC route tables.

options.text: Verify that the private subnet has a NAT gateway for the VPN clients to reach the servers.
options.rationale: NAT gateways provide outbound internet access. VPN clients do not need them to reach private resources.

options.text: Verify that the Client VPN endpoint uses split tunneling for all traffic to use the tunnel.
options.rationale: Split tunneling sends only VPC-bound traffic through the VPN, which is the opposite of what this option says, and it does not grant access to subnets.

questions.question:
A company attached an AWS Lambda function to private subnets so that the function can reach an Amazon RDS database. Since then, the function times out when it calls a third-party payment API on the internet.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Add a NAT gateway path for the function's private subnets. Keep the function in the VPC.
options.rationale: Lambda functions that are attached to a VPC get only private IP addresses, so they need a NAT gateway (zonal or regional) to reach the internet. Routing the function's subnets through NAT keeps database access and restores internet access.

options.text: Assign a public IP address to the function's network interfaces through the Lambda console.
options.rationale: Lambda does not support public IP addresses on the network interfaces that it creates.

options.text: Move the function into a public subnet to use the internet gateway route of the subnet.
options.rationale: Even in a public subnet, the function's network interfaces have no public IP addresses, so the internet gateway route does not help.

options.text: Increase the function timeout to 15 minutes to give the payment API call time to complete.
options.rationale: The call fails because there is no network path, so a longer timeout only delays the failure.

questions.question:
A company uses a single AWS Direct Connect connection to reach its VPCs. During a recent fiber cut, all connectivity to AWS was lost for 6 hours. The company needs a low-cost backup path that takes over automatically.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Add an AWS Site-to-Site VPN to the same virtual private gateway or transit gateway. Use BGP for failover.
options.rationale: A Site-to-Site VPN over the internet is a low-cost backup for Direct Connect. When both use BGP with the same gateway, AWS prefers the Direct Connect path while it is up and fails over to the VPN automatically when the Direct Connect BGP session goes down.

options.text: Order a second Direct Connect connection in the same location on the same router at the same speed.
options.rationale: A second connection on the same router and in the same location shares the same failure points, and it costs more than a VPN.

options.text: Configure Direct Connect SiteLink.
options.rationale: SiteLink connects on-premises sites to each other through Direct Connect locations. It does not back up a single failed connection.

options.text: Ask the on-premises team to route traffic through the public internet to the instances' public IPs.
options.rationale: Routing to public IP addresses over the internet exposes resources and is not an automatic, private failover.

questions.question:
A CloudOps engineer tries to create a VPC peering connection between VPC A (10.0.0.0/16) and VPC B (10.0.128.0/17). The request fails.

Why does the request fail?

options.text: The CIDR blocks of the two VPCs overlap, and peering does not allow overlapping CIDR blocks.
options.rationale: 10.0.128.0/17 falls inside 10.0.0.0/16, so the ranges overlap. A VPC peering connection cannot be created between VPCs with overlapping IPv4 CIDR blocks. Re-addressing one VPC, or using PrivateLink for specific services, solves this.

options.text: The two VPCs must be in different AWS Regions before any peering connection between them can be created.
options.rationale: Peering works both within a Region and across Regions.

options.text: VPC peering requires that both VPCs use exactly the same CIDR block size, such as /16.
options.rationale: Peered VPCs can use different CIDR block sizes as long as the ranges do not overlap.

options.text: VPC peering is allowed only between VPCs that are in two different AWS accounts.
options.rationale: Peering works between VPCs in the same account or in different accounts.

questions.question:
A company has an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate. Tasks stop shortly after they start, and the reason is not visible. The task definition does not configure any logging.

What should a CloudOps engineer do to see the container's output?

options.text: Add the awslogs log driver to the task definition.
options.rationale: The awslogs log driver, or FireLens for routing to other destinations, sends the container's stdout and stderr to CloudWatch Logs. The task's stopped reason and the container exit code in the ECS console also help explain why tasks stop. The task execution role needs permission to write the logs.

options.text: Connect to the Fargate host with SSH, and read the Docker logs in the host's /var/log directory.
options.rationale: Fargate hosts are managed by AWS, so there is no SSH access to them.

options.text: Configure VPC Flow Logs for the task's network interface to see the output that the container wrote.
options.rationale: Flow logs record network traffic metadata, not application output.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for ECS.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records ECS API calls, not container output.

questions.question:
A company's application on Amazon EC2 instances intermittently fails to receive connections. A CloudOps engineer must determine whether security groups or network ACLs are rejecting traffic to the instances' network interfaces. The CloudOps engineer must be able to query the results.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a VPC flow log with the REJECT filter that publishes to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Query the logs by using CloudWatch Logs Insights.
options.rationale: VPC Flow Logs capture information about the IP traffic to and from network interfaces, including whether security groups and network ACLs accepted or rejected the traffic. Publishing to CloudWatch Logs lets the engineer query the records with Logs Insights.

options.text: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail with data events for the VPC that publishes to Amazon S3. Query the events by using Amazon Athena.
options.rationale: CloudTrail records API calls, not network traffic. Rejected packets do not appear in a trail.

options.text: Enable detailed monitoring on the instances. Create an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that shows the NetworkPacketsIn metric.
options.rationale: NetworkPacketsIn counts packets that the instance received. It does not show packets that were rejected before reaching the instance.

options.text: Enable access logs on the security groups and network ACLs. Query the access logs by using Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights.
options.rationale: Security groups and network ACLs do not have their own access logs. VPC Flow Logs provide this information.
